#### 070. `orchestrate`

- Kind: verb. Banned forms: `orchestrate`, `orchestrates`, `orchestrated`, `orchestrating`, `orchestration`, `orchestrator`.
- Why it reads as machine text: Two habits again: generated résumés (`orchestrated a company-wide launch`) and infrastructure copy (`orchestrate your containers`). The musical image suggests one conductor in control of many parts. In résumés it inflates coordination; in docs it hides which tool schedules what. Agent frameworks use it for a loop that calls tools in order, which is easier to describe as a loop.
- Where it shows up: résumés, DevOps product pages, architecture docs, AI agent frameworks.

```slop
Orchestrated a cross-team product launch across 5 regions.
Orchestrate your microservices with ease.
The agent orchestrates multiple tools to complete tasks.
```

Replace with:

- `coordinated`, `planned`, `ran` in résumés, with scope.
- Name the scheduler or the control flow: "Kubernetes schedules", "a loop calls".
- `runs`, `calls`, `starts`, in order.
- `schedule`, for jobs with a time or a trigger.

Rewrites:

```slop
Orchestrated a cross-team product launch across 5 regions.
```

After: Ran the launch plan for 5 regions: 14 teams, one shared checklist, all live on the same day.

```slop
Orchestrate your microservices with ease.
```

After: Kubernetes restarts failed containers and spreads replicas across 3 zones.

```slop
The agent orchestrates multiple tools to complete tasks.
```

After: The agent calls search, reads the top 3 pages, writes the answer, and stops after 10 steps.

- Literal use: for music, write "arrange" or "score for orchestra"; for container schedulers, name the tool (Kubernetes, Nomad) or keep the term in inline code (`orchestration`).

### 7.2 Entries 071 to 140: adjectives, part one

#### 071. `seamless`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `seamless`, `seamlessly`, `seamlessness`.
- Why it reads as machine text: models attach `seamless` to every integration, handoff and sync, and `seamlessly integrates with` is one of the most repeated strings in generated product copy. It borrows the language of tailoring to suggest that nothing breaks where two systems meet. It never names that boundary, and it hides the steps that remain, such as an OAuth prompt or a field-mapping screen.
- Where it shows up: integration pages, onboarding emails, README feature lists.

```slop
Seamlessly integrates with your existing tools.
Enjoy a seamless experience across all your devices.
Our API ensures seamless data synchronization.
```

Replace with:

- The step count: "connects to GitHub in two clicks, with no API key". Use when setup is short enough to count.
- The step that no longer happens: "no second login when you switch from Mail to Calendar". Use for single sign-on and shared sessions.
- The delay: "edits reach your other devices within 2 seconds". Use for sync claims.
- The named list: "works with Slack, Linear and Jira". Use when the claim was about compatibility.
- Cut it when the sentence still says what connects to what without it.

Rewrites:

```slop
Seamlessly integrates with your existing tools.
```

After: Imports issues from GitHub, Linear and Jira. Setup takes one OAuth prompt per service.

```slop
Enjoy a seamless experience across all your devices.
```

After: Drafts sync between phone and laptop within 2 seconds of the last keystroke.

```slop
Our API ensures seamless data synchronization.
```

After: The API writes each change to both databases in one transaction, so a failed write changes neither.

- Literal use: for a garment or surface with no joins, write "without seams" or "knitted in one piece".

#### 072. `robust`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `robust`, `robustly`, `robustness`.
- Why it reads as machine text: models call any code with a try/catch `robust`, and any platform the reader is meant to trust. The word fakes an engineering review that never happened: no load test, no failure injection, no uptime figure. In generated READMEs it sits in a row with "scalable" and "secure", three words that tell an evaluator nothing.
- Where it shows up: README openers, architecture docs, pull request descriptions.

```slop
A robust and scalable framework for building APIs.
Added robust error handling to the upload flow.
Our robust infrastructure keeps your data safe.
```

Replace with:

- The failure it survives: "retries failed uploads 3 times with exponential backoff". Use for error handling.
- The measured limit: "tested at 12,000 requests per second on one 4-core node". Use for performance.
- The uptime record: "99.95% uptime over the last 12 months, status page linked". Use for hosting.
- The test that tried to break it: "fuzzed with 2 million malformed inputs, no crashes". Use for parsers and protocols.
- Cut it when the sentence describes a feature and the adjective only adds praise.

Rewrites:

```slop
A robust and scalable framework for building APIs.
```

After: A Go framework for HTTP APIs. It serves 12,000 requests per second on one 4-core node.

```slop
Added robust error handling to the upload flow.
```

After: Uploads now retry 3 times with exponential backoff and show the server's error if the last attempt fails.

```slop
Our robust infrastructure keeps your data safe.
```

After: Data is stored in two regions, with nightly backups kept for 30 days.

- Literal use: for the statistical sense, name the method ("a median-based estimate that ignores outliers"), or put a library parameter such as `robust=True` in inline code.

#### 073. `comprehensive`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `comprehensive`, `comprehensively`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `comprehensive` is how a model introduces a guide, test suite or product tier without stating its scope. It promises completeness, which no reader can check, so they discount it at once. Generated docs open with `This comprehensive guide covers` and then cover five topics.
- Where it shows up: tutorial intros, test plan summaries, pricing tier descriptions.

```slop
This comprehensive guide covers everything you need to know about Docker.
We added comprehensive test coverage for the billing module.
A comprehensive suite of tools for growing teams.
```

Replace with:

- The count: "covers 14 commands, from `docker build` to `docker compose down`". Use for guides.
- The coverage figure: "line coverage for `billing/` went from 41% to 88%". Use for tests.
- The scope and its edge: "covers Linux and macOS; Windows is out of scope". Use when readers need to know what is missing.
- The named parts: "invoicing, payroll and expense reports". Use for product suites.
- Cut it when the list that follows already shows the scope.

Rewrites:

```slop
This comprehensive guide covers everything you need to know about Docker.
```

After: This guide covers 14 Docker commands for building, running and debugging containers on Linux and macOS.

```slop
We added comprehensive test coverage for the billing module.
```

After: Added 63 tests for `billing/`. Line coverage is now 88%, up from 41%.

```slop
A comprehensive suite of tools for growing teams.
```

After: Invoicing, payroll and expense reports in one account, for teams of 5 to 200.

- Literal use: when an insurance product or exam has the word in its official name, quote the name in inline code, as in `comprehensive coverage`.

#### 074. `cutting-edge`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `cutting-edge`, `cutting edge`.
- Why it reads as machine text: models reach for `cutting-edge` when a product should sound new but there is no release date or benchmark to cite. It fakes the register of a trade-press headline. It also ages badly: copy that called a 2021 model `cutting-edge` reads as stale two years later, and the reader cannot tell which year the claim meant.
- Where it shows up: AI product landing pages, conference bios, company "About" pages.

```slop
Built on cutting-edge AI technology.
Our team works at the cutting edge of machine learning.
Experience cutting-edge design with our new dashboard.
```

Replace with:

- The named technology and its date: "uses Whisper large-v3, released November 2023". Use for model and AI claims.
- The benchmark: "scores 71% on SWE-bench Verified". Use when a public benchmark exists.
- The first: "the first open-source tool to read Parquet files in the browser". Use only when you can show it was first.
- What the team publishes or ships: "2 to 3 papers a year on speech recognition". Use for bios.
- Cut it when the sentence already names the technology.

Rewrites:

```slop
Built on cutting-edge AI technology.
```

After: Transcribes audio with Whisper large-v3 and summarizes it with a model that runs on your own server.

```slop
Our team works at the cutting edge of machine learning.
```

After: Our team publishes research on speech recognition. The last paper appeared at Interspeech 2024.

```slop
Experience cutting-edge design with our new dashboard.
```

After: The new dashboard puts the 4 numbers you check every morning in the top row.

- Literal use: for a blade or tool, write "the blade's edge" or "the cutting surface".

#### 075. `innovative`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `innovative`, `innovatively`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `innovative` is what a model writes when asked to describe a company it knows nothing about. Every competitor uses it too, so it separates the product from no one. It claims novelty without naming the new thing or the old thing it replaced.
- Where it shows up: company boilerplate, grant applications, launch posts.

```slop
An innovative approach to project management.
We are an innovative company passionate about design.
Our innovative platform changes how teams collaborate.
```

Replace with:

- The departure from the default: "tasks have no due dates; each gets a weekly time budget instead". Use when there is a real departure.
- The old way it replaces: "a 3-line written update instead of the weekly status meeting". Use for process products.
- The patent or paper: "patent US 11,234,567 covers the sorting method". Use only when it exists.
- Cut it when you cannot name the new thing, because then the word is false.

Rewrites:

```slop
An innovative approach to project management.
```

After: Projects have no Gantt charts. Each task gets a weekly time budget, and the board shows what is over.

```slop
We are an innovative company passionate about design.
```

After: We are a 9-person studio in Lyon that builds booking software for clinics.

```slop
Our innovative platform changes how teams collaborate.
```

After: Teams post a 3-line update each Friday instead of holding a status meeting.

- Literal use: when an award category or grant form uses the word as its official title, put that title in inline code.

#### 076. `groundbreaking`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `groundbreaking`, `ground-breaking`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `groundbreaking` is press-release vocabulary that models apply to minor releases, such as a new export option. It claims a shift in a whole field, which a reader expects to see confirmed by people outside the company. When the subject is one feature, the gap between word and evidence makes the whole page look inflated.
- Where it shows up: launch announcements, research summaries, investor updates.

```slop
Introducing a groundbreaking new way to manage your inbox.
The study presents groundbreaking findings on sleep and memory.
This groundbreaking release changes everything.
```

Replace with:

- The result with its size: "participants recalled 23% more words after 8 hours of sleep than after 4". Use for research.
- The change in plain terms: "the inbox now groups mail by sender, not by date". Use for features.
- Outside confirmation: "cited by 140 papers since 2022". Use only when true.
- Cut it in release notes and list the changes instead.

Rewrites:

```slop
Introducing a groundbreaking new way to manage your inbox.
```

After: The inbox now groups messages by sender, so a newsletter takes one row instead of forty.

```slop
The study presents groundbreaking findings on sleep and memory.
```

After: Participants who slept 8 hours recalled 23% more words than those who slept 4 (n = 212).

```slop
This groundbreaking release changes everything.
```

After: Version 3.0 adds offline mode, CSV export and a keyboard shortcut for every menu item.

- Literal use: for the ceremony at the start of construction, write "the first-dig ceremony" or "the start of construction".

#### 077. `game-changing`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `game-changing`, `game changing`.
- Why it reads as machine text: models use `game-changing` to mark a feature as important when they cannot say why. The phrase comes from sports commentary and pitch decks, and technical readers read it as hype. It takes the place of the before-and-after comparison that would prove the point.
- Where it shows up: launch-day posts, sales emails, feature announcement threads.

```slop
Our AI assistant is a game-changing tool for developers.
This game-changing feature will transform your workflow.
Get ready for game-changing results.
```

Replace with:

- The before and after: "builds that took 11 minutes now take 90 seconds". Use when you have a timing.
- The task it removes: "you no longer write migration files by hand". Use when a manual step disappears.
- A named customer's number: "Acme cut duplicate tickets by 30% in the first month". Use with the customer's permission.
- Cut it when the next sentence gives the result, since the phrase only delays it.

Rewrites:

```slop
Our AI assistant is a game-changing tool for developers.
```

After: The assistant drafts unit tests from a function signature, and you review and edit them.

```slop
This game-changing feature will transform your workflow.
```

After: Schema changes now generate their own migration files, so you stop writing them by hand.

```slop
Get ready for game-changing results.
```

After: Beta teams filed 30% fewer duplicate support tickets in their first month.

- Literal use: for the play that decided a match, describe it: "the interception in the 88th minute decided the match".

#### 078. `transformative`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `transformative`, `transformatively`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `transformative` is consulting and grant-writing vocabulary that models carry into product and policy text. It claims a deep change in a person or an organization and gives no measure of it. Readers of annual reports know it as the word used before the outcome has been measured.
- Where it shows up: nonprofit reports, course descriptions, executive summaries.

```slop
A transformative learning experience for future leaders.
AI will have a transformative impact on healthcare.
Our partnership has been truly transformative.
```

Replace with:

- The outcome with a number: "82% of last year's cohort were promoted within 18 months". Use for education.
- The process that changed: "urgent scans are read first, cutting the wait from 9 days to 2". Use for operations.
- What the partner paid for or did: "3 new clinics and 40 trained nurses in 2024". Use for partnerships.
- Cut it when there is no outcome yet; say what you expect and when you will measure it.

Rewrites:

```slop
A transformative learning experience for future leaders.
```

After: A 12-week course on running a team. 82% of last year's cohort were promoted within 18 months.

```slop
AI will have a transformative impact on healthcare.
```

After: Software that flags urgent scans could cut the wait for a radiology report from 9 days to 2. A trial runs through 2026.

```slop
Our partnership has been truly transformative.
```

After: The partnership paid for 3 new clinics and trained 40 nurses in 2024.

- Literal use: for a change of shape in geometry, name the operation: rotation, reflection or scaling.

#### 079. `revolutionary`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `revolutionary`, `revolutionaries`.
- Why it reads as machine text: models use `revolutionary` for products that are incremental. It borrows the weight of political history to describe, often, a new settings screen. It claims the old way is now obsolete, which a reader can disprove by looking at what competitors still sell.
- Where it shows up: hero headlines, crowdfunding pages, keynote scripts.

```slop
A revolutionary new way to take notes.
Our revolutionary battery technology lasts all day.
Join the revolutionary movement in personal finance.
```

Replace with:

- The mechanism: "type [[ and a title to link two notes". Use for software features.
- The new spec beside the old one: "18 hours of video playback, up from 11". Use for hardware.
- What the person does: "set a limit per category and the card declines past it". Use for consumer finance.
- Cut it in any headline. A headline needs a verb and a noun more than it needs praise.

Rewrites:

```slop
A revolutionary new way to take notes.
```

After: Notes that link to each other: type [[ and a title, and the link works in both directions.

```slop
Our revolutionary battery technology lasts all day.
```

After: 18 hours of video playback on one charge, up from 11 on the previous model.

```slop
Join the revolutionary movement in personal finance.
```

After: Set a monthly limit per category, and the card declines purchases once you reach it.

- Literal use: for history, name the event or group: "the 1848 uprisings", "the Continental Army".

#### 080. `pivotal`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `pivotal`, `pivotally`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `pivotal` is how a model raises the stakes of a sentence, and `plays a pivotal role` appears in generated essays on almost any subject. It asserts importance without showing what depends on the thing. The pair is frequent enough in model output that AI-text detectors give it weight.
- Where it shows up: student essays, biographies, company histories.

```slop
She played a pivotal role in the company's early growth.
Data plays a pivotal role in today's decision-making.
2019 was a pivotal year for the team.
```

Replace with:

- What the person did: "she signed the first 40 customers herself". Use for biographies.
- The dependency: "no price change ships until the analytics team checks it". Use for process descriptions.
- The event of that year: "in 2019 the team moved from contracts to subscriptions". Use for timelines.
- Cut it whenever "role" follows, and write the role.

Rewrites:

```slop
She played a pivotal role in the company's early growth.
```

After: She signed the first 40 customers herself and hired the sales team that followed.

```slop
Data plays a pivotal role in today's decision-making.
```

After: No price change ships until the analytics team checks it against the last 90 days of orders.

```slop
2019 was a pivotal year for the team.
```

After: In 2019 the team dropped one-off contracts and started selling subscriptions.

- Literal use: for a part that turns on a pin, write "turns on a pivot" or "hinged".

#### 081. `crucial`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `crucial`, `crucially`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `crucial` is the default intensifier models use for "important", most often in `it is crucial to` before an instruction. It sounds urgent but never says what happens if the reader ignores the advice. Generated tutorials put it on every second step, so it stops marking anything.
- Where it shows up: tutorials, onboarding checklists, policy summaries.

```slop
It is crucial to back up your database before upgrading.
The survey offers crucial insights into customer behavior.
Communication is crucial for remote teams.
```

Replace with:

- The consequence: "upgrading without a backup can lose every row since the last snapshot". Use for warnings.
- The imperative alone: "Back up the database before you upgrade." Use for instructions; the order of the steps is the emphasis.
- The finding: "62% of carts are abandoned on the shipping-cost page". Use for research summaries.
- The practice: "post a written update by 10:00 each day". Use for advice.
- Cut it whenever `it is crucial to` opens a sentence, and start with the verb.

Rewrites:

```slop
It is crucial to back up your database before upgrading.
```

After: Back up the database before you upgrade. The 4.0 migration cannot be undone.

```slop
The survey offers crucial insights into customer behavior.
```

After: 62% of carts are abandoned on the page that first shows shipping costs.

```slop
Communication is crucial for remote teams.
```

After: On a remote team, post a written update by 10:00 each day so nobody waits for a call to learn the status.

- Literal use: for the deciding experiment in science, write "the deciding test".

#### 082. `vital`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `vital`, `vitally`, `vitals`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `vital` is a model's second choice after `crucial`, used to rotate synonyms through a long answer. It borrows the medical sense of life and death to make routine advice sound urgent. It also slips into technical text through `Core Web Vitals`, so put that metric name in inline code when you cite it.
- Where it shows up: health and wellness copy, security advice, web performance docs.

```slop
Sleep is vital for your overall well-being.
It is vital to keep your dependencies up to date.
Proper hydration plays a vital role in performance.
```

Replace with:

- The effect with a figure and source: "below 6 hours of sleep, reaction times slow". Use for health claims.
- The risk: "the CVE fixed in lodash 4.17.21 allows prototype pollution". Use for security advice.
- The metric by name: "Largest Contentful Paint under 2.5 s". Use for performance.
- Cut it when the advice stands on its own.

Rewrites:

```slop
Sleep is vital for your overall well-being.
```

After: Adults need 7 to 9 hours of sleep a night. Below 6, reaction times slow measurably.

```slop
It is vital to keep your dependencies up to date.
```

After: Update dependencies weekly, and run `npm audit` in CI so a known CVE fails the build.

```slop
Proper hydration plays a vital role in performance.
```

After: Losing 2% of body weight in water lowers endurance. Drink 500 ml two hours before exercise.

- Literal use: for medical signs, list them ("heart rate, blood pressure, temperature and breathing rate") or write `vital signs` in inline code.

#### 083. `essential`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `essential`, `essentials`, `essentially`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `essential` is the most common way models mark an item as required, and it is often wrong: the `essential tools` list includes optional ones. It fakes editorial selection, as if someone had cut everything else. It also heads listicle titles like `10 Essential Tips`, the format readers now associate with filler.
- Where it shows up: listicle titles, setup guides, packing and shopping lists.

```slop
10 Essential VS Code Extensions for Every Developer.
Git is an essential tool for any developer.
Essential features include dark mode and notifications.
```

Replace with:

- Required or optional, stated as such: "Required: Node 20. Optional: Docker, for the local database." Use in setup guides.
- The count and whose list it is: "the 6 extensions I install on every new machine". Use for lists.
- What breaks without it: "without Git you cannot open a pull request". Use when necessity is the point.
- Cut it in feature lists and list the features.

Rewrites:

```slop
10 Essential VS Code Extensions for Every Developer.
```

After: 6 VS Code extensions I install on every new machine, and what each one does.

```slop
Git is an essential tool for any developer.
```

After: You need Git to clone the repository and open pull requests.

```slop
Essential features include dark mode and notifications.
```

After: Includes dark mode and push notifications.

- Literal use: for chemistry and nutrition terms, use inline code (`essential oil`, `essential amino acid`) or give the compound's name.

#### 084. `paramount`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `paramount`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `paramount` appears when a model wants to sound formal about priorities, nearly always in `your privacy is paramount` or `security is of paramount importance`. It is an old legal word that claims a ranking without showing what ranked below. Readers have seen it in breach apology letters, so it now invites distrust.
- Where it shows up: privacy pages, security statements, company values pages.

```slop
Your privacy is paramount to us.
Security is of paramount importance.
Customer satisfaction remains our paramount concern.
```

Replace with:

- The practice: "we do not sell personal data, and we delete accounts within 30 days of a request". Use for privacy.
- The control: "data encrypted at rest with AES-256; staff access requires a hardware key". Use for security.
- The tradeoff you made: "we delayed launch 6 weeks to finish the security audit". Use when you can prove the ranking.
- Cut it when the sentence only says that something matters to you.

Rewrites:

```slop
Your privacy is paramount to us.
```

After: We do not sell personal data. Ask us to delete your account and we erase it within 30 days.

```slop
Security is of paramount importance.
```

After: Data is encrypted at rest with AES-256. Staff access requires a hardware key and every access is logged.

```slop
Customer satisfaction remains our paramount concern.
```

After: If you are unhappy in the first 60 days, we refund the full amount.

- Literal use: for the film studio, put the name in inline code: `Paramount Pictures`.

#### 085. `multifaceted`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `multifaceted`, `multi-faceted`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `multifaceted` lets a model avoid choosing which parts of a topic matter. It appears in `a multifaceted issue` before a list that often has two items. It fakes depth by asserting that a subject has many sides without naming them.
- Where it shows up: essays, policy briefs, cover letters.

```slop
Climate change is a multifaceted challenge.
She brings a multifaceted skill set to the team.
Our approach to security is multifaceted.
```

Replace with:

- The named parts: "rising food prices, insurance costs and migration". Use for issues.
- The specific skills: "she has shipped iOS apps and run a 6-person support team". Use for people.
- The layers: "single sign-on, per-role permissions and audit logs". Use for security.
- Cut it when a list follows, because the list is the proof.

Rewrites:

```slop
Climate change is a multifaceted challenge.
```

After: Climate change is raising food prices, home insurance costs and the number of people who move for work.

```slop
She brings a multifaceted skill set to the team.
```

After: She has shipped two iOS apps and managed a 6-person support team.

```slop
Our approach to security is multifaceted.
```

After: Security has three layers: single sign-on, per-role permissions and an audit log of every export.

- Literal use: for a cut stone or crystal, write "with many facets" or give the count: "57 facets".

#### 086. `intricate`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `intricate`, `intricately`.
- Why it reads as machine text: models use `intricate` for patterns, systems and plots, usually beside "details" or "web". It treats complexity as praise but never says how many parts there are or how they connect. In code explanations it often covers for logic the writer did not trace.
- Where it shows up: craft and product descriptions, fiction blurbs, code walkthroughs.

```slop
The codebase is an intricate web of dependencies.
The rug features intricate hand-woven patterns.
The plot is an intricate tapestry of betrayal and loyalty.
```

Replace with:

- The count: "the service imports 14 packages, 3 of them in a cycle". Use for systems.
- The measurable detail: "120 knots per square inch, dyed with madder and indigo". Use for craft.
- The structure: "two timelines, 1962 and 2012, that meet in the last chapter". Use for plots.
- Cut it when the noun already implies many parts.

Rewrites:

```slop
The codebase is an intricate web of dependencies.
```

After: The billing service imports 14 internal packages, and 3 of them import each other.

```slop
The rug features intricate hand-woven patterns.
```

After: Hand-knotted wool at 120 knots per square inch, dyed with madder and indigo.

```slop
The plot is an intricate tapestry of betrayal and loyalty.
```

After: The novel alternates between 1962 and 2012, and the two timelines meet in the last chapter.

- Literal use: when you mean hard to follow, say which part is hard: "the retry logic is spread across 3 files".

#### 087. `nuanced`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `nuanced`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `nuanced` is a model describing its own thinking: `a nuanced view`, `a nuanced understanding`. It praises the reasoning instead of stating it. It is often used to soften a position until it cannot be wrong, which leaves the reader with nothing to act on.
- Where it shows up: essay conclusions, performance reviews, chat answers about contested topics.

```slop
This is a nuanced topic with no easy answers.
He has a nuanced understanding of the market.
We take a nuanced approach to content moderation.
```

Replace with:

- The conditions: "remote work raised output for senior writers and lowered it for new hires". Use when the answer depends on cases.
- The demonstrated knowledge: "he priced 3 product lines and predicted the 2023 drop". Use for people.
- The rule and its exception: "we remove slurs; we keep quoted slurs in news reporting". Use for policies.
- Cut it when you give the cases anyway.

Rewrites:

```slop
This is a nuanced topic with no easy answers.
```

After: It depends on the team. Remote work raised output for senior writers and lowered it for new hires in their first 6 months.

```slop
He has a nuanced understanding of the market.
```

After: He set prices for 3 product lines and predicted the 2023 drop in EU orders a quarter early.

```slop
We take a nuanced approach to content moderation.
```

After: We remove posts with slurs. A post that quotes a slur in news reporting stays up with a warning label.

- Literal use: when a distinction is fine, name it: "the difference between affect and effect".

#### 088. `holistic`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `holistic`, `holistically`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `holistic` comes from wellness marketing and management consulting, and models apply it to any plan that touches more than one area. It claims the parts were considered together without saying which parts or how they interact. In product copy it usually means "we added several features".
- Where it shows up: wellness sites, consulting proposals, benefits pages.

```slop
A holistic approach to employee wellbeing.
We take a holistic view of your marketing strategy.
Holistic health solutions for mind and body.
```

Replace with:

- The components: "counseling sessions, a gym stipend and one no-meeting Friday a month". Use for benefits.

- The specific services: "physiotherapy and sleep coaching". Use for health providers.


After: We set your ad budget from last quarter's sales by channel, not from impression counts.

```slop

```

After: Physiotherapy, sleep coaching and nutrition advice from licensed staff.

- Literal use: where "holism" is a named position in philosophy or medicine, name the school or write `holism` in inline code.

#### 089. `dynamic`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `dynamic`, `dynamically`, `dynamics`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `dynamic` has an exact meaning in programming, and models blur it with the advertising sense of "lively". In copy it describes teams, markets and dashboards and says nothing about any of them. In technical docs it hides whether a value is computed at runtime, fetched from a server or edited by the user, which are three different things.
- Where it shows up: job listings, dashboard feature lists, framework docs.

```slop
Join our dynamic team in a fast-paced environment.
Create dynamic dashboards that update in real time.
A dynamic platform for dynamic businesses.
```

Replace with:

- The team facts: "8 engineers, release every Tuesday, on call one week in six". Use for job listings.
- The refresh rule: "charts reload every 30 seconds from the live database". Use for dashboards.
- The runtime behavior: "routes are read from `routes.json` at startup". Use for technical docs.
- Cut it in pairs and repeats, where it adds rhythm and no meaning.

Rewrites:

```slop
Join our dynamic team in a fast-paced environment.
```

After: Join a team of 8 engineers. We release every Tuesday, and each person is on call one week in six.

```slop
Create dynamic dashboards that update in real time.
```

After: Charts reload every 30 seconds from the production database, without a page refresh.

```slop
A dynamic platform for dynamic businesses.
```

After: Accounting software for shops with 1 to 50 staff.

- Literal use: for a value computed at runtime, write "computed at runtime" or name the mechanism in inline code, such as `import()` or a framework's `dynamic` option.

#### 090. `vibrant`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `vibrant`, `vibrantly`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `vibrant` is the travel-guide adjective models attach to cities, communities and color palettes. It claims liveliness without one observed detail. In design copy it usually means saturated color, which a hex value states better.
- Where it shows up: travel writing, community pages, design system docs.

```slop
Join our vibrant community of 10,000 makers.
A vibrant color palette that pops.
```

Replace with:

- The observed detail: "tram 28 climbs past tiled house fronts to the castle". Use for places.
- The activity: "members post 300 projects a week and meet monthly in 12 cities". Use for communities.
- The values: "accent #B4441C on page #F7F5F0". Use for color.
- Cut it when the noun is already a place name or a number.

Rewrites:

```slop
Explore the vibrant streets of Lisbon.
```

After: Ride tram 28 up the hill past tiled house fronts to the castle.

```slop
Join our vibrant community of 10,000 makers.
```

After: 10,000 members post about 300 projects a week and meet monthly in 12 cities.

```slop
A vibrant color palette that pops.
```

After: One saturated accent, #B4441C, on an off-white page, #F7F5F0, with ink at #1A1A18.

- Literal use: for color science, give the values: hue, saturation and lightness, or the OKLCH chroma.

#### 091. `bustling`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `bustling`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `bustling` is a fixed pairing in model travel and fiction output: `bustling city`, `bustling market`, `bustling streets`. It is stock description that fits every city on earth. It takes the place of the one sound or count that would put the reader there.

#### 092. `thriving`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `thriving`.

#### 093. `meticulous`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `meticulous`, `meticulously`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `meticulous` is self-praise that models write into cover letters and studio pages, and into accounts of their own work (`I meticulously reviewed`). It asserts care while giving no evidence of it. A reader cannot check care; they can check an error rate or a checklist.
- Where it shows up: cover letters, studio "About" pages, assistants describing their own process.

```slop

Every product is meticulously crafted by hand.
```

Replace with:

- The error rate or audit result: "no billing errors across 3,000 invoices in 2024". Use for CVs.
- The process step: "one person stitches each bag and a second checks it against 12 points". Use for products.
- What was checked and what was not: "read all 4 changed files and ran the tests; did not check the migrations". Use for code review.
- Cut it when describing yourself, and give the record.

```slop
I am a meticulous professional with a keen eye for detail.
```

```slop
Every product is meticulously crafted by hand.
```

After: One person stitches each bag, and a second checks it against a 12-point list before it ships.

```slop
I have meticulously reviewed your code for errors.
```

After: I read all 4 changed files and ran the tests. Two fail, both in `parse_date`. I did not check the SQL migrations.

#### 094. `unparalleled`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `unparalleled`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `unparalleled` is a superlative that models apply to ordinary products. It says nothing else compares, which invites the reader to name a competitor. Advertising regulators in several countries treat unsupported superlatives as claims that need evidence, so it is also a legal risk.
- Where it shows up: hotel and travel listings, enterprise sales pages, luxury goods.

```slop
Enjoy unparalleled views of the Alps.
Unparalleled performance at an unbeatable price.
We offer unparalleled customer support.
```

Replace with:

- The fact behind the view: "every room faces south toward Mont Blanc". Use for hospitality.
- The benchmark with the rival named: "40% faster than Postgres 16 on TPC-H, same hardware". Use for performance, with the scripts published.
- The support terms: "a named engineer replies within 1 hour, any time of day". Use for service.
- Cut it when you have no comparison, because a superlative without one is empty.

Rewrites:

```slop
Enjoy unparalleled views of the Alps.
```

After: Every room faces south toward Mont Blanc.

```slop
Unparalleled performance at an unbeatable price.
```

After: Runs TPC-H 40% faster than Postgres 16 on the same hardware, for 20 USD a month. The benchmark scripts are in the repository.

```slop
We offer unparalleled customer support.
```

After: A named engineer replies within 1 hour, 24 hours a day, on every plan.

- Literal use: for lines in geometry, write "not parallel" or give the angle between them.

#### 095. `unprecedented`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `unprecedented`, `unprecedentedly`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `unprecedented` became a cliche in 2020, and models absorbed it at that frequency. It claims something has never happened before, which is rarely checked and often false. It turns a normal increase into a historic one.
- Where it shows up: news-style summaries, investor letters, crisis emails.

```slop
In these unprecedented times, we are here for you.
The platform saw unprecedented growth last quarter.
An unprecedented level of personalization.
```

Replace with:

- The record and the previous record: "1.2 million sign-ups, three times the old monthly high". Use for growth.
- The practical facts of the crisis: "stores closed until 15 May; orders still ship in 2 days". Use for customer emails.
- What changes per user: "the homepage reorders around the last 20 items you viewed". Use for personalization.
- Cut it in openers; the reader knows what year it is.

Rewrites:

```slop
In these unprecedented times, we are here for you.
```

After: Our stores are closed until 15 May. Online orders still ship within 2 days.

```slop
The platform saw unprecedented growth last quarter.
```

After: 1.2 million people signed up last quarter, three times the previous record.

```slop
An unprecedented level of personalization.
```

After: The homepage reorders itself around the last 20 items you viewed.

- Literal use: in law, write "without precedent" and cite the search: "the court found no earlier ruling on this question".

#### 096. `unwavering`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `unwavering`, `unwaveringly`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `unwavering` appears in model output as a fixed pair: `unwavering commitment`, `unwavering support`, `unwavering dedication`. It is the language of award speeches and condolence letters. In company copy it promises a constancy no one can test.

- What the person did: "you read every draft within a day for 3 years". Use for thanks.
- The events: "she rebuilt the lab twice, after the floods of 2011 and 2014". Use for tributes.

```slop

```

After: She rebuilt the lab twice, after the floods of 2011 and 2014.

#### 097. `unmatched`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `unmatched`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `unmatched` is the shorter cousin of `unparalleled`, and models alternate the two to avoid repeating themselves. It claims no competitor matches the product while naming none. To a developer, `unmatched` first suggests a bracket with no partner.

#### 098. `compelling`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `compelling`, `compellingly`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `compelling` is how a model praises an argument, story or offer without stating it. `A compelling case` usually comes right before a weak one. It claims the reader will be persuaded, which is the reader's call to make.

- The trait of the story: "open on one named customer and one problem, in under 50 words". Use for writing advice.

```slop
We make a compelling case for switching.
```


```slop
The data paints a compelling picture.
```

#### 099. `captivating`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `captivating`, `captivatingly`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `captivating` is a model's default praise for visuals, performances and stories. It claims an effect on the reader's attention that the writer cannot know. In image captions and portfolio blurbs it usually sits beside `stunning`.

#### 100. `stunning`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `stunning`, `stunningly`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `stunning` is the most common praise word in model-written image prompts, captions and template copy. It reports the writer's claimed reaction, not a property of the object. When every template on a marketplace is `stunning`, the word means "has a picture".

#### 101. `breathtaking`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `breathtaking`, `breathtakingly`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `breathtaking` is travel and property filler that models add to any view. It claims a physical reaction that no reader will have from text. Paired with "views", it appears in thousands of rental listings and adds no fact to any of them.

#### 104. `remarkable`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `remarkable`.


#### 105. `exceptional`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `exceptional`, `exceptionally`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `exceptional` is how models praise service, quality and talent, in a register borrowed from hotel reviews and HR forms. It claims a rank above the rule without stating the rule. Every company calls its service `exceptional`, so the word now reads as average.

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `extraordinary`, `extraordinarily`.

#### 108. `invaluable`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `invaluable`, `invaluably`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `invaluable` is the default word in model-written thank-you notes, testimonials and acknowledgements. It says the value cannot be counted, which is a reason to count it. Some readers also misread it as "not valuable", so it can fail even as praise.
- Where it shows up: testimonials, acknowledgements, survey prompts.

```slop
Your feedback is invaluable to us.
An invaluable resource for beginners.
Her contributions have been invaluable to the project.
```

Replace with:

- What the feedback changed: "three reports like yours led to the fixes in 2.3.1". Use for thanks and survey prompts.
- Who it helps and how: "explains each Git command with one diagram". Use for resources.
- The contribution: "she wrote the parser and reviewed 300 pull requests". Use for credit.
- Cut it in survey prompts and ask the question.

Rewrites:

```slop
Your feedback is invaluable to us.
```

After: Tell us what broke. Last month, three reports like yours led to the fixes in 2.3.1.

```slop
An invaluable resource for beginners.
```

After: Explains each Git command with one diagram, for people in their first month of using it.

```slop
Her contributions have been invaluable to the project.
```

After: She wrote the parser and reviewed more than 300 pull requests.

- Literal use: when worth really is unknown, say so: "no one has priced it".

#### 109. `indispensable`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `indispensable`, `indispensably`.
- Why it reads as machine text: models use `indispensable` to claim a product or person cannot be done without. It is rarely true and easy to disprove: the reader managed without it yesterday. It is catalog-sales register, carried into tool roundups and reference letters.
- Where it shows up: tool roundups, product pages, reference letters.

```slop
An indispensable tool for every designer.
He quickly became an indispensable member of the team.
Indispensable tips for first-time founders.
```

Replace with:

- How often it is used: "I open it about 40 times a day". Use for tool reviews.
- What the person owns: "within 3 months he owned the billing service and its on-call rotation". Use for references.
- The count and the source: "7 lessons from founders who raised a seed round in 2023". Use for lists.
- Cut it whenever a working alternative exists.

Rewrites:

```slop
An indispensable tool for every designer.
```

After: A color picker I open about 40 times a day. It reads values from any window on screen.

```slop
He quickly became an indispensable member of the team.
```

After: Within 3 months he owned the billing service and its on-call rotation.

```slop
Indispensable tips for first-time founders.
```

After: 7 lessons from founders who raised a seed round in 2023.

- Literal use: for a hard dependency, write "required" and name it: "requires `libssl` 3.0".

#### 110. `instrumental`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `instrumental`, `instrumentally`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `instrumental` appears in model text as `was instrumental in`, a phrase that credits someone without saying what they did. It is common in award citations, obituaries and professional-network posts. The construction lets the writer skip the verb, and the verb is the claim.
- Where it shows up: performance reviews, award citations, professional-network posts.

```slop
He was instrumental in launching the new product.
Our partners have been instrumental to our success.
She was instrumental in driving adoption.
```

Replace with:

- The verb of what they did: "wrote the launch plan and ran the beta with 40 customers". Use for credit.
- The partner's act: "resold the product to 300 schools". Use for partnerships.
- The action and its result: "ran the training that took weekly users from 200 to 1,400". Use for adoption.
- Cut it every time it comes with "in", and write the verb.

Rewrites:

```slop
He was instrumental in launching the new product.
```

After: He wrote the launch plan and ran the beta with 40 customers.

```slop
Our partners have been instrumental to our success.
```

After: Our partners resold the product to 300 schools in the first year.

```slop
She was instrumental in driving adoption.
```

After: She ran the training sessions that took weekly users from 200 to 1,400.

- Literal use: for music with no vocals, write "no vocals" or put the genre label in inline code: `instrumental`.

#### 111. `integral`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `integral`, `integrally`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `integral` arrives in `an integral part of`, a model construction that claims something belongs without saying how it connects. It is filler in job ads and company histories. In technical writing it also collides with the calculus term, so readers stop to check which sense is meant.
- Where it shows up: job descriptions, company pages, engineering process docs.

```slop
You will be an integral part of our team.
Testing is an integral part of our development process.
Sustainability is integral to everything we do.
```

Replace with:

- The role: "you will own the checkout service and join on-call in month 2". Use for job ads.
- The rule: "no pull request merges unless CI passes and one reviewer approves". Use for process.
- The practice with a number: "52% of our packaging is recycled cardboard". Use for policy claims.
- Cut it when "part of" can be replaced by a verb.

Rewrites:

```slop
You will be an integral part of our team.
```

After: You will own the checkout service and join the on-call rotation in your second month.

```slop
Testing is an integral part of our development process.
```

After: No pull request merges until CI passes and one reviewer approves.

```slop
Sustainability is integral to everything we do.
```

After: 52% of our packaging is recycled cardboard. We aim to reach 90% by 2027.

- Literal use: in mathematics, write the expression in inline code, such as `\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx`, or say "the area under the curve".

#### 112. `intuitive`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `intuitive`, `intuitively`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `intuitive` is the default interface adjective in model-written product copy. It claims people will understand the interface without learning it, which only a usability test can show. Designers distrust it because it usually means "familiar to the person who built it".
- Where it shows up: SaaS landing pages, app store descriptions, design reviews.

```slop
An intuitive interface that anyone can use.
Intuitive drag-and-drop editing.
The dashboard is intuitive and easy to navigate.
```

Replace with:

- The test result: "5 of 6 first-time users sent an invoice without help". Use when you ran a test.
- The interaction: "drag a block to move it; press Delete to remove it". Use for editors.
- The borrowed convention: "the same keyboard shortcuts as Google Docs". Use when it follows a known model.
- Cut it in design reviews and describe what a first-time user did.

Rewrites:

```slop
An intuitive interface that anyone can use.
```

After: In testing, 5 of 6 first-time users sent an invoice without help, in a median of 2 minutes.

```slop
Intuitive drag-and-drop editing.
```

After: Drag a block to move it. Press Delete to remove it.

```slop
The dashboard is intuitive and easy to navigate.
```

After: Every report is one click from the sidebar, and search finds any customer by name or email.

- Literal use: for judgment without formal reasoning, write "a gut estimate" or "an untested guess".

#### 113. `user-friendly`

- Kind: compound adjective. Banned forms: `user-friendly`, `user friendly`, `user-friendliness`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `user-friendly` is a 1980s computing phrase that models still apply to APIs, forms and apps. It claims ease without naming the user or the task. In feature grids it fills the slot where a measurable claim should go.
- Where it shows up: feature grids, procurement answers, app store listings.

```slop
A user-friendly interface for managing your finances.
Our API is simple and user-friendly.
User-friendly design that puts you first.
```

Replace with:

- The task and the time: "connect a bank and see last month's spending in under 3 minutes". Use for apps.
- The developer facts: "one POST request per charge; every error names the field to fix". Use for APIs.
- The accessibility facts: "every action reachable by keyboard, tested with VoiceOver and NVDA". Use for procurement.
- Cut it when the reader can try the product instead of reading about it.

Rewrites:

```slop
A user-friendly interface for managing your finances.
```

After: Connect a bank account and see last month's spending by category in under 3 minutes.

```slop
Our API is simple and user-friendly.
```

After: Create a charge with one POST request. Every error message names the field to fix.

```slop
User-friendly design that puts you first.
```

After: Text at 16 px or larger, every action reachable by keyboard, tested with VoiceOver and NVDA.

- Literal use: none; if a buyer's form asks for the phrase, answer with test results like the ones above.

#### 114. `frictionless`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `frictionless`, `frictionlessly`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `frictionless` is startup and payments vocabulary that models apply to sign-up, checkout and onboarding. It claims zero effort, which is never true: someone still types a card number. It hides the steps a designer should be counting.
- Where it shows up: checkout pages, fintech pitch decks, SDK docs.

```slop
Frictionless checkout for your customers.
A frictionless onboarding experience.
Make payments frictionless with our SDK.
```

Replace with:

- The screen count: "checkout on one screen, with Apple Pay and saved cards". Use for payments.
- The removed step: "no email confirmation before your first project". Use for onboarding.
- The integration size: "card payments in 14 lines of code". Use for SDKs.
- Cut it whenever steps remain, and count them instead.

Rewrites:

```slop
Frictionless checkout for your customers.
```

After: Checkout fits on one screen, with Apple Pay, Google Pay and saved cards.

```slop
A frictionless onboarding experience.
```

After: Start a project before confirming your email. We ask for it when you invite someone.

```slop
Make payments frictionless with our SDK.
```

After: Add card payments in 14 lines of code with the iOS or Android SDK.

- Literal use: in physics, write "with friction ignored" or "assuming zero friction".

#### 115. `effortless`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `effortless`, `effortlessly`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `effortless` appears in model output for workflows, clothing and fitness alike. It promises no work, which the reader knows is false, so it lowers trust in the claims around it. `effortlessly` also papers over steps the writer chose not to describe.
- Where it shows up: productivity tools, fashion copy, how-to intros.

```slop
Effortlessly manage your projects in one place.
Effortless style for every occasion.
Deploy your app effortlessly.
```

Replace with:

- The setup time: "a project board from a template in about 4 minutes". Use for tools.
- The garment facts: "linen-cotton, machine wash at 30 C, no ironing". Use for clothing.
- The command and its duration: "`fly deploy` builds and ships in about 90 seconds". Use for developer tools.
- Cut it in how-tos; the steps show how much effort the task takes.

Rewrites:

```slop
Effortlessly manage your projects in one place.
```

After: Set up a project board from a template in about 4 minutes.

```slop
Effortless style for every occasion.
```

After: A linen-cotton shirt that goes in the machine at 30 C and needs no ironing.

```slop
Deploy your app effortlessly.
```

After: Run `fly deploy` in the project folder. It builds and ships in about 90 seconds.

- Literal use: for a motion with no visible strain, describe it: "she lifted the 20 kg bag with one hand".

#### 116. `delightful`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `delightful`, `delightfully`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `delightful` is a design-industry word that models copy from product blogs, as in `delightful experiences` and `delightful details`. It claims an emotion in the user and names no detail that causes it. In UI copy it often accompanies animation that slows people down.
- Where it shows up: design blog posts, launch notes, onboarding screens.

```slop
Delightful micro-interactions throughout the app.
A delightful way to plan your week.
We sweat the details to make every moment delightful.
```

Replace with:

- The specific detail: "the checkbox fills in 120 ms and the task moves to Done". Use for interaction design.
- The product's job: "drag tasks onto days and see hours left per day". Use for apps.
- The list of care details: "undo on every action, drafts saved every 5 seconds". Use for quality claims.
- Cut it in product UI; users do not need to be told how to feel.

Rewrites:

```slop
Delightful micro-interactions throughout the app.
```

After: Checking a task fills the box in 120 ms and moves the task to Done.

```slop
A delightful way to plan your week.
```

After: Drag tasks onto days, and the week view shows how many hours each day has left.

```slop
We sweat the details to make every moment delightful.
```

After: Every action can be undone, and drafts save every 5 seconds.

- Literal use: for your own pleasure in a personal letter, write "I enjoyed it" or "I was glad".

#### 117. `sleek`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `sleek`, `sleekly`, `sleeker`, `sleekness`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `sleek` is a model's default for hardware and interfaces with little ornament. It says how something looks without one dimension, material or color. In UI kit listings it signals the generic dark dashboard with glowing accents.
- Where it shows up: hardware product pages, UI kit listings, gadget reviews.

```slop
A sleek, modern design that fits any workspace.
Sleek dashboard UI kit with dark mode.
The sleek aluminum body weighs just 1.2 kg.
```

Replace with:

- Dimensions and material: "14 mm thick, aluminum, 1.2 kg". Use for hardware.
- What the kit contains: "48 components, light and dark themes, Figma and React". Use for UI kits.
- The design decision: "no visible screws; one USB-C port on the back". Use for reviews.
- Cut it when a measurement is in the sentence.

Rewrites:

```slop
A sleek, modern design that fits any workspace.
```

After: 14 mm thick and 42 cm wide, in gray or black aluminum.

```slop
Sleek dashboard UI kit with dark mode.
```

After: A dashboard kit with 48 components in light and dark themes, for Figma and React.

```slop
The sleek aluminum body weighs just 1.2 kg.
```

After: The aluminum body weighs 1.2 kg and has no visible screws.

- Literal use: for hair or fur, write "smooth" or "glossy".

#### 118. `elegant`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `elegant`, `elegantly`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `elegant` is the praise models give to code, fonts and answers. In engineering it approves code without naming the virtue, which might be fewer lines, fewer branches or no shared state. In design copy it pairs with `minimal` and `timeless` as generic luxury.
- Where it shows up: code review comments, font and template marketplaces, wedding copy.

```slop
An elegant solution to a complex problem.
This elegant serif font is perfect for branding.
The code is clean and elegant.
```

Replace with:

- The code property: "3 nested loops replaced by one dictionary lookup, 40 lines to 12". Use for code.
- The font specs: "high-contrast serif, 6 weights, small caps and old-style figures". Use for type.
- The readability rule it meets: "each function under 20 lines, no shared mutable state". Use for review comments.
- Cut it when you mean "I like it", and say what to keep.

Rewrites:

```slop
An elegant solution to a complex problem.
```

After: Replaces 3 nested loops with one dictionary lookup, cutting the function from 40 lines to 12.

```slop
This elegant serif font is perfect for branding.
```

After: A high-contrast serif in 6 weights, with small caps and old-style figures.

```slop
The code is clean and elegant.
```

After: Each function is under 20 lines, and none of them share mutable state.

- Literal use: in mathematics, say what makes the proof short: "a proof with no case analysis".

#### 119. `modern`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `modern`, `modernize`, `modernization`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `modern` is the most frequent design adjective in model output, as in `modern UI`, `modern stack` and `modern teams`. It ages the day it is written and describes nothing a reader can check. In design prompts it reliably produces the same look: Inter, an `indigo-500` accent and `rounded-2xl` cards with soft shadows.
- Where it shows up: design prompts, tech-stack READMEs, SaaS hero lines.

```slop
A modern, responsive landing page.
Built with a modern tech stack.
Modern tools for modern teams.
```

Replace with:

- The design spec: "IBM Plex Sans at 16 px, 2px radius, one accent #B4441C, borders not shadows". Use for design prompts.
- The named stack and versions: "React 19, Vite 6, Postgres 17". Use for READMEs.
- The audience and the job: "invoicing for freelancers who bill by the hour". Use for hero lines.
- Cut it every time; the word is never the claim.

Rewrites:

```slop
A modern, responsive landing page.
```

After: A landing page in IBM Plex Sans at 16 px, one burnt-orange accent, 1px borders, no shadows, readable at 320 px wide.

```slop
Built with a modern tech stack.
```

After: Built with React 19, Vite 6 and Postgres 17.

```slop
Modern tools for modern teams.
```

After: Time tracking and invoicing for freelancers who bill by the hour.

- Literal use: for a historical period, give the dates ("since 1945"); for a proper name such as `Modern Greek`, use inline code.

#### 120. `next-generation`

- Kind: compound adjective. Banned forms: `next-generation`, `next generation`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `next-generation` claims a product belongs to a new generation without naming the old one. Models attach it to firewalls, databases and AI tools, and it is a fixed vendor phrase in security marketing. Because every vendor uses it, buyers skip it.
- Where it shows up: security vendor pages, analyst briefings, hardware launches.

```slop
A next-generation firewall for the cloud era.
Next-generation analytics for data-driven teams.
Meet the next generation of project management.
```

Replace with:

- The difference from the last version: "inspects TLS traffic at 10 Gbps; version 3 managed 2". Use for upgrades.
- The capability: "query events with SQL within 5 seconds of arrival". Use for analytics.
- The change in method: "plans in 2-week budgets, not dated milestones". Use for new product categories.
- Cut it in headings and name the product.

Rewrites:

```slop
A next-generation firewall for the cloud era.
```

After: A firewall that inspects encrypted traffic at 10 Gbps, five times the rate of version 3.

```slop
Next-generation analytics for data-driven teams.
```

After: Query event data with SQL within 5 seconds of it arriving.

```slop
Meet the next generation of project management.
```

After: Project planning in 2-week budgets instead of dated milestones.

- Literal use: for families and demographics, write "their children" or "people born after 2000".

#### 121. `next-gen`

- Kind: compound adjective. Banned forms: `next-gen`, `next gen`, `nextgen`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `next-gen` is the clipped, gaming-press form of `next-generation`, and models use it to sound casual and current. It refers to a console cycle that readers of a developer blog may not share. It carries all the vagueness of the long form plus slang that dates within a year.
- Where it shows up: gaming copy, crypto pages, developer tool announcements.

```slop
Next-gen graphics on any device.
The next-gen platform for decentralized finance.
A next-gen CLI for modern developers.
```

Replace with:

- The rendering spec: "ray-traced shadows at 60 fps on a 2022 laptop GPU". Use for graphics.
- The mechanism and cost: "trades settle on-chain in about 12 seconds, fees under 0.01 USD". Use for finance.
- The feature the old tool lacks: "runs tests in parallel and skips unchanged files". Use for CLIs.
- Cut it in all cases; no reader needs it.

Rewrites:

```slop
Next-gen graphics on any device.
```

After: Ray-traced shadows at 60 fps on a 2022 laptop GPU.

```slop
The next-gen platform for decentralized finance.
```

After: Trades settle on-chain in about 12 seconds, with fees under 0.01 USD.

```slop
A next-gen CLI for modern developers.
```

After: A CLI that runs tests in parallel and skips files whose hash has not changed.

- Literal use: for a console generation, name the hardware: "PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X".

#### 122. `state-of-the-art`

- Kind: compound adjective. Banned forms: `state-of-the-art`, `state of the art`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `state-of-the-art` has an exact use in machine learning papers, the best published result on a benchmark, and models spread it to products, clinics and security. In marketing it claims the top current level with no benchmark. In research it often appears without a date, which matters because records on popular benchmarks fall every few months.
- Where it shows up: ML paper abstracts, clinic and hospital pages, security pages.

```slop
Our state-of-the-art model outperforms existing approaches.
A state-of-the-art facility with the latest equipment.
State-of-the-art security for your peace of mind.
```

Replace with:

- The benchmark, score and date: "81.2 on MMLU, 1.4 points above the best published result as of March 2025". Use for ML.
- The named equipment: "a 3 tesla MRI scanner installed in 2024". Use for facilities.
- The controls: "authenticator app or hardware key; SOC 2 Type II report on request". Use for security.
- Cut it when you have no comparison to show.

Rewrites:

```slop
Our state-of-the-art model outperforms existing approaches.
```

After: Our model scores 81.2 on MMLU, 1.4 points above the best published result as of March 2025.

```slop
A state-of-the-art facility with the latest equipment.
```

After: The clinic has a 3 tesla MRI scanner, installed in 2024.

```slop
State-of-the-art security for your peace of mind.
```

After: Sign-in requires an authenticator app or a hardware key. Our SOC 2 Type II report is available on request.

- Literal use: in a results table, write "best published result as of" a date, or keep the abbreviation `SOTA` in inline code.

#### 123. `world-class`

- Kind: compound adjective. Banned forms: `world-class`, `world class`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `world-class` is a ranking claim that names no ranking. Models use it for teams, support, chefs and infrastructure. Readers know it usually means the writer had no credential to cite.
- Where it shows up: team pages, hiring posts, hospitality copy.

```slop
A world-class team of engineers and designers.
World-class support, around the clock.
Enjoy world-class dining at our resort.
```

Replace with:

- Credentials: "two Postgres committers and a former Rust compiler maintainer". Use for teams.
- The service terms: "phone support 24 hours a day, median wait 40 seconds". Use for support.
- The outside rating: "one Michelin star since 2019". Use only for ratings that exist.
- Cut it when no ranking stands behind it.

Rewrites:

```slop
A world-class team of engineers and designers.
```

After: Our 14 engineers include two Postgres committers and a former Rust compiler maintainer.

```slop
World-class support, around the clock.
```

After: Phone support 24 hours a day. The median wait last month was 40 seconds.

```slop
Enjoy world-class dining at our resort.
```

After: The resort's restaurant has held one Michelin star since 2019.

- Literal use: for sport, cite the ranking body and position: "ranked 12th by World Athletics".

#### 124. `best-in-class`

- Kind: compound adjective. Banned forms: `best-in-class`, `best in class`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `best-in-class` comes from analyst reports and procurement language, and models use it to sound like an enterprise vendor. It claims a category win without naming the category or the judge. In comparison tables it tends to appear in the vendor's own column only.
- Where it shows up: enterprise sales pages, RFP answers, comparison tables.

```slop
Best-in-class security and compliance.
We deliver best-in-class customer experiences.
Best-in-class performance for mission-critical workloads.
```

Replace with:

- The certification list: "SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, HIPAA BAA on request". Use for compliance.
- The service figure: "94% of 12,000 tickets rated resolved in 2024". Use for support claims.
- The benchmark with rivals named and the method linked. Use for performance.
- Cut it in RFP answers; procurement staff score evidence, not adjectives.

Rewrites:

```slop
Best-in-class security and compliance.
```

After: SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 certified. We sign HIPAA BAAs on request.

```slop
We deliver best-in-class customer experiences.
```

After: Customers rated 94% of our 12,000 support tickets in 2024 as resolved.

```slop
Best-in-class performance for mission-critical workloads.
```

After: p99 write latency of 4 ms at 50,000 writes per second. The benchmark scripts are public.

- Literal use: for a dog show or a car race, name the class and the event: "won the terrier class at Crufts 2024".

#### 125. `industry-leading`

- Kind: compound adjective. Banned forms: `industry-leading`, `industry leading`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `industry-leading` is a market-position claim that models attach to features, uptime and margins. It names neither the industry nor the measure. In regulated markets, an unsupported leadership claim can draw a complaint to the advertising regulator.
- Where it shows up: investor decks, press releases, B2B landing pages.

```slop
Industry-leading uptime and reliability.
An industry-leading provider of HR software.
Our industry-leading AI delivers results.
```

Replace with:

- The figure and the promise: "99.99% uptime in 2024 against a 99.9% SLA". Use for availability.
- The market share with its source: "used by 31% of US hospitals with over 500 beds". Use for position.
- What the AI does and how often it works: "agents send 55% of drafted replies unedited". Use for AI features.
- Cut it in press releases; journalists delete it anyway.

Rewrites:

```slop
Industry-leading uptime and reliability.
```

After: 99.99% uptime in 2024, measured by an outside monitor, against a 99.9% SLA.

```slop
An industry-leading provider of HR software.
```

After: HR software used by 31% of US hospitals with more than 500 beds.

```slop
Our industry-leading AI delivers results.
```

After: The assistant drafts replies, and agents send 55% of them without edits.

- Literal use: none; a lead is always a comparison, so state the comparison.

#### 126. `enterprise-grade`

- Kind: compound adjective. Banned forms: `enterprise-grade`, `enterprise grade`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `enterprise-grade` claims a product meets the demands of large companies but never lists the demands. Models use it for security, support and scale. Enterprise buyers work from a checklist, and the word skips every item on it.
- Where it shows up: pricing pages, security pages, upgrade prompts in developer tools.

```slop
Enterprise-grade security for teams of all sizes.
Get enterprise-grade features on every plan.
Enterprise-grade reliability you can trust.
```

Replace with:

- The checklist items: "SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning, audit log export, EU data residency". Use for security and admin.
- The contract terms: "99.9% SLA with service credits, 1-hour response for severity 1". Use for support.
- The limits: "up to 50,000 users per workspace". Use for scale.
- Cut it when the plan table already lists the features.

Rewrites:

```slop
Enterprise-grade security for teams of all sizes.
```

After: SAML single sign-on and audit logs on every plan, including the 5-seat one.

```slop
Get enterprise-grade features on every plan.
```

After: SCIM provisioning, EU data residency and audit log export on every plan.

```slop
Enterprise-grade reliability you can trust.
```

After: A 99.9% uptime SLA with service credits, and a 1-hour response for severity 1 incidents.

- Literal use: none; a buyer needs the list, so give the list.

#### 127. `mission-critical`

- Kind: compound adjective. Banned forms: `mission-critical`, `mission critical`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `mission-critical` came from aerospace and defense, where a failure ends the mission. Models apply it to any production workload or internal tool. It raises the stakes without stating the cost of downtime, which is the number that decides budgets.
- Where it shows up: infrastructure marketing, incident postmortems, architecture docs.

```slop
Built for mission-critical workloads.
Email is a mission-critical application for our business.
Monitoring for your mission-critical systems.
```

Replace with:

- The recovery targets: "recovery point 5 minutes, recovery time 30 minutes". Use for architecture docs.
- The cost of downtime: "the 3-hour outage in March delayed 120 quotes". Use for business cases.
- The tier and its response: "Tier 1 pages the on-call engineer within 60 seconds". Use for incident policy.
- Cut it when the sentence already says "production".

Rewrites:

```slop
Built for mission-critical workloads.
```

After: Designed for workloads that need a 5-minute recovery point and a 30-minute recovery time.

```slop
Email is a mission-critical application for our business.
```

After: When email is down, sales cannot send quotes. The 3-hour outage last March delayed 120 of them.

```slop
Monitoring for your mission-critical systems.
```

After: Alerts for your Tier 1 services page the on-call engineer within 60 seconds.

- Literal use: in aerospace and defense documents where it is a formal class, use the document's own term in inline code.

#### 128. `powerful`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `powerful`, `powerfully`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `powerful` is among the most frequent adjectives in model-written READMEs and feature grids. It claims capability without naming one. It usually comes paired as `powerful yet simple`, a stock contrast that cancels itself.
- Where it shows up: library READMEs, feature grids, AI tool launches.

```slop
A powerful yet simple library for data validation.
Powerful features to help you grow.
Unlock powerful insights from your data.
```

Replace with:

- What it does that a smaller tool does not: "validates nested JSON and reports every error with its path". Use for libraries.
- The specific feature: "a follow-up email after 3 days without a reply". Use for feature grids.
- The question it answers: "which 10 customers are most likely to cancel next month". Use for analytics.
- Cut it in pairs with "simple".

Rewrites:

```slop
A powerful yet simple library for data validation.
```

After: Validates nested JSON against a schema and reports every error with its path, such as `items[3].price`.

```slop
Powerful features to help you grow.
```

After: Sends a follow-up email when a lead has not replied in 3 days.

```slop
Unlock powerful insights from your data.
```

After: See which 10 customers are most likely to cancel next month, and the usage drop behind each one.

- Literal use: for physical power, give the unit: "a 250 W motor", "a 1,000 W power supply".

#### 129. `bleeding-edge`

- Kind: compound adjective. Banned forms: `bleeding-edge`, `bleeding edge`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `bleeding-edge` is the developer-flavored version of `cutting-edge`, used by models to sound like an insider. It originally meant unstable pre-release software, which is the opposite of what a sales page wants to say. Readers cannot tell which sense the writer meant.
- Where it shows up: developer tool landing pages, release channel docs, hiring posts.

```slop
Stay on the bleeding edge with our nightly builds.
Work with bleeding-edge technologies.
A bleeding-edge framework for building web apps.
```

Replace with:

- The release channel and its risk: "nightly builds from `main`, breaking changes about weekly". Use for release docs.
- The tech list with versions: "Rust, WebGPU, Postgres 17". Use for hiring.
- What the framework does by default: "renders on the server and streams HTML". Use for framework pages.
- Cut it when the reader would rather know the stability guarantee.

Rewrites:

```slop
Stay on the bleeding edge with our nightly builds.
```

After: Nightly builds come straight from `main`. Expect a breaking change about once a week.

```slop
Work with bleeding-edge technologies.
```

After: You will work in Rust and WebGPU, with Postgres 17 for storage.

```slop
A bleeding-edge framework for building web apps.
```

After: A web framework that renders on the server by default and streams HTML as each part is ready.

- Literal use: when you mean unstable, write "pre-release" or "unstable" and name the channel in inline code, as in `nightly`.

#### 130. `top-notch`

- Kind: compound adjective. Banned forms: `top-notch`, `top notch`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `top-notch` is casual praise that models use to sound friendly in service and staffing copy. It is a grade with no scale. Its informal register clashes with the formal claims around it, which makes the page read as assembled from parts.
- Where it shows up: small-business websites, freelancer profiles, replies to reviews.

```slop
We provide top-notch service at affordable prices.
Top-notch developers ready to join your team.
Thanks for the review. We strive for top-notch quality.
```

Replace with:

- The service terms: "same-day callback, 2-year warranty on every repair". Use for small businesses.
- The vetting step: "each developer passed a 4-hour paid trial project". Use for staffing.
- The specific reply: "sorry the hinge broke; a replacement ships today". Use for review replies.
- Cut it everywhere; it carries nothing a reader can check.

Rewrites:

```slop
We provide top-notch service at affordable prices.
```

After: Same-day callback and a 2-year warranty on every repair, from 60 EUR.

```slop
Top-notch developers ready to join your team.
```

After: Every developer we place has passed a 4-hour paid trial project.

```slop
Thanks for the review. We strive for top-notch quality.
```

After: Thanks for the review. Sorry the hinge broke; a replacement ships today.

- Literal use: none; if a real ranking exists, give the rank and who set it.

#### 131. `premium`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `premium`, `premiums`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `premium` is pricing vocabulary that models apply to materials, plans and content. It claims higher quality through a price signal alone. In product UI it also labels the paid tier, where the plan name and its price would be clearer.
- Where it shows up: pricing pages, consumer goods copy, paywall labels.

```slop
Upgrade to Premium for exclusive features.
Made from premium materials.
Premium templates for professionals.
```

Replace with:

- The plan name, price and contents: "Pro, 8 USD a month: unlimited projects and version history". Use for pricing.
- The material: "18-gauge stainless steel, 3-ply base". Use for goods.
- What the template includes: "40 pages, print-ready bleeds, a style guide". Use for templates.
- Cut it when the price is visible, because the price already says it.

Rewrites:

```slop
Upgrade to Premium for exclusive features.
```

After: Pro costs 8 USD a month and adds unlimited projects and 90 days of version history.

```slop
Made from premium materials.
```

After: 18-gauge stainless steel with a 3-ply base.

```slop
Premium templates for professionals.
```

After: 40-page templates with print-ready bleeds and a style guide.

- Literal use: for insurance, write "the monthly payment", or keep the term in inline code: `premium`.

#### 132. `bespoke`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `bespoke`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `bespoke` is British tailoring vocabulary that models use to make any custom work sound expensive. It claims something was made for one client, which is often false: a template with a swapped logo is not that. In agency copy it signals the price, not the process.
- Where it shows up: agency websites, luxury goods, consulting proposals.

```slop
Bespoke software solutions for your business.
A bespoke shopping experience made just for you.
We create bespoke marketing strategies.
```

Replace with:

- What is custom and what is reused: "a booking system built on our open-source scheduler". Use for agencies.
- The input that changes the output: "recommendations change with every order and return". Use for retail.
- The deliverable and its source data: "a 12-month channel plan from your last 2 years of sales". Use for consulting.
- Cut it when the work starts from a template; say "custom" only if it is.

Rewrites:

```slop
Bespoke software solutions for your business.
```

After: We build booking and inventory systems for clinics, on top of our open-source scheduler.

