- A rule people can apply: "if a design fails WCAG AA, it does not ship".
- Cut it when the goal has no number or rule attached.

Rewrites:

```slop
Customer happiness is our north star.
```

After: Our main goal for 2025 is a support CSAT of 4.6 out of 5, up from 4.2.

```slop
Weekly active users is the north star metric for the growth team.
```

After: The growth team is judged on weekly active users; the target is 120,000 by December.

```slop
Let accessibility be the north star for every design decision.
```

After: No design ships if any text fails WCAG AA contrast or any control lacks a keyboard path.

- Literal use: for the star itself, write "Polaris" or "the pole star".

#### 240. `moonshot`

- Kind: noun. Banned forms: `moonshot`, `moonshots`, `moon shot`.
- Why it reads as machine text: Models attach `moonshot` to any ambitious project, borrowing from the Apollo program and from Google X branding. The word claims both difficulty and importance, and it excuses the lack of a plan, since such projects are expected to fail. It hides the goal, the budget and the odds.
- Where it shows up: R&D announcements, founder interviews, corporate lab pages.

```slop
Our moonshot is to make every website accessible by 2030.
The team is working on a secret moonshot project.
Fusion energy is the ultimate moonshot.
```

Replace with:

- "long-shot project" or "high-risk project" when risk is the point, with the odds if known.
- The goal as a number with a date.
- "research project" for work with no product yet.
- Cut it when the sentence is only about ambition.

Rewrites:

```slop
Our moonshot is to make every website accessible by 2030.
```

After: Our goal is to bring 1 million websites to WCAG AA by 2030; so far our scanner has fixed issues on 40,000.

```slop
The team is working on a secret moonshot project.
```

After: Six engineers are prototyping an on-device speech model; it is not on the roadmap yet.

```slop
Fusion energy is the ultimate moonshot.
```

After: A fusion experiment first released more energy than its lasers delivered in December 2022; a working power plant is still decades away.

- Literal use: for the Apollo missions, write "the Moon landing" or the mission name ("Apollo 11").

#### 241. `holy grail`

- Kind: noun phrase. Banned forms: `holy grail`, `Holy Grail`.
- Why it reads as machine text: The phrase names a goal everyone wants and nobody reaches, and models use it for layout problems, metrics and products (`the holy grail of productivity`). It treats a problem with known partial answers as mythical, which hides the approaches that already exist. In CSS writing it is also a real layout name, which models then stretch to cover anything.
- Where it shows up: tech blogs, product marketing, research summaries.

```slop
Zero-downtime deploys are the holy grail of DevOps.
Finding product-market fit is the holy grail for every startup.
Inbox zero, the holy grail of productivity, is finally within reach.
```

Replace with:

- "hard goal" or "long-standing goal", with why it is hard.
- The existing approaches and their limits.
- "ideal" for a target state, followed by how close you are.
- Cut it when the topic is a known technique with documentation.

Rewrites:

```slop
Zero-downtime deploys are the holy grail of DevOps.
```

After: Zero-downtime deploys need blue-green or rolling releases, plus database migrations that work with both the old and the new code.

```slop
Finding product-market fit is the holy grail for every startup.
```

After: One common test for product-market fit is whether 40% of surveyed users say they would be very disappointed to lose the product.

```slop
Inbox zero, the holy grail of productivity, is finally within reach.
```

After: The app files newsletters and receipts into folders, so most people's inbox drops below 20 messages.

- Literal use: for the CSS pattern, write `holy grail layout` in inline code or "three-column layout with header and footer"; for the Arthurian object, write "the Grail".

#### 242. `silver bullet`

- Kind: noun phrase. Banned forms: `silver bullet`, `silver bullets`.
- Why it reads as machine text: Models write `there is no silver bullet` as a reflex hedge, and `a silver bullet for X` as a claim to deny or, in marketing, to make. The phrase comes from Fred Brooks's 1986 essay, which lends it borrowed authority. Both uses are filler: the denial hides which partial fixes help, and the claim is never true.
- Where it shows up: closing paragraphs of advice posts, architecture debates, vendor pitches.

```slop
There is no silver bullet for technical debt.
Microservices are not a silver bullet.
Our platform is the silver bullet for slow page loads.
```

Replace with:

- "no single fix", then the 2 or 3 fixes that do help.
- The trade-off: "microservices add network calls and deploy overhead".
- For a product claim, the measured result on a stated workload.
- Cut it when the hedge closes a paragraph that already listed the options.

Rewrites:

```slop
There is no silver bullet for technical debt.
```

After: Technical debt shrinks when teams budget 20% of each sprint for it and delete dead code first.

```slop
Microservices are not a silver bullet.
```

After: Microservices let each team deploy alone, at the cost of network calls, distributed tracing and more on-call work.

```slop
Our platform is the silver bullet for slow page loads.
```

After: On our test set of 50 store pages, the CDN cut median load time from 3.1 s to 1.4 s.

- Literal use: when citing Brooks, give the essay title in inline code, `No Silver Bullet` (1986); for werewolf folklore, put `silver bullet` in inline code.

#### 243. `low-hanging fruit`

- Kind: noun phrase. Banned forms: `low-hanging fruit`, `low hanging fruit`.
- Why it reads as machine text: The phrase is the stock consultant's term for easy wins, and models put it at the top of every improvement plan. It suggests low effort and high payoff without measuring either. It also implies the list was ranked, when it usually was not.
- Where it shows up: audit reports, roadmap docs, performance and SEO advice.

```slop
Let's start with the low-hanging fruit: image compression and caching.
There's plenty of low-hanging fruit in our onboarding flow.
Fixing alt text is low-hanging fruit for accessibility.
```

Replace with:

- "quick fixes" or "easy changes", with time estimates.
- A table with the change, the effort in hours and the expected gain.
- "Start with", plus the item and its numbers.
- Cut it when the list that follows already shows effort and gain.

Rewrites:

```slop
Let's start with the low-hanging fruit: image compression and caching.
```

After: Start with image compression (1 day, about 400 KB less per page) and cache headers (2 hours).

```slop
There's plenty of low-hanging fruit in our onboarding flow.
```

After: Three onboarding changes take under a day each: drop the team-size question, prefill the workspace name, and remove the second email check.

```slop
Fixing alt text is low-hanging fruit for accessibility.
```

After: Adding alt text to the 38 product images takes an afternoon and clears our largest group of audit failures.

- Literal use: for fruit on a low branch, write "fruit within reach" or "the lower branches".

#### 244. `best practices`

- Kind: noun phrase. Banned forms: `best practices`. The singular `best practice` passes the linter but has the same problem.
- Why it reads as machine text: Models write `follow best practices` when they do not know the practice or do not want to state it. It is the most common empty instruction in generated code reviews and READMEs. It claims a consensus that rarely exists and hides which source, version or team agreed on it.
- Where it shows up: code review comments, README and contributing guides, security and SEO advice.

```slop
Make sure to follow best practices when handling user input.
This template follows industry best practices for accessibility.
We adhere to security best practices at every layer.
```

Replace with:

- The rule itself: "parameterize every SQL query".
- The source: "meets WCAG 2.2 AA", "passes OWASP ASVS level 2".
- "conventions" for team or language norms, with a link.
- Cut it when the list that follows states the rules.

Rewrites:

```slop
Make sure to follow best practices when handling user input.
```

After: Escape user input in templates, and pass it to SQL only as bound parameters.

```slop
This template follows industry best practices for accessibility.
```

After: The template meets WCAG 2.2 AA: 4.5:1 text contrast, visible focus rings, and a label on every input.

```slop
We adhere to security best practices at every layer.
```

After: We encrypt data at rest with AES-256, require SSO for staff, and rotate keys every 90 days.

- Literal use: when citing a published document with the phrase in its title, put the title in inline code.

#### 245. `thought leader`

- Kind: noun phrase. Banned forms: `thought leader`, `thought leaders`. `thought leadership` has its own entry.
- Why it reads as machine text: `thought leader` is a self-awarded title from conference and LinkedIn culture, and models give it to anyone with a blog. It claims influence without naming what the person thought or who followed. Many readers now take it as a mild insult, so it works against the person it praises.
- Where it shows up: speaker bios, press releases, LinkedIn summaries.

```slop
Dana is a recognized thought leader in product design.
Hear from top thought leaders in AI.
We position our CEO as a thought leader in fintech.
```

Replace with:

- The person's job and work: "head of design at X, author of Y".
- "expert", only with the evidence next to it: books, papers, systems built.
- "speaker" for event lineups, with the talk title.
- Cut it when the bio already lists the work.

Rewrites:

```slop
Dana is a recognized thought leader in product design.
```

After: Dana led design at a payroll company for 8 years and wrote a book on form design.

```slop
Hear from top thought leaders in AI.
```

After: Hear talks from 12 researchers who build and evaluate language models.

```slop
We position our CEO as a thought leader in fintech.
```

After: Our CEO publishes a monthly report on card fraud rates across our 3,000 merchants.

- Literal use: the phrase has no literal sense; describe the person's work.

#### 246. `thought leadership`

- Kind: noun phrase. Banned forms: `thought leadership`.
- Why it reads as machine text: Marketing teams file their blog posts and white papers under `thought leadership content`, and models repeat the label as if it were a genre. It names content by the status it hopes to earn, not by what it says. It hides the format (report, essay, talk) and the topic.
- Where it shows up: marketing plans, agency service pages, content calendars.

```slop
We publish thought leadership on the future of work.
Our thought leadership content drives brand awareness.
Download our latest thought leadership report.
```

Replace with:

- The format: "essay", "report", "research", "talk".
- The topic and the data source.
- "articles by our staff" for a company blog.
- Cut it when the title of the piece already tells the reader what it is.

Rewrites:

```slop
We publish thought leadership on the future of work.
```

After: We publish a quarterly report on remote hiring, based on 8,000 job posts.

```slop
Our thought leadership content drives brand awareness.
```

After: Our engineers write two posts a month about running Postgres at scale; those posts bring in about 30% of trial signups.

```slop
Download our latest thought leadership report.
```

After: Download the 2025 report on checkout abandonment across 400 online stores.

- Literal use: the phrase has no literal sense; name the format and the topic.

#### 247. `value proposition`

- Kind: noun phrase. Banned forms: `value proposition`, `value propositions`, `value prop`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `value proposition` is MBA vocabulary that models bring into every piece of landing-page and pitch advice. Writers then talk about the term instead of stating the offer. The term belongs in an internal planning doc at most; in text a customer reads, it is a sign the actual offer was never written down.
- Where it shows up: pitch decks, landing page briefs, product marketing docs.

```slop
Our value proposition is simple: we save you time.
The new pricing strengthens our value proposition for small teams.
Make sure your hero section communicates a clear value proposition.
```

Replace with:

- The offer: what the customer gets, at what price, in how much time.
- "why customers buy" in internal docs, followed by the reasons heard on sales calls.
- "offer" or "pitch" when you need a noun.
- Cut it when the next sentence states the offer.

Rewrites:

```slop
Our value proposition is simple: we save you time.
```

After: Payroll for 10 people takes 5 minutes a month and costs $8 per person.

```slop
The new pricing strengthens our value proposition for small teams.
```

After: Teams under 10 people now pay nothing for the first year.

```slop
Make sure your hero section communicates a clear value proposition.
```

After: Make the hero headline say what the product does and for whom, such as "Payroll for restaurants, filed in 5 minutes".

- Literal use: in a marketing framework document that defines the term, put `value proposition` in inline code.

#### 248. `bandwidth`

- Kind: noun. Banned forms: `bandwidth`, `bandwidths`.
- Why it reads as machine text: Models use `bandwidth` for a person's time or attention: `I don't have the bandwidth`, `free up bandwidth`. It borrows a network term to make a scheduling problem sound technical. It hides the actual constraint, hours in a week or people on a team, and it makes a refusal vaguer than it needs to be.
- Where it shows up: Slack messages and emails, staffing memos, project plans.

```slop
I don't have the bandwidth to take this on right now.
Hiring a contractor will free up bandwidth for the core team.
Our team has limited bandwidth this quarter.
```

Replace with:

- "time", with hours: "I have 4 free hours this week".
- "capacity" for teams, with headcount or points.
- A plain "no" or "not before", with a date.
- Cut it when the refusal works without a reason.

Rewrites:

```slop
I don't have the bandwidth to take this on right now.
```

After: I can't take this before the 20th; the release needs all my time until then.

```slop
Hiring a contractor will free up bandwidth for the core team.
```

After: The contractor will handle billing support, which gives the 3 core engineers back about 10 hours a week.

```slop
Our team has limited bandwidth this quarter.
```

After: Two of our five engineers are on the migration until March, so we will take on one new feature this quarter.

- Literal use: for network capacity, write "throughput" or give the figure in Mbps or Gbps; in signal processing, give the range in Hz.

#### 249. `touchpoint`

- Kind: noun. Banned forms: `touchpoint`, `touchpoints`, `touch point`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `touchpoint` comes from customer-experience consulting, where it means any moment a customer meets the brand. Models use it to make a list of emails, screens and calls sound like a planned system. It hides which channel and which moment, which are exactly what a designer or writer needs to know.
- Where it shows up: CX strategy docs, marketing plans, customer flow maps.

```slop
We optimize every touchpoint across the customer journey.
Email remains a key touchpoint for retention.
Each touchpoint should reflect our brand values.
```

Replace with:

- The channel and the moment: "the welcome email", "the cancel screen", "the renewal call".
- "step" for a flow, numbered.
- "contact" for support conversations.
- Cut it when the list of screens or emails already exists.

Rewrites:

```slop
We optimize every touchpoint across the customer journey.
```

After: We tested the signup page, the welcome email and the first-invoice screen, and rewrote the copy on all three.

```slop
Email remains a key touchpoint for retention.
```

After: The renewal reminder, sent 14 days before the term ends, brings back 1 in 5 lapsed customers.

```slop
Each touchpoint should reflect our brand values.
```

After: The receipt, the shipping email and the return label use the same typeface, logo and tone.

- Literal use: the word has no literal sense in product work; name the screen, email or call.

#### 250. `narrative`

- Kind: noun, also an adjective. Banned forms: `narrative`, `narratives`.
- Why it reads as machine text: Models use `narrative` for any story, message or explanation, and `control the narrative` or `the narrative around X` for public opinion. It borrows the tone of media studies and turns a set of claims into one shape without stating the claims. In product writing, `our narrative` usually means a message nobody has written down.
- Where it shows up: PR and communications plans, essays on public debate, launch docs.

```slop
We need to own the narrative around the outage.
The deck tells a compelling narrative about our growth.
This challenges the dominant narrative about remote work.
```

Replace with:

- "story" for a sequence of events.
- "explanation", "account" or "message", with the content stated.
- "the common view that", followed by the view.
- Cut it when you can write the claims themselves.

Rewrites:

```slop
We need to own the narrative around the outage.
```

After: Publish the outage timeline and root cause within 24 hours, before others guess at them.

```slop
The deck tells a compelling narrative about our growth.
```

After: The deck shows revenue growing from $1M to $6M in two years and names the 3 deals behind it.

```slop
This challenges the dominant narrative about remote work.
```

After: Most coverage says remote teams ship slower; our data from 200 teams shows no difference in cycle time.

- Literal use: for a form section with that title, such as a grant application or police report, put `Narrative` in inline code or write "written account".

#### 251. `storytelling`

- Kind: noun. Banned forms: `storytelling`, `storyteller`, `storytellers`.
- Why it reads as machine text: Models apply `storytelling` to any communication with a beginning and an end: `data storytelling`, `brand storytelling`, `visual storytelling`. It promises emotional pull and hides the plain task, which is usually "explain this chart" or "write the about page". It turns ordinary writing advice into a branded skill.
- Where it shows up: data visualization advice, brand guidelines, design conference talks.

```slop
Great dashboards are all about data storytelling.
Our brand storytelling brings our values to life.
Use visual storytelling to guide users through onboarding.
```

Replace with:

- "explain", "show" or "write", plus the object.
- For charts, the one finding the chart must show, placed in its title.
- "sequence" or "order of steps" for onboarding.
- Cut it when the method described is just writing.

Rewrites:

```slop
Great dashboards are all about data storytelling.
```

After: Give each dashboard chart a title that states its finding, such as "Refunds doubled after the March price change".

```slop
Our brand storytelling brings our values to life.
```

After: The about page says who founded the company, why, and what it has made since 2015.

```slop
Use visual storytelling to guide users through onboarding.
```

After: Onboarding shows one screen per step, 4 steps in total, each with one illustration and one sentence.

- Literal use: for the oral craft or performance, write "telling stories" or put `storytelling` in inline code.

#### 252. `passion`

- Kind: noun. Banned forms: `passion`, `passions`, and avoid `passionate` for the same reason.
- Why it reads as machine text: `passion` is the default way models express commitment: `our passion for quality`, `passionate about`. Every company and every candidate claims it, so it tells the reader nothing about this team. It replaces evidence of care, such as hours spent or details fixed, with a feeling.
- Where it shows up: about pages, cover letters and bios, job ads.

```slop
Our passion for design drives everything we do.
I have a deep passion for clean code.
Join a team with a passion for innovation.
```

Replace with:

- What the person or team has done that shows care: hours, projects, details.
- "interest" or "focus" when a neutral noun is needed.
- "I like" or "I care about" in personal writing, followed by an example.
- Cut it when the sentence states a feeling and nothing else.

Rewrites:

```slop
Our passion for design drives everything we do.
```

After: We test every screen at 320px wide and with a screen reader before release.

```slop
I have a deep passion for clean code.
```

After: I maintain two open source linters and have reviewed about 600 pull requests on them.

```slop
Join a team with a passion for innovation.
```

After: The team ships to production about 30 times a week and joins a customer call every Friday.

- Literal use: for the fruit, write "maracuja" or put `passion fruit` in inline code; in art history or theology, put `Passion` in inline code.

#### 253. `endeavor`

- Kind: noun and verb. Banned forms: `endeavor`, `endeavors`, `endeavored`, `endeavoring`, and the British `endeavour`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `endeavor` is a formal word for "try" or "project" that models use to sound earnest, above all in sign-offs (`best of luck in your future endeavors`). As a noun it inflates ordinary work into a grand attempt and hides what the work is. As a verb (`we endeavor to`) it hedges a promise the writer could make or decline.
- Where it shows up: email closings, mission statements, cover letters.

```slop
Best of luck in all your future endeavors.
We endeavor to respond to every inquiry within 24 hours.
Building a startup is a challenging endeavor.
```

Replace with:

- "try" or "aim" for the verb, and drop it entirely when you can promise.
- "project", "work" or "job" for the noun.
- The next thing, named: "good luck at the clinic".
- Cut it when the sentence is a sign-off; end the email on the last useful line.

Rewrites:

```slop
Best of luck in all your future endeavors.
```

After: Good luck with the new job at the clinic.

```slop
We endeavor to respond to every inquiry within 24 hours.
```

After: We reply to every email within 24 hours on weekdays.

```slop
Building a startup is a challenging endeavor.
```

After: Starting a company means raising money, hiring and selling, often in the same week.

- Literal use: for the Space Shuttle or the ship, write `Endeavour` in inline code.

#### 254. `harmony`

- Kind: noun. Banned forms: `harmony`, `harmonies`. The adjective `harmonious` has its own entry.
- Why it reads as machine text: Models use `harmony` for things that fit together and for calm among people. In design writing, `visual harmony` and `color harmony` stand in for actual rules about spacing, scale and contrast. The word names a good feeling about the result and hides how it was reached.
- Where it shows up: design system docs, color and type advice, team culture copy.

```slop
The palette creates visual harmony across the interface.
Our tools work in harmony with your existing stack.
We believe in harmony between work and life.
```

Replace with:

- The rule: "one accent color, used only for primary actions".
- "consistent", with what is consistent: the spacing scale, the type scale.
- "works with", plus the named tools.
- Cut it when the sentence is about mood; state the policy instead.

Rewrites:

```slop
The palette creates visual harmony across the interface.
```

After: The palette has one accent, `#B4441C`, used only for primary buttons and links; everything else is ink on paper.

```slop
Our tools work in harmony with your existing stack.
```

After: The CLI reads your existing `package.json` scripts and `.env` files; nothing has to move.

```slop
We believe in harmony between work and life.
```

After: No meetings after 4 pm, and every on-call week ends with a day off.

- Literal use: in music theory, name the chords or intervals, or put `harmony` in inline code; for color schemes, name the scheme ("complementary", "analogous").

#### 255. `essence`

- Kind: noun. Banned forms: `essence`, `essences`.
- Why it reads as machine text: Models write `the essence of X` or `capture the essence` to sound as if they reduced something to its center without doing the reduction. It appears in summaries and in brand copy for products and places. It hides the actual property, which is what the reader came for.
- Where it shows up: brand and travel copy, summaries, design critique.

```slop
Our logo captures the essence of the brand.
The essence of good design is simplicity.
This dish captures the essence of Tuscan cooking.
```

Replace with:

- The property: "the logo is a single line drawing of a bridge".
- "main point" or "core idea" when summarizing, then the idea itself.
- The features that make it typical: ingredients, methods, materials.
- Cut it when the next sentence states the property; start there.

Rewrites:

```slop
Our logo captures the essence of the brand.
```

After: The logo is a single-weight line drawing of the Tyne Bridge, set beside the name in IBM Plex Sans.

```slop
The essence of good design is simplicity.
```

After: A good form asks only for the data the next step needs; ours went from 14 fields to 6.

```slop
This dish captures the essence of Tuscan cooking.
```

After: The soup uses stale bread, white beans, kale and olive oil, as Tuscan farm cooks made it.

- Literal use: for a plant oil or flavoring, write "extract" or "oil" ("vanilla extract", "rose oil").

#### 256. `forefront`

- Kind: noun. Banned forms: `forefront`. The phrase `at the forefront` has its own entry.
- Why it reads as machine text: `at the forefront of` is a stock claim of leadership that models attach to any company on an about page. It asserts rank without a source or a comparison. The word also appears in `bring to the forefront`, a padded way to say "make visible".
- Where it shows up: about pages, press releases, research center descriptions.

```slop
We are at the forefront of sustainable fashion.
The pandemic brought remote work to the forefront.
Our lab is at the forefront of quantum research.
```

Replace with:

- The evidence: what you did first, papers, patents, market share.
- "led" or "first", with the date.
- "made common" or "made visible" for the "bring to" form.
- Cut it when there is no evidence of rank.

Rewrites:

```slop
We are at the forefront of sustainable fashion.
```

After: Since 2021, 80% of our fabric has been recycled cotton or deadstock.

```slop
The pandemic brought remote work to the forefront.
```

After: In 2020, the share of our staff working from home went from 5% to 90%.

```slop
Our lab is at the forefront of quantum research.
```

After: The lab has published 40 papers on error correction since 2019 and runs a 72-qubit device.

- Literal use: for the front of a group or object, write "front".

#### 257. `cusp`

- Kind: noun. Banned forms: `cusp`, `cusps`. The phrase `on the cusp` has its own entry.
- Why it reads as machine text: Models write `on the cusp of` to announce that something is about to happen, which lets them make a prediction with no date. It is common in trend pieces and launch posts (`on the cusp of a new era`). The word's exact meaning in geometry and dentistry lends the prose a precision it does not have.
- Where it shows up: trend articles, investor updates, launch announcements.

```slop
We are on the cusp of a new era in personal computing.
The company is on the cusp of profitability.
Quantum computing sits on the cusp of mainstream adoption.
```

Replace with:

- "about to" or "close to", with the date or the gap.
- The current number and the threshold: "$40k a month short of break-even".
- "expected in", plus a quarter and a source.
- Cut it when there is no date or number; the claim is a guess.

Rewrites:

```slop
We are on the cusp of a new era in personal computing.
```

After: Three phone makers plan to ship on-device assistants in the second half of 2025.

```slop
The company is on the cusp of profitability.
```

After: The company expects to break even in Q3, when monthly revenue passes $2.1M.

```slop
Quantum computing sits on the cusp of mainstream adoption.
```

After: Several cloud providers rent quantum hardware today; few companies run production work on it.

- Literal use: in geometry or dentistry, put `cusp` in inline code ("the `cusp` of a molar"); in astrology, write "the border between two signs".

#### 258. `crossroads`

- Kind: noun. Banned forms: `crossroads`, and the phrase `at a crossroads`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `at a crossroads` lets a model dramatize a decision without describing the options. It is common in opinion essays and in company updates written before a change. It hides the choice, the trade-offs and the deadline, which are the three things a reader of a decision needs.
- Where it shows up: opinion essays, all-hands notes, industry analysis.

```slop
The web is at a crossroads.
Our company stands at a crossroads.
Open source finds itself at a crossroads between community and commerce.
```

Replace with:

- "has to choose between X and Y", with both options named.
- "decision", plus the date it must be made.
- A table of the options with their costs.
- Cut it when the following paragraph lists the options; start there.

Rewrites:

```slop
The web is at a crossroads.
```

After: Browser makers disagree on third-party cookies; Safari and Firefox block them by default, and Chrome does not.

```slop
Our company stands at a crossroads.
```

After: By June we must decide whether to raise a Series B or cut costs to break even on current revenue.

```slop
Open source finds itself at a crossroads between community and commerce.
```

After: Maintainers of popular projects choose between staying unpaid, charging for hosting, or changing the license, as Redis did in 2024.

- Literal use: for a road junction, write "junction" or "intersection".

#### 259. `underpinning`

- Kind: noun. Banned forms: `underpinning`, `underpinnings`. The verb `underpin` has its own entry.
- Why it reads as machine text: `the underpinnings of` is a model's phrase for the theory or structure behind something. It sounds rigorous, like an engineering drawing, and then usually introduces a summary at a basic level. It hides which ideas or components the writer means.
- Where it shows up: explainer intros, academic-style essays, architecture overviews.

```slop
This chapter explores the theoretical underpinnings of reinforcement learning.
The technical underpinnings of the platform are built on Kubernetes.
Understanding the psychological underpinnings of habit formation helps designers.
```

Replace with:

- "basis", "theory" or "foundations" for ideas, then name them.
- "runs on" or "is built from" for systems, with the component list.
- "causes" or "reasons" for behavior.
- Cut it when the next sentence names the theory.

Rewrites:

```slop
This chapter explores the theoretical underpinnings of reinforcement learning.
```

After: This chapter covers Markov decision processes, the Bellman equation and policy gradients.

```slop
The technical underpinnings of the platform are built on Kubernetes.
```

After: The platform runs on Kubernetes 1.30, with Postgres for state and NATS for messages.

```slop
Understanding the psychological underpinnings of habit formation helps designers.
```

After: Habits form when a cue, an action and a reward repeat in the same order; designers control where the cue appears.

- Literal use: in a construction spec for supporting a foundation, put `underpinning` in inline code or write "foundation support".

#### 260. `arsenal`

- Kind: noun. Banned forms: `arsenal`, `arsenals`.
- Why it reads as machine text: Models label a set of tools, features or skills `arsenal` to make it sound strong and ready. It pulls in a military register that almost no product needs. It hides the count and the contents, and it often comes right before a vague list.
- Where it shows up: tool roundups, feature pages, career advice.

```slop
Add this tool to your design arsenal.
Our platform gives marketers a full arsenal of analytics features.
A good debugger is the most important weapon in your arsenal.
```

Replace with:

- "toolkit" or "set of tools", only with the list.
- The tools, named, with what each does.
- "features", with a count.
- Cut it when the noun before it already says what the thing is.

Rewrites:

```slop
Add this tool to your design arsenal.
```

After: This plugin exports Figma frames as SVG files named to match your component files.

```slop
Our platform gives marketers a full arsenal of analytics features.
```

After: Marketers get funnels, cohort charts and A/B test results on one page.

```slop
A good debugger is the most important weapon in your arsenal.
```

After: Learn to set breakpoints and step through code; it finds most bugs faster than print statements.

- Literal use: for a weapons store, write "armory"; for the football club, write `Arsenal` in inline code.

#### 261. `blueprint`

- Kind: noun. Banned forms: `blueprint`, `blueprints`.
- Why it reads as machine text: Models put the label `blueprint` on any plan, template or guide, borrowing the authority of architects' drawings. `a blueprint for success` is a fixed model phrase. It hides whether the reader is getting a checklist, a template or an essay.
- Where it shows up: guide titles, strategy docs, template marketplaces.

```slop
Download our blueprint for scaling your SaaS to $10M ARR.
This article provides a blueprint for building accessible forms.
Our 2025 roadmap is a blueprint for growth.
```

Replace with:

- "plan", "template", "checklist" or "guide", whichever it is.
- "spec" or "design doc" in engineering.
- The steps themselves.
- Cut it when the title can name the content.

Rewrites:

```slop
Download our blueprint for scaling your SaaS to $10M ARR.
```

After: Download the checklist of 12 steps we took from $1M to $10M ARR.

```slop
This article provides a blueprint for building accessible forms.
```

After: This article gives a form template with labels, error text and a tested focus order.

```slop
Our 2025 roadmap is a blueprint for growth.
```

After: The 2025 roadmap has 4 projects, each with a target and an owner.

- Literal use: for an architect's print, write "drawing" or "floor plan"; for Unreal Engine, write `Blueprint` in inline code.

#### 262. `solution`

- Kind: noun. Banned forms: `solution`, `solutions`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `solution` is the default noun in B2B copy for any product, and models carry it everywhere: `our solution`, `end-to-end solutions`, `the solution for teams`. It avoids saying what the product is: a database, an app, a service. In technical answers, `Here's a solution` adds nothing before the code.
- Where it shows up: B2B landing pages, sales emails, model answers to coding questions.

```slop
Our all-in-one solution helps teams collaborate better.
We provide enterprise solutions for supply chain management.
Here's a solution that should fix your issue.
```

Replace with:

- The product type: "app", "API", "database", "service", "plugin".
- "fix", "answer" or "workaround" in support and code answers.
- "way" when you mean a method: "one way to do this is".
- Cut it when the code or steps follow directly; start with them.

Rewrites:

```slop
Our all-in-one solution helps teams collaborate better.
```

After: A shared inbox app for support teams, with assignments and internal notes.

```slop
We provide enterprise solutions for supply chain management.
```

After: We sell inventory and shipping software to warehouses with 50 to 500 staff.

```slop
Here's a solution that should fix your issue.
```

After: Set `"moduleResolution": "bundler"` in `tsconfig.json`, and the import error goes away.

- Literal use: in chemistry, give the mix ("0.9% saline") or put `solution` in inline code; for a Visual Studio project file, write `.sln` in inline code; in math, write "answer" or give the value.

#### 263. `innovation`

- Kind: noun. Banned forms: `innovation`, `innovations`. The adjective `innovative` has its own entry.
- Why it reads as machine text: `innovation` is the most common abstract noun in corporate and model-written copy: `driving innovation`, `a culture of innovation`, `innovation hub`. It claims newness without naming any new thing. Readers have seen it on every about page, so it carries no weight.
- Where it shows up: about pages, job ads, R&D and government announcements.

```slop
We foster a culture of innovation across every team.
The new campus will serve as a hub for innovation.
Innovation is in our DNA.
```

Replace with:

- The new thing, named: product, method or patent, with a date.
- "new", "first" or "change" when a plain word works.
- "research" for R&D, with the budget or headcount.
- Cut it when the sentence contains no new thing.

Rewrites:

```slop
We foster a culture of innovation across every team.
```

After: Every engineer gets one day every two weeks for their own projects; 3 of our current products started that way.

```slop
The new campus will serve as a hub for innovation.
```

After: The new campus houses 400 researchers working on battery chemistry and grid storage.

```slop
Innovation is in our DNA.
```

After: We have filed 22 patents since 2018, most of them on low-power radio.

- Literal use: in economics papers that measure it, write "new products and processes" or put `innovation` in inline code.

#### 264. `engagement`

- Kind: noun. Banned forms: `engagement`, `engagements`. The adjective `engaging` has its own entry.
- Why it reads as machine text: `engagement` is the metric word models use for any user activity, and `drive engagement` is a top phrase in product and marketing text. It hides what users actually do: click, reply, return, pay. It also lets teams count attention-grabbing features as success.
- Where it shows up: product metric docs, social media reports, HR surveys (`employee engagement`).

```slop
The redesign increased engagement by 40%.
Push notifications are a great way to boost engagement.
We measure employee engagement every quarter.
```

Replace with:

- The action counted: "daily active users", "replies per post", "sessions per week".
- "use" or "activity" in a general sense, with the metric next to it.
- For staff surveys, the questions or the score.
- Cut it when there is no metric; the sentence is a slogan.

Rewrites:

```slop
The redesign increased engagement by 40%.
```

After: After the redesign, the share of users who return within 7 days rose from 30% to 42%.

```slop
Push notifications are a great way to boost engagement.
```

After: Users who turn on the weekly digest email open the app on 2 more days a month.

```slop
We measure employee engagement every quarter.
```

After: Each quarter, staff rate 12 statements such as "I know what is expected of me" on a 1 to 5 scale.

- Literal use: for a betrothal, write "engaged" or "betrothal"; for a speaking slot, write "booking"; for combat, write "battle"; for gears, put `engagement` in inline code.

#### 265. `delight`

- Kind: noun and verb. Banned forms: `delight`, `delights`, `delighted`, `delighting`. The adjective `delightful` has its own entry.
- Why it reads as machine text: `Delight your users` and `moments of delight` come from 2010s product design culture, and models repeat them as a goal for every feature. The word aims at a feeling nobody measures and hides the usual case, in which the user wants the task to finish. It also justifies confetti and bouncy animation over speed.
- Where it shows up: product principles, design critiques, marketing copy.

```slop
Small animations add moments of delight to the experience.
We're obsessed with delighting our customers.
You'll be delighted by how easy setup is.
```

Replace with:

- The task outcome: "the export finishes in 3 seconds".
- "pleased", "glad" or "happy" in personal messages, when the feeling is real.
- The detail users notice: "the form keeps your input after an error".
- Cut it when the sentence promises the reader a feeling.

Rewrites:

```slop
Small animations add moments of delight to the experience.
```

After: The save button confirms in place within 100 ms, with a 120 ms fade and no other animation.

```slop
We're obsessed with delighting our customers.
```

After: We reply to every support email within 4 business hours and call every customer who cancels.

```slop
You'll be delighted by how easy setup is.
```

After: Setup takes 3 steps: connect GitHub, pick a repo, and press deploy.

- Literal use: for the sweet, write "lokum" or put `Turkish delight` in inline code.

#### 266. `magic`

- Kind: noun, also used as an adjective. Banned forms: `magic`, `magics`. The adjective `magical` has its own entry.
- Why it reads as machine text: Models attach `magic` to any automated step: `let the magic happen`, `like magic`, `AI magic`. The word hides the mechanism, which is the one thing a technical reader needs in order to trust the output and debug it. It also signals that the writer may not know how the thing works.
- Where it shows up: copy for AI features, onboarding screens, docs that skip the mechanism.

```slop
Just upload your CSV and let the magic happen.
Our AI works its magic on your photos.
Here's where the magic happens: the build() function.
```

Replace with:

- What happens, step by step: "we detect column types, then match them to your fields".
- "automatically", with what is automatic.
- The function or model, named, with its limits.
- Cut it when the next sentence explains the mechanism.

Rewrites:

```slop
Just upload your CSV and let the magic happen.
```

After: Upload a CSV; we detect column types from the first 100 rows, match them to your fields, and ask you to confirm.

```slop
Our AI works its magic on your photos.
```

After: The model removes noise and corrects exposure; it does not change faces or add objects.

```slop
Here's where the magic happens: the build() function.
```

After: The `build()` function reads the config, compiles each page, and writes the output to `dist/`.

- Literal use: for stage acts, write "conjuring" or "illusion"; in code, write `magic number`, `magic bytes` or `__magic__` in inline code; for the card game, write `Magic: The Gathering` in inline code.

#### 267. `wow factor`

- Kind: noun phrase. Banned forms: `wow factor`, `wow-factor`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `wow factor` is a model's way to praise a visual effect or a demo without saying what it does. It shows up in design advice (`add a wow factor to your hero`) that leads to gradients, glows and parallax. It ranks first impression above use and gives no detail anyone can check.
- Where it shows up: design feedback, real estate and event copy, pitch advice.

```slop
Add some wow factor to your landing page with a 3D hero.
The kitchen has serious wow factor.
Our demo needs more wow factor for the investor meeting.
```

Replace with:

- The feature that draws attention: the size, the material, the result shown.
- "first impression" when that is the point, with what the viewer sees in the first 5 seconds.
- For demos, the result the buyer wants, shown with real data.
- Cut it when the advice would add decoration; drop the effect as well.

Rewrites:

```slop
Add some wow factor to your landing page with a 3D hero.
```

After: Put a 5-second screen recording of the product at the top of the landing page.

```slop
The kitchen has serious wow factor.
```

After: The kitchen has a 4-meter marble island and a window over the garden.

```slop
Our demo needs more wow factor for the investor meeting.
```

After: Open the investor demo with a real customer's dashboard and their 30% drop in costs.

- Literal use: the phrase has no literal sense; describe what produces the reaction.

#### 268. `prowess`

- Kind: noun. Banned forms: `prowess`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `prowess` is an old word for skill in battle, and models use it to praise technical or athletic skill in a grand tone: `engineering prowess`, `culinary prowess`. It names a level of skill without showing a single result. It is common in bios and in sentences about a company's strength.
- Where it shows up: bios, press releases, sports and food writing.

```slop
The team's engineering prowess is evident in every release.
Showcase your design prowess with a standout portfolio.
Her culinary prowess earned her a loyal following.
```

Replace with:

- "skill", plus the evidence.
- The result: release count, defect rate, awards.
- The specific craft: "she cures her own ham".
- Cut it when the evidence is already in the next sentence.

Rewrites:

```slop
The team's engineering prowess is evident in every release.
```

After: The team ships every two weeks, and the last 20 releases needed no rollback.

```slop
Showcase your design prowess with a standout portfolio.
```

After: Show 3 projects in your portfolio, each with the problem, your sketches and the result.

```slop
Her culinary prowess earned her a loyal following.
```

After: She bakes 200 loaves a day, and the bakery sells out by 10 am.

- Literal use: in historical writing about combat, write "skill at arms" or put `prowess` in inline code.

#### 269. `excellence`

- Kind: noun. Banned forms: `excellence`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `excellence` is the abstract noun on every values page (`committed to excellence`, `center of excellence`). Models produce it whenever asked for company values or a mission statement. It claims quality without a standard to measure it against, so no reader can check it.
- Where it shows up: values pages, award names, internal team names.

```slop
We are committed to excellence in everything we do.
Our Center of Excellence drives best practices across the org.
Excellence is not an act but a habit.
```

Replace with:

- The standard: "every PR gets two reviews", "99.9% uptime".
- "quality", with a measure next to it.
- For team names, what the team does: "the platform team", "the design systems group".
- Cut it when the sentence is a value with no standard.

Rewrites:

```slop
We are committed to excellence in everything we do.
```

After: Every change gets two reviews, and we publish our uptime and incident reports.

```slop
Our Center of Excellence drives best practices across the org.
```

After: The platform team writes the shared CI templates and reviews each new service before launch.

```slop
Excellence is not an act but a habit.
```

After: Delete the quote; it is Will Durant's paraphrase of Aristotle, and it says nothing about your team.

- Literal use: for an award or institution with the word in its name, put the name in inline code.

#### 270. `transformation`

- Kind: noun. Banned forms: `transformation`, `transformations`. The adjective `transformative` has its own entry.
- Why it reads as machine text: `transformation` is consulting vocabulary (`digital transformation`, `business transformation`) that models use for any change larger than a bug fix. It claims a total change of form while hiding what changed and by how much. Most projects given the label are migrations or reorganizations.
- Where it shows up: consulting pages, annual reports, case studies.

```slop
We guide enterprises through digital transformation.
The redesign was a complete transformation of the user experience.
Our transformation journey began in 2020.
```

Replace with:

- "migration", "rewrite", "redesign" or "reorganization", whichever it was.
- Before and after numbers.
- "change" when a plain noun is enough.
- Cut it when the sentence only announces change; list the changes.

Rewrites:

```slop
We guide enterprises through digital transformation.
```

After: We move companies off on-premise ERP systems to cloud accounting, usually in 6 to 9 months.

```slop
The redesign was a complete transformation of the user experience.
```

After: The redesign cut checkout from 5 screens to 2 and halved the number of support tickets about payment.

```slop
Our transformation journey began in 2020.
```

After: In 2020 we moved our 30 internal apps to one cloud provider and closed both data centers.

- Literal use: for data, geometry or CSS, name the operation (`transform: rotate(45deg)`, "ETL step", "matrix multiplication") or put `transformation` in inline code.

#### 271. `masterpiece`

- Kind: noun. Banned forms: `masterpiece`, `masterpieces`.
- Why it reads as machine text: Models give the label `masterpiece` to well-made things in reviews, product copy and even code review (`a masterpiece of engineering`). It is the highest possible rating applied to ordinary work, so it reads as flattery. It hides what is good about the work.
- Where it shows up: product reviews, portfolio copy, praise in pull request comments.

```slop
This watch is a masterpiece of Swiss engineering.
Your refactor is a masterpiece.
The new campus is an architectural masterpiece.
```

Replace with:

- The qualities, named: precision, materials, measured performance.
- "well made" or "good", with the reason.
- In code review, the specific change you liked and why.
- Cut it when the praise has no reason.

Rewrites:

```slop
This watch is a masterpiece of Swiss engineering.
```

After: The watch movement keeps time within 2 seconds a day and has 28 jewels.

```slop
Your refactor is a masterpiece.
```

After: Splitting `parseOrder` into 3 functions made the tests readable, and the error cases are now covered.

```slop
The new campus is an architectural masterpiece.
```

After: The campus uses timber frames and planted roofs, and its 6 buildings share one heat pump plant.

- Literal use: for the guild sense or in art history, write "major work" or put `masterpiece` in inline code.

#### 272. `vibe`

- Kind: noun and verb. Banned forms: `vibe`, `vibes`, `vibed`, `vibing`, `vibey`, and the phrases `vibe coding`, `the vibe is`, `good vibes`, `vibe check`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `vibe` moved from social media slang into model output, and it now fills design briefs, product copy and posts about code. It names a mood instead of a property, so a designer cannot build from it and a reviewer cannot check it. `vibe coding` hides whether anyone read, ran or tested the code.
- Where it shows up: design briefs and moodboards, landing page and office copy, posts about AI-written code.

```slop
The vibe is minimal but warm, like a Scandinavian coffee shop.
I vibe coded the whole backend over a weekend.
Our office has great vibes and a ping-pong table.
```

Replace with:

- The properties: palette hex values, typeface, spacing, corner radius.
- "mood" or "tone" in a brief, followed by those specifics.
- For code, how it was made and checked: "generated with an assistant, not reviewed, no tests".
- Cut it when the sentence describes only a feeling.

Rewrites:

```slop
The vibe is minimal but warm, like a Scandinavian coffee shop.
```

After: Use `#F7F5F0` for the page, one serif for headings, 2px corners, light oak photos, and no shadows.

```slop
I vibe coded the whole backend over a weekend.
```

After: I generated the backend with a coding assistant over a weekend; it has no tests yet and nobody has reviewed it.

```slop
Our office has great vibes and a ping-pong table.
```

After: The office has a quiet floor, lunch on Fridays, and a ping-pong table.

- Literal use: for the instrument in music writing, write "vibraphone"; the word has no other literal sense.

#### 273. `furthermore`

- Kind: adverb, connective. Banned forms: `furthermore`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `furthermore` is one of the connectives models put at the start of the second or third paragraph of an answer, in a register nobody uses in speech. It signals "here is another point" without saying how the point relates to the last one. Stacked with `moreover` and `additionally`, it dresses a list as an argument.
- Where it shows up: essay-style answers, cover letters, documentation written as prose.

```slop
Furthermore, the API supports pagination.
The tool is fast. Furthermore, it is free.
Furthermore, it is important to consider security implications.
```

Replace with:

- Start with the claim: "The API supports pagination."
- "and" or "also" inside the sentence when the two points belong together.
- A bulleted list when you have 3 or more parallel points.
- Cut it when the next sentence plainly adds to the last; the reader already knows it is an addition.

Rewrites:

```slop
Furthermore, the API supports pagination.
```

After: The API paginates results with a `cursor` parameter, 100 items per page.

```slop
The tool is fast. Furthermore, it is free.
```

After: The tool is fast and free.

```slop
Furthermore, it is important to consider security implications.
```

After: Uploads accept any file type, so scan files before you serve them to other users.

- Literal use: the word has no technical sense; inside quoted legal text, keep the quote in inline code.

#### 274. `moreover`

- Kind: adverb, connective. Banned forms: `moreover`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `moreover` claims the next point strengthens the last one, and models use it even when the next point is unrelated. It is rare in speech and common in generated essays, where it can open every third paragraph. It pushes the reader to read a list as a building case.
- Where it shows up: essay answers, persuasive copy, academic-style summaries.

```slop
Moreover, the library has excellent documentation.
The plan is cheaper. Moreover, it includes support.
Moreover, this approach scales well.
```

Replace with:

- Start the sentence with the claim; its position already marks it as the next point.
- "also" for a point of similar weight: "The plan also includes support."
- "and" to join two short claims in one sentence.
- Cut it when the connective is propping up a weak point; drop the point too.

Rewrites:

```slop
Moreover, the library has excellent documentation.
```

After: The library documents every function with an example that runs.

```slop
The plan is cheaper. Moreover, it includes support.
```

After: The plan is cheaper and includes email support.

```slop
Moreover, this approach scales well.
```

After: The same setup handled 50,000 requests a minute on 4 servers in our load test.

- Literal use: the word has no literal sense; start with the claim, or use "also" or "and".

#### 275. `additionally`

- Kind: adverb, connective. Banned forms: `additionally`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `additionally` is the model's formal version of "also", and it often opens a sentence that would read better joined to the one before. In generated docs, every feature paragraph after the first starts with it. It adds five syllables and no meaning.
- Where it shows up: feature lists written as prose, README files, emails.

```slop
Additionally, you can export reports as PDF.
Additionally, the plugin supports dark mode.
The service is HIPAA-compliant. Additionally, data is encrypted at rest.
```

Replace with:

- "also" in the middle of the sentence: "You can also export reports as PDF."
- One bulleted list, when there are 3 or more items.
- "and" to join two related facts.
- Cut it when the sentence starts a new paragraph; the break already signals a new point.

Rewrites:

```slop
Additionally, you can export reports as PDF.
```

After: Reports export as PDF or CSV.

```slop
Additionally, the plugin supports dark mode.
```

After: The plugin follows the system dark mode setting.

```slop
The service is HIPAA-compliant. Additionally, data is encrypted at rest.
```

After: The service is HIPAA-compliant and encrypts data at rest with AES-256.

- Literal use: the word has no literal sense; for an amount added, write "extra" or give the number.

#### 276. `notably`

- Kind: adverb, connective. Banned forms: `notably`, `most notably`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `notably` tells the reader that the next item matters more than the others without saying why. Models use it to introduce an example or to fake emphasis. When every paragraph has one, the reader can no longer tell what deserves attention.
- Where it shows up: summaries, comparison posts, release notes.

```slop
Several large companies use it, notably two of the biggest US banks.
Notably, the update includes a new caching layer.
The model performed well, most notably on reasoning tasks.
```

Replace with:

- "including" or "such as" for examples.
- Why it matters: "the cache halves p95 latency".
- The most important item placed first, with no adverb.
- Cut it when the sentence works without it, which is nearly always.

Rewrites:

```slop
Several large companies use it, notably two of the biggest US banks.
```

After: About 300 companies use it in production, including two of the five largest US banks.

```slop
Notably, the update includes a new caching layer.
```

After: The update adds a caching layer that cuts p95 latency from 200 ms to 90 ms.

```slop
The model performed well, most notably on reasoning tasks.
```

After: The model scored highest on the reasoning tasks, 71% against a 58% average.

- Literal use: the word has no technical sense; "notable" (worth notice) is allowed when followed by the reason.

#### 277. `importantly`

- Kind: adverb, connective. Banned forms: `importantly`, `more importantly`, `most importantly`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `importantly` is a model's flag for "pay attention here", most often as `more importantly` or `most importantly`. It ranks without explaining, and in generated text it marks a point no more important than the rest. If the point matters, the reader needs the consequence, not the label.
- Where it shows up: instructions, summaries, persuasive answers.

```slop
Importantly, you must back up your data before upgrading.
More importantly, the change improves accessibility.
Most importantly, have fun with it.
```

Replace with:

- The consequence: "the upgrade deletes the old index, so back up first".
- The most important point placed first in the paragraph or list.
- A warning callout in docs, with the failure stated.
- Cut it when the point is not the most important one, which is most of the time.

Rewrites:

```slop
Importantly, you must back up your data before upgrading.
```

After: Back up your data before upgrading; the upgrade rewrites the database and cannot be undone.

```slop
More importantly, the change improves accessibility.
```

After: The change adds a label to every form field, so screen readers announce each one.

```slop
Most importantly, have fun with it.
```

After: Delete the line; a closing pep talk adds nothing to a tutorial.

- Literal use: the word has no literal sense; "important" as an adjective is allowed when the sentence says why.

#### 278. `crucially`

- Kind: adverb, connective. Banned forms: `crucially`, and the adjective `crucial` (its own entry).
- Why it reads as machine text: `crucially` is a louder `importantly`, and models use it to raise the stakes of an ordinary step. It is a form of `crucial`, one of the most overused model adjectives. It tells the reader to worry without saying what fails.
- Where it shows up: tutorials, policy explainers, analysis essays.

```slop
Crucially, the function must be called before render.
Crucially, the agreement includes a non-compete clause.
The team, crucially, had buy-in from leadership.
```

Replace with:

- The failure: "if you call it after render, the first frame shows unstyled text".
- "because", to show why the fact matters.
- The condition placed in a numbered step or a warning.
- Cut it when the fact carries its own weight.

Rewrites:

```slop
Crucially, the function must be called before render.
```

After: Call `init()` before `render()`; otherwise the first frame draws without styles.

```slop
Crucially, the agreement includes a non-compete clause.
```

After: The agreement bars you from working for a competitor for 12 months after you leave.

```slop
The team, crucially, had buy-in from leadership.
```

After: The VP of engineering approved the plan, so the team got 2 extra hires for it.

- Literal use: the word has no literal sense; write "because" and the reason.

#### 279. `ultimately`

- Kind: adverb, connective. Banned forms: `ultimately`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `ultimately` is the most common closing adverb in model answers, as in `Ultimately, the choice depends on your needs`. It promises a final verdict and then hands the decision back to the reader. It also opens closing paragraphs that restate the body.
- Where it shows up: last paragraphs of comparison answers, opinion pieces, recommendations.

```slop
Ultimately, the best framework depends on your specific needs.
Ultimately, it's up to you to decide.
The goal is ultimately to make users happy.
```

Replace with:

- The verdict, with its condition: "pick Vue if your team knows templates; pick React if you need React Native".
- "in the end" or "finally", only for order in time.
- A tie-breaker rule when the options are close.
- Cut it when the sentence works without it, which it nearly always does; delete sentences that hand the choice back.

Rewrites:

```slop
Ultimately, the best framework depends on your specific needs.
```

After: Use SvelteKit for a small site you build alone; use Next.js if you need its larger hiring pool and plugin count.

```slop
Ultimately, it's up to you to decide.
```

After: If both options pass your tests, pick the one with fewer dependencies.

```slop
The goal is ultimately to make users happy.
```

After: The goal is that a new user finishes setup in under 5 minutes.

- Literal use: for the last step in a sequence, write "finally" or "in the end".

#### 280. `essentially`

- Kind: adverb, connective. Banned forms: `essentially`, and the adjective `essential` (its own entry).
- Why it reads as machine text: `essentially` lets a model simplify without saying what it left out. It opens sentences that restate the previous one in looser words (`Essentially, what this means is`), so it signals repetition. It is also a form of `essential`, which is banned on its own.
- Where it shows up: explanations of technical concepts, summaries, support answers.

```slop
Essentially, a closure is a function that remembers its scope.
The new plan is essentially the same as the old one.
Essentially, what this means is that you need to restart the server.
```

Replace with:

- The full definition, including the edge that the adverb skipped.
- "nearly" or "the same except", with the difference named.
- "basically" has the same problem; do not swap one for the other.
- Cut it when the sentence restates the last one; delete the restatement.

Rewrites:

```slop
Essentially, a closure is a function that remembers its scope.
```

After: A closure is a function together with the variables of the scope where it was created; it can read and change them after that scope returns.

```slop
The new plan is essentially the same as the old one.
```

After: The new plan matches the old one, except that support moves from email to chat.

```slop
Essentially, what this means is that you need to restart the server.
```

After: Restart the server to apply the change.

- Literal use: the word has no literal sense; state the definition, or write "in short" before a one-line summary.

### 7.5 Entries 281 to 350: adverbs, connectives and stock phrases

These 70 entries sit between claims. They are intensifiers, hedges, formal connectives, and the openers and closers that chat assistants wrap around an answer. Most of them are removed, not replaced: delete the word, read the sentence again, and add the number or the name the word was standing in for.

#### 281. `fundamentally`

- Kind: adverb. Banned forms: `fundamentally`, sentence-initial `Fundamentally,`.
- Why it reads as machine text: Models put `fundamentally` in front of a definition to make it sound deeper than it is, as in `X is fundamentally about Y`. The sentence that follows is usually a paraphrase of the topic name, so the word adds pitch and no fact. Generated explainers open section after section this way.
- Where it shows up: the first line of an explainer section, the "Overview" of an architecture doc, and pitch copy about what a product is.

```slop
React is fundamentally a library for building user interfaces.
Fundamentally, caching is about trading memory for speed.
The outage was fundamentally a problem of ownership between two teams.
```

Replace with:

- A direct definition with a verb that does work: "renders", "stores", "blocks". Use it when the sentence defines a thing.
- The cause, named: "The cause was X." Use it when you separate a symptom from its source.
- A number that shows the tradeoff, when the sentence claims one.
- Cut it when the sentence stays true without it, which is nearly always.

Rewrites:

```slop
React is fundamentally a library for building user interfaces.
```

After: React renders a UI tree from component state and patches the DOM when that state changes.

```slop
Fundamentally, caching is about trading memory for speed.
```

After: The cache keeps 2 GB of query results in memory so repeat requests skip a 40ms database call.

```slop
The outage was fundamentally a problem of ownership between two teams.
```

After: Neither team owned the billing webhook, so nobody fixed it when it began failing on 3 March.

- Literal use: for the physics or music term, write "fundamental frequency"; it names a measured quantity and is not an intensifier.

#### 282. `arguably`

- Kind: adverb. Banned forms: `arguably`, `arguably the best`, `arguably one of`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `arguably` lets a model make a ranking claim and withdraw it in the same word. It signals that an argument exists without making it. Model output pairs it with superlatives (`arguably the most popular`) because the training data rewards confident tone and penalizes unsupported claims, and this word satisfies both.
- Where it shows up: framework comparisons, "top 10" listicles, and the opening line of a README that ranks its own project.

```slop
Postgres is arguably the best open-source database available today.
This is arguably one of the most important changes in the release.
Tailwind is arguably the fastest way to style a React app.
```

Replace with:

- The evidence for the ranking: a benchmark, a download count, a survey with its year.
- "I think" or "We picked X because" when the claim is an opinion and the reader should know whose.
- A narrower true claim in place of the superlative: "the only one of the three with X".
- Cut it when you cannot name the argument; then the ranking goes too.

Rewrites:

```slop
Postgres is arguably the best open-source database available today.
```

After: We picked Postgres over MySQL for its JSONB indexes and row-level security.

```slop
This is arguably one of the most important changes in the release.
```

After: This change removes the 30-second lock on large tables during migration.

```slop
Tailwind is arguably the fastest way to style a React app.
```

After: With Tailwind we style a component without opening a second file; the tradeoff is long class strings.

- Literal use: in legal or academic text where a position can be argued, write "one could argue X, because Y" and supply Y.

#### 283. `undeniably`

- Kind: adverb. Banned forms: `undeniably`, `it is undeniable that`.
- Why it reads as machine text: A writer only says a claim cannot be denied when the claim has not been shown. The word asks the reader to skip the proof. Generated essays use it in the second paragraph to escalate a thesis the first paragraph only stated.
- Where it shows up: opinion posts, conclusion paragraphs, and sales pages that cite no source.

```slop
TypeScript has undeniably changed how teams write JavaScript.
The new design is undeniably faster and easier to use.
It is undeniable that remote work is here to stay.
```

Replace with:

- The measurement: "Load time fell from 2.4s to 1.1s."
- The source: "The 2025 Stack Overflow survey puts TypeScript at 38%."
- A scoped claim: "On our team" or "in the 14 interviews we ran".
- Cut it when the fact is plain; a plain fact needs no guard.

Rewrites:

```slop
TypeScript has undeniably changed how teams write JavaScript.
```

After: Since moving to TypeScript, our PRs catch type errors in CI instead of in production.

```slop
The new design is undeniably faster and easier to use.
```

After: In testing, the new checkout took 41 seconds on median, down from 68.

```slop
It is undeniable that remote work is here to stay.
```

After: 62% of our hires in 2025 work fully remote.

- Literal use: none. If a fact is uncontested, cite it and let it stand.

#### 284. `undoubtedly`

- Kind: adverb. Banned forms: `undoubtedly`, `without a doubt`, `no doubt`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `undoubtedly` usually sits on a forecast, the claim most open to doubt. Models append it to predictions (`will undoubtedly shape`) because a forecast without a hedge or an intensifier reads as flat to them. The result is certainty about the future with no basis.
- Where it shows up: trend posts, the last paragraph of a product announcement, and generated cover letters.

```slop
AI will undoubtedly change the way we write software.
This feature will undoubtedly save your team hours every week.
She is undoubtedly the right person for the role.
```

Replace with:

- A forecast with its basis: "Based on the pilot, we expect X."
- A measured past result in place of a future promise.
- The specific qualification for a person: years, projects, outcomes.
- Cut it when the sentence is a prediction you cannot support; cut the prediction too.

Rewrites:

```slop
AI will undoubtedly change the way we write software.
```

After: Half our new tests in Q3 were drafted by a code model and edited by a person.

```slop
This feature will undoubtedly save your team hours every week.
```

After: In the pilot, bulk edit cut the weekly price update from 3 hours to 20 minutes.

```slop
She is undoubtedly the right person for the role.
```

After: She ran the payments migration for 4 years and led the 2024 PCI audit.

- Literal use: none. Doubt is either addressed with evidence or admitted.

#### 285. `indeed`

- Kind: adverb, connective. Banned forms: `indeed`, `Indeed,`, `yes indeed`, `very X indeed`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `indeed` confirms what the previous sentence already said, so it signals a repeat. Chat models use `Indeed,` to open an agreement with the user, and generated essays use it to start a sentence that restates the thesis with an example. Few people use the word in speech, so it reads as borrowed formality.
- Where it shows up: the first word of a chat reply that agrees with the user, the middle of an essay paragraph, and code review replies.

```slop
Indeed, the function does mutate its input.
This approach is indeed faster, as the benchmarks show.
The error is very confusing indeed.
```

Replace with:

- "Yes" when you are answering a question.
- The evidence itself, with no confirming word before it.
- "In fact" only when you correct a wrong belief, and say what the belief was.
- Cut it when the sentence before already made the point.

Rewrites:

```slop
Indeed, the function does mutate its input.
```

After: Yes. `sortUsers` sorts the array in place, so callers see their list reordered.

```slop
This approach is indeed faster, as the benchmarks show.
```

After: The batched insert runs in 180ms against 2.1s for the loop.

```slop
The error is very confusing indeed.
```

After: The error says "undefined is not a function" and names no file, so it is hard to trace.

- Literal use: none. The confirming sense is the only sense.

#### 286. `truly`

- Kind: adverb. Banned forms: `truly`, `truly unique`, `truly scalable`, `yours truly`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `truly` is an intensifier placed before an adjective that is already doing too much (`truly unique`, `truly seamless`). Its job is to tell the reader that this time the adjective is meant, which concedes that adjectives elsewhere are not. Marketing copy generated from a brief adds it to every claim in the hero.
- Where it shows up: landing page heroes, feature bullets, and thank-you notes.

```slop
Our platform is truly built for scale.
We are truly grateful for your support.
This is a truly unique approach to state management.
```

Replace with:

- The number behind "scale": requests per second, tenants, rows.
- A specific thanks that names what the person did.
- The one property that differs from the usual approach, named.
- Cut it when the adjective after it can stand alone; if it cannot, replace the adjective.

Rewrites:

```slop
Our platform is truly built for scale.
```

After: One cluster serves 40,000 requests per second across 1,200 tenants.

```slop
We are truly grateful for your support.
```

After: Thank you for the 14 bug reports you filed during the beta.

```slop
This is a truly unique approach to state management.
```

After: The store keeps state in the URL, so every view can be bookmarked and shared.

- Literal use: to say a statement is correct, write "true" or "correct"; sign a letter with your name.

#### 287. `genuinely`

- Kind: adverb. Banned forms: `genuinely`, `genuinely useful`, `I genuinely`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `genuinely` is a sincerity marker. It tells the reader the writer means it, which is only needed when the reader has reason to think otherwise. Chat assistants use it to warm up praise and empathy (`I genuinely understand`), and the word marks those lines as scripted.
- Where it shows up: chat replies that praise the user's code, product reviews, and apology emails.

```slop
This is a genuinely useful tool for frontend developers.
I genuinely understand how frustrating this bug must be.
The docs are genuinely helpful once you get past the setup.
```

Replace with:

- The use: what task the tool does and for whom.
- An acknowledgment of the cost to the user, followed by the fix.
- The specific page or section that helped.
- Cut it when the sentence carries a claim; the claim is enough.

Rewrites:

```slop
This is a genuinely useful tool for frontend developers.
```

After: It flags unused CSS classes in a Next.js build in under a second.

```slop
I genuinely understand how frustrating this bug must be.
```

After: That bug cost you a day of debugging. The fix is in 2.3.1, released today.

```slop
The docs are genuinely helpful once you get past the setup.
```

After: The "Migrations" page answered every question I had after setup.

- Literal use: for authenticity of an object or signature, write "authentic" or "real" and say how it was checked.

#### 288. `incredibly`

- Kind: adverb. Banned forms: `incredibly`, `incredible`, `incredibly fast`, `incredibly easy`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `incredibly` means "not believable", and it is placed before claims that should be believed. Models use it as the default intensifier for speed and ease (`incredibly fast`, `incredibly easy`), where a number would carry the claim. Three uses on one landing page are common in generated copy.
- Where it shows up: performance claims, onboarding copy, and reviews.

```slop
The new build system is incredibly fast.
Setting up the SDK is incredibly easy.
Our team has been incredibly busy this quarter.
```

Replace with:

- The measured value with its baseline: "builds in 4s, down from 38s".
- A count of steps or minutes for ease.
- The work itself, listed, in place of "busy".
- Cut it when there is no number; then cut the claim it was propping up.

Rewrites:

```slop
The new build system is incredibly fast.
```

After: A cold build of the 900-file monorepo takes 4 seconds, down from 38.

```slop
Setting up the SDK is incredibly easy.
```

After: Install the package, add one API key, and call `init()`. Setup takes about 5 minutes.

```slop
Our team has been incredibly busy this quarter.
```

After: This quarter we shipped SSO, the audit log, and 3 regional data centers.

- Literal use: for a claim that is hard to believe, say so plainly: "This number looks wrong, so we ran it 3 times."

#### 289. `remarkably`

- Kind: adverb. Banned forms: `remarkably`, `Remarkably,`, `remarkably simple`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `remarkably` marks a surprise without saying what was expected. Models use it to dress an ordinary result as a finding, as in `Remarkably, the change reduced errors.` The reader cannot judge the surprise because the baseline is missing.
- Where it shows up: postmortems, research summaries, and product updates.

```slop
Remarkably, the fix reduced error rates across the board.
The API is remarkably simple to integrate.
The model performs remarkably well on long documents.
```

Replace with:

- The expectation and the result: "We expected a 5% drop; errors fell 60%."
- The integration measured in lines of code or calls.
- The score and the benchmark name.
- Cut it when there was no expectation to break.

Rewrites:

```slop
Remarkably, the fix reduced error rates across the board.
```

After: We expected the retry fix to help checkout only, but 5xx errors fell 60% on every endpoint.

```slop
The API is remarkably simple to integrate.
```

After: A working integration is 12 lines: create a client, sign the request, read the JSON.

```slop
The model performs remarkably well on long documents.
```

After: On 50-page contracts the model finds 91% of the clauses a lawyer marked.

- Literal use: to say something deserves comment, write "unusual" or "unexpected" and state the usual case.

#### 290. `profoundly`

- Kind: adverb. Banned forms: `profoundly`, `profoundly changed`, `profoundly impact`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `profoundly` claims a deep change and gives no depth. It is paired with abstract verbs ("affect", "shape", "impact") so neither half of the phrase can be checked. Generated essays use it in the thesis sentence and again in the last paragraph.
- Where it shows up: essays about technology and society, company history pages, and keynote scripts.

```slop
Smartphones have profoundly changed how we communicate.
This decision will profoundly impact our users.
The book profoundly shaped my approach to design.
```

Replace with:

- The before and after, each stated: "In 2010 we did X. Now we do Y."
- Who is affected, how many, and in what way.
- The specific idea you took from the book and where you applied it.
- Cut it when the verb after it is abstract; replace the verb.

Rewrites:

```slop
Smartphones have profoundly changed how we communicate.
```

After: Most of our support contacts now come by chat on a phone; in 2012 most came by email.

```slop
This decision will profoundly impact our users.
```

After: Removing the free tier moves 18,000 accounts to a 14-day trial.

```slop
The book profoundly shaped my approach to design.
```

After: From that book I took one rule: design the empty state before the full one.

- Literal use: for medical severity, write the clinical term ("severe hearing loss", "deaf") and its measure.

#### 291. `inherently`

- Kind: adverb. Banned forms: `inherently`, `inherently insecure`, `inherently complex`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `inherently` claims a property is built into a thing, which would need a reason, and then gives none. Models use it to end a debate (`inherently insecure`) without showing the mechanism. The claim is often false: the property comes from a default, not from the thing.
- Where it shows up: security advice, architecture debates, and arguments against a tool.

```slop
Storing tokens in localStorage is inherently insecure.
Distributed systems are inherently complex.
```
