```slop
Microservices are inherently harder to debug than a monolith.
```

Replace with:

- The mechanism: what makes it so, in one clause starting with "because".
- The specific failure mode the property causes.
- A condition: "when X" or "unless Y", if the property depends on setup.
- Cut it when the reason follows; the reason carries the claim.

Rewrites:

```slop
Storing tokens in localStorage is inherently insecure.
```

After: Any script on the page can read localStorage, so one XSS bug exposes every token.

```slop
Distributed systems are inherently complex.
```

After: With 3 replicas, a write can succeed on one node and fail on two, and the client has to handle both.

```slop
Microservices are inherently harder to debug than a monolith.
```

After: A request that crosses 6 services needs a trace ID to follow; a monolith has one stack trace.

- Literal use: in philosophy or law, "inherent" as a defined term is fine; outside those fields, give the reason.

#### 292. `invariably`

- Kind: adverb. Banned forms: `invariably`, `invariably leads to`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `invariably` claims a rule with no exceptions from what is usually a handful of cases. Models reach for it to make advice sound like law (`invariably leads to bugs`). Readers who know one counterexample stop trusting the rest of the page.
- Where it shows up: engineering advice posts, code review comments, and management writing.

```slop
Skipping tests invariably leads to production bugs.
Large PRs invariably get rubber-stamped in review.
Users invariably ignore onboarding tooltips.
```

Replace with:

- A frequency with its sample: "in 9 of our last 12 incidents".
- "Always" when it is a rule of the system, and name the rule.
- "Often" or "usually" with an example, when you have no count.
- Cut it when the claim works as a tendency; most claims do.

Rewrites:

```slop
Skipping tests invariably leads to production bugs.
```

After: 9 of our last 12 incidents shipped in a PR with no new tests.

```slop
Large PRs invariably get rubber-stamped in review.
```

After: PRs over 800 lines got a median of 1 review comment; PRs under 200 got 6.

```slop
Users invariably ignore onboarding tooltips.
```

After: In session recordings, 4 of 5 new users closed the first tooltip within 2 seconds.

- Literal use: for a value that never changes, use the noun "invariant" and state it: "Invariant: `balance >= 0`."

#### 293. `interestingly`

- Kind: adverb. Banned forms: `interestingly`, `Interestingly,`, `interestingly enough`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `interestingly` tells the reader how to feel about the next fact instead of making the fact interesting. Models use it as a transition when the next point has no logical link to the last. It is a filler slot for "here is another thing".
- Where it shows up: data summaries, research write-ups, and chat answers that list findings.

```slop
Interestingly, mobile users converted at a higher rate.
Interestingly enough, the bug only appears in Safari.
The results were interestingly mixed across regions.
```

Replace with:

- The expectation it breaks: "We expected X; we saw Y."
- A causal link: "because", "so", or "which means".
- The fact alone, with its numbers, so the reader judges it.
- Cut it when nothing was expected; the fact stands without a frame.

Rewrites:

```slop
Interestingly, mobile users converted at a higher rate.
```

After: Mobile users converted at 3.1% against 2.4% on desktop, the reverse of last year.

```slop
Interestingly enough, the bug only appears in Safari.
```

After: The bug only appears in Safari, which does not support `:has()` inside `@supports` before 15.4.

```slop
The results were interestingly mixed across regions.
```

After: Signups rose 12% in Europe and fell 4% in North America.

- Literal use: none. Interest is the reader's to decide.

#### 294. `overall`

- Kind: adverb, adjective. Banned forms: `overall`, `Overall,`, `overall experience`, `overall performance`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `Overall,` opens the summary sentence of a generated paragraph, the one that restates the paragraph at lower resolution. As an adjective (`overall experience`) it claims to cover everything and so names nothing. Model reviews and reports end almost every section with it.
- Where it shows up: the last sentence of a paragraph, review verdicts, and performance reports.

```slop
Overall, the migration went smoothly.
The overall user experience has improved significantly.
Overall performance is good, with a few exceptions.
```

Replace with:

- The result with its measure: "The migration finished in 4 hours with no downtime."
- The specific parts that changed, by name.
- The exceptions first, since they are the news.
- Cut it when the paragraph already made the point.

Rewrites:

```slop
Overall, the migration went smoothly.
```

After: The migration finished in 4 hours, 2 under the window, with no failed writes.

```slop
The overall user experience has improved significantly.
```

After: Search now returns in 200ms and the settings page loads without a spinner.

```slop
Overall performance is good, with a few exceptions.
```

After: Every page loads under 1s except Reports (3.2s) and Billing (2.6s).

- Literal use: for a total dimension in a spec, write "total width" or "outer width" and give the value: "outer width 1,280px".

#### 295. `thereby`

- Kind: adverb, connective. Banned forms: `thereby`, `, thereby reducing`, `, thereby ensuring`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `thereby` hangs a consequence on the end of a sentence as an "-ing" clause, so one sentence carries an action and its effect. Models produce this shape constantly (`X does Y, thereby reducing Z`) because it packs a claim of benefit into the tail where it is rarely checked. The register is legal, not technical.
- Where it shows up: design docs, PR descriptions, and generated commit messages.

```slop
The cache stores results in memory, thereby reducing database load.
We added retries, thereby improving reliability.
The new flow removes a step, thereby ensuring a smoother checkout.
```

Replace with:

- Two sentences: the action, then the effect with its number.
- "so" between the clauses when the effect is short.
- The effect alone, if the action is obvious from context.
- Cut it when the consequence is a vague benefit; state the measured one or drop it.

Rewrites:

```slop
The cache stores results in memory, thereby reducing database load.
```

After: The cache stores results in memory. Database reads fell from 1,200 to 300 per second.

```slop
We added retries, thereby improving reliability.
```

After: We retry failed uploads 3 times with backoff, so a dropped connection no longer loses the file.

```slop
The new flow removes a step, thereby ensuring a smoother checkout.
```

After: The new flow drops the address confirmation page; checkout is now 3 screens.

- Literal use: in a contract, keep the drafting style your lawyer uses; in product and code text, use "so".

#### 296. `whereby`

- Kind: relative adverb. Banned forms: `whereby`, `a process whereby`, `a system whereby`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `whereby` introduces a clause that defines a process, and it comes with a vague noun in front (`a mechanism whereby`). The construction delays the verb and hides who acts. Models use it to sound formal when describing any workflow.
- Where it shows up: policy pages, architecture docs, and glossary definitions.

```slop
We use a system whereby each request is assigned a unique ID.
This is a process whereby users verify their email.
The protocol defines a mechanism whereby nodes agree on a leader.
```

Replace with:

- An active sentence with the actor as subject: "The gateway assigns each request an ID."
- "in which" or "where" if you must keep the clause.
- A numbered list when the process has steps.
- Cut it when the noun before it ("system", "process") adds nothing.

Rewrites:

```slop
We use a system whereby each request is assigned a unique ID.
```

After: The gateway assigns each request a UUID and passes it in the `X-Request-Id` header.

```slop
This is a process whereby users verify their email.
```

After: To verify an email, the user clicks a link we send that expires after 24 hours.

```slop
The protocol defines a mechanism whereby nodes agree on a leader.
```

After: Nodes elect a leader by majority vote; a node that hears no heartbeat for 300ms starts an election.

- Literal use: none outside legal drafting. Use "where" or "in which".

#### 297. `albeit`

- Kind: conjunction. Banned forms: `albeit`, `albeit with`, `albeit slowly`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `albeit` tucks a concession into a short tail so the main claim keeps its weight and the limitation goes unread. Models use it to sound balanced while saying little about the cost (`albeit with some limitations`). The word is rare in spoken English and stands out in casual text.
- Where it shows up: comparison tables, review summaries, and changelogs.

```slop
The feature works, albeit with some limitations.
Performance improved, albeit slightly.
The new API is faster, albeit less flexible.
```

Replace with:

- "but" followed by the specific limitation.
- Two sentences when the limitation matters as much as the claim.
- The number, when "slightly" is the concession.
- Cut it when the concession is vague; name it or delete it.

Rewrites:

```slop
The feature works, albeit with some limitations.
```

After: Export works for files under 50 MB. Larger files time out.

```slop
Performance improved, albeit slightly.
```

After: Median response time fell from 210ms to 195ms.

```slop
The new API is faster, albeit less flexible.
```

After: The new API is 3 times faster but cannot filter on nested fields.

- Literal use: none. "Although" and "but" cover every case.

#### 298. `aforementioned`

- Kind: adjective. Banned forms: `aforementioned`, `the aforementioned`, `abovementioned`, `said` as in "said function".
- Why it reads as machine text: `aforementioned` points back at something instead of naming it, which makes the reader scroll up. It is legal register applied to software. Models use it to avoid repeating a noun, though repeating the noun is clearer.
- Where it shows up: long docs that refer back to earlier sections, support replies, and generated reports.

```slop
The aforementioned function should be called before rendering.
Please refer to the aforementioned documentation.
To avoid the aforementioned issues, pin your dependencies.
```

Replace with:

- The noun again: "`initTheme()`", "the timeout issue".
- "this" or "that" when the referent is in the previous sentence.
- A link to the section, when the referent is far away.
- Cut it when "the" alone points clearly enough.

Rewrites:

```slop
The aforementioned function should be called before rendering.
```

After: Call `initTheme()` before the first render.

```slop
Please refer to the aforementioned documentation.
```

After: See the "Auth tokens" section of the API reference.

```slop
To avoid the aforementioned issues, pin your dependencies.
```

After: Pin your dependencies to avoid the lockfile drift described in step 2.

- Literal use: none outside contracts. Name the thing.

#### 299. `in conclusion`

- Kind: closer. Banned forms: `in conclusion`, `In conclusion,`, `to conclude`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `In conclusion,` comes from the school essay template, and models trained on essays reproduce it at the top of the last paragraph. The paragraph that follows restates the points above in the same order. A reader can skip it without losing anything, which they will.
- Where it shows up: the last paragraph of a generated blog post, chat answers longer than 300 words, and reports.

```slop
In conclusion, choosing the right database depends on your needs.
In conclusion, accessibility should be part of every project.
To conclude, the new pipeline offers many benefits.
```

Replace with:

- Nothing. End on the last new fact or the last step.
- A decision or recommendation, stated as the final line: "Use Postgres unless you need X."
- A summary at the top (TL;DR) instead of the bottom, for long documents.
- Cut it when the final paragraph only restates; cut the paragraph too.

Rewrites:

```slop
In conclusion, choosing the right database depends on your needs.
```

After: Use Postgres unless you need more than 50,000 writes per second; then test Cassandra.

```slop
In conclusion, accessibility should be part of every project.
```

After: Add an axe check to CI so contrast and label errors fail the build.

```slop
To conclude, the new pipeline offers many benefits.
```

After: The new pipeline deploys in 6 minutes instead of 25 and rolls back in one command.

- Literal use: for the closing section of a paper, use the heading "Conclusions" and state findings, not a recap.

#### 300. `in summary`

- Kind: closer. Banned forms: `in summary`, `In summary,`, `in sum`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `In summary,` marks a paragraph that repeats the answer, and chat models attach one to nearly every long reply. The summary sits at the end, after the reader has already read everything it repeats. It often adds a vague benefit the body never claimed.
- Where it shows up: chat answers, generated documentation pages, and code review summaries.

```slop
In summary, hooks make React components easier to reuse.
In summary, there are several ways to fix this error.
In summary, the PR looks good with a few minor changes.
```

Replace with:

- The answer in the first sentence, so no summary is needed.
- A TL;DR line at the top of long pages.
- A list of the specific changes requested, for reviews.
- Cut it when the body is under a screen long.

Rewrites:

```slop
In summary, hooks make React components easier to reuse.
```

After: Move the fetch logic into `useUser()` and both pages can share it.

```slop
In summary, there are several ways to fix this error.
```

After: Fix it by adding `"type": "module"` to package.json; if you cannot, rename the file to `.mjs`.

```slop
In summary, the PR looks good with a few minor changes.
```

After: Approve after two changes: rename `tmp2` and add a test for the empty list.

- Literal use: for a section that sums up a report, title it "Summary" and place it first.

#### 301. `to summarize`

- Kind: closer, transition. Banned forms: `to summarize`, `to sum up`, `summarizing`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `To summarize,` is the same closing move as `in summary` with a verb in front, and models alternate the two to avoid repeating themselves. It announces a recap the reader did not ask for. In chat answers it often follows a bulleted list and repeats the bullets as prose.
- Where it shows up: chat replies, tutorial endings, and meeting notes.

```slop
To summarize, you need to update your config and restart the server.
To sum up, the redesign improves usability and performance.
To summarize the discussion, we agreed to revisit this later.
```

Replace with:

- The steps as a numbered list, once, with no prose recap.
- The specific change, measured.
- Decisions and owners, for meeting notes: "Decision: X. Owner: Ana. Date: 20 Oct."
- Cut it when the summary would repeat the last 5 lines.

Rewrites:

```slop
To summarize, you need to update your config and restart the server.
```

After: Set `cache: false` in `vite.config.ts`, then restart the dev server.

```slop
To sum up, the redesign improves usability and performance.
```

After: The redesign cuts the settings page from 4 tabs to 1 and loads it in 300ms.

```slop
To summarize the discussion, we agreed to revisit this later.
```

After: No decision. Ana will bring cost numbers to the 28 October review.

- Literal use: in a docstring for a function that condenses data, write what it returns: "Returns a one-line digest per log file."

#### 302. `all in all`

- Kind: closer. Banned forms: `all in all`, `All in all,`, `all things considered`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `All in all` is a folksy wrap-up that weighs pros and cons without showing the weights. Models use it to end reviews with a verdict that matches the average sentiment of the text above. The verdict is usually "good, with room to improve".
- Where it shows up: product reviews, retrospectives, and chat answers comparing tools.

```slop
All in all, it was a successful launch.
All in all, Svelte is a great choice for small projects.
All things considered, the trip was worth it.
```

Replace with:

- The verdict with the deciding factor: "Svelte, because the bundle is 40% smaller."
- The result against the goal: "We aimed for 500 signups and got 820."
- The one thing that tipped the decision.
- Cut it when the verdict is already clear from the text above.

Rewrites:

```slop
All in all, it was a successful launch.
```

After: The launch brought 820 signups against a goal of 500, with 2 support tickets.

```slop
All in all, Svelte is a great choice for small projects.
```

After: For a 5-page site, pick Svelte: the bundle is 40% smaller and there is no virtual DOM to learn.

```slop
All things considered, the trip was worth it.
```

After: The trip cost 2 days and closed the Lyon contract.

- Literal use: none. Give the deciding factor.

#### 303. `at its core`

- Kind: opener. Banned forms: `at its core`, `at their core`, `at the core of`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `At its core,` promises that the sentence after it is the one definition that matters, then gives a broad paraphrase. Models start explainers with it (`At its core, Kubernetes is a container orchestrator`) because it frames a definition as a reveal. The reader learns nothing that the product name did not already say.
- Where it shows up: the first sentence of an explainer, "About" pages, and onboarding copy.

```slop
At its core, Kubernetes is a system for managing containers.
At its core, our product is about helping teams collaborate.
At the core of the design is a commitment to simplicity.
```

Replace with:

- The definition, starting with the subject and a concrete verb.
- The one action the product performs, for whom.
- The specific design rule, stated as a rule.
- Cut it when what follows is a definition; definitions need no frame.

Rewrites:

```slop
At its core, Kubernetes is a system for managing containers.
```

After: Kubernetes starts containers on a pool of machines and restarts them when they fail.

```slop
At its core, our product is about helping teams collaborate.
```

After: Teams use the app to review designs and leave comments pinned to a layer.

```slop
At the core of the design is a commitment to simplicity.
```

After: Each screen has one primary action and no more than 5 inputs.

- Literal use: for a CPU, write "per core" or "on each core"; for a reactor or an apple, "the core" without the "at its" frame.

#### 304. `at the end of the day`

- Kind: closer, phrase. Banned forms: `at the end of the day`, `when all is said and done`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `at the end of the day` introduces a statement meant to override the details before it, usually a platitude ("users just want it to work"). Models use it to close debates with a value nobody disputes. It sounds like speech, but it is a spoken filler copied into writing.
- Where it shows up: the last paragraph of opinion posts, design debates, and management email.

```slop
At the end of the day, users just want things to work.
At the end of the day, it's about shipping value to customers.
When all is said and done, the choice of framework matters less than the team.
```

Replace with:

- The specific priority that wins, and what it beats: "We fix the crash before the redesign."
- The decision rule: "If X, choose A."
- Nothing, when the line is a platitude.
- Cut it when the sentence after it could close any article.

Rewrites:

```slop
At the end of the day, users just want things to work.
```

After: Fix the 3 crash bugs before starting the new theme.

```slop
At the end of the day, it's about shipping value to customers.
```

After: Ship the CSV export first; 40 customers asked for it last month.

```slop
When all is said and done, the choice of framework matters less than the team.
```

After: Pick the framework the team already knows; switching costs about 2 months.

- Literal use: for time, give the time: "by 18:00" or "before the nightly build at 02:00".

#### 305. `needless to say`

- Kind: opener. Banned forms: `needless to say`, `it goes without saying`, `obviously`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `needless to say` introduces a statement the writer then says, so the phrase contradicts itself. It also implies a reader who did not know the fact should have. Models use it to bridge into an obvious consequence of the last sentence.
- Where it shows up: the middle of first-person posts, incident write-ups, and support replies.

```slop
Needless to say, the deployment failed.
It goes without saying that you should back up your data first.
Needless to say, we were thrilled with the results.
```

Replace with:

- The fact alone.
- An instruction with its reason, when the fact is a warning.
- The result with its number, for reactions.
- Cut it every time; the phrase never carries meaning.

Rewrites:

```slop
Needless to say, the deployment failed.
```

After: The deployment failed at the migration step.

```slop
It goes without saying that you should back up your data first.
```

After: Back up the database before you run the upgrade; the migration cannot be reversed.

```slop
Needless to say, we were thrilled with the results.
```

After: Signups doubled in the first week.

- Literal use: none.

#### 306. `worth noting`

- Kind: phrase. Banned forms: `worth noting`, `it's worth noting that`, `it is worth noting`, `worth mentioning`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `It's worth noting that` spends five words to say the next clause matters. Models insert it before caveats and side facts, often several times in one reply. The phrase signals that the writer has not decided where the fact belongs.
- Where it shows up: chat answers, documentation caveats, and pull request descriptions.

```slop
It's worth noting that this API is deprecated.
It is worth noting that the free plan has a rate limit.
Worth mentioning: the build may take longer on Windows.
```

Replace with:

- The fact, stated where it applies.
- A labeled warning block in docs ("Warning" or "Note") when the reader must not miss it.
- The fact moved to the first line, if it changes the answer.
- Cut it when the clause after it can stand alone, which is always.

Rewrites:

```slop
It's worth noting that this API is deprecated.
```

After: This API is deprecated and will be removed in v5. Use `fetchUsers()` instead.

```slop
It is worth noting that the free plan has a rate limit.
```

After: The free plan allows 60 requests per minute.

```slop
Worth mentioning: the build may take longer on Windows.
```

After: On Windows the build takes about 4 minutes because file watching is slower.

- Literal use: none. If the fact matters, state it where it applies.

#### 307. `important to note`

- Kind: phrase. Banned forms: `important to note`, `it's important to note`, `it is important to remember`, `keep in mind that`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `It's important to note` claims priority for a statement and then buries it mid-paragraph. Chat models attach it to safety caveats and edge cases out of habit, so it appears on things that are not important. When everything is flagged, nothing is.
- Where it shows up: chat answers, how-to articles, and generated README warnings.

```slop
It's important to note that this command deletes all data.
It is important to remember that results may vary.
Keep in mind that the token expires after one hour.
```

Replace with:

- A warning placed before the step it affects, in its own block.
- The specific condition, in place of "results may vary".
- The fact stated in the step where the reader needs it.
- Cut it when the fact is not a risk; put it in the body.

Rewrites:

```slop
It's important to note that this command deletes all data.
```

After: Warning: `db:reset` deletes every table. Run `db:dump` first.

```slop
It is important to remember that results may vary.
```

After: Results depend on image size; above 4,000px the model misses small text.

```slop
Keep in mind that the token expires after one hour.
```

After: The token expires after 60 minutes. Call `refresh()` before then.

- Literal use: none. Put the important thing first.

#### 308. `in today's`

- Kind: opener. Banned forms: `in today's`, `in today's fast-paced world`, `in today's competitive market`, `in this day and age`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `In today's` opens a generated article by placing the topic in a present that is never dated. The noun after it is a stock phrase (`world`, `market`, `landscape`), and the sentence states a trend nobody disputes. The paragraph could open any post on any subject.
- Where it shows up: the first line of blog posts, cover letters, and product pages.

```slop
In today's fast-paced world, developers need tools that keep up.
In today's competitive market, a good website is a must.
In this day and age, security cannot be an afterthought.
```

Replace with:

- The specific fact with its date: "In 2026, 70% of our traffic is mobile."
- The problem the reader has, in their terms.
- Nothing; start with the second sentence.
- Cut it when the sentence would be equally true in 2005.

Rewrites:

```slop
In today's fast-paced world, developers need tools that keep up.
```

After: Our team ships 40 PRs a day, and a 12-minute CI run blocks every one.

```slop
In today's competitive market, a good website is a must.
```

After: 8 of 10 customers in our survey looked at a competitor's site before calling us.

```slop
In this day and age, security cannot be an afterthought.
```

After: Run the dependency audit on every PR; last year two CVEs reached production.

- Literal use: for the actual day, name it: "in this morning's standup" or "in the 14 October release".

#### 309. `digital age`

- Kind: phrase. Banned forms: `digital age`, `in the digital age`, `information age`, `digital era`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `the digital age` names a period without dates and a change without details. Models use it as a backdrop for any claim about technology. It reads as dated, since the phrase belongs to 1990s press copy.
- Where it shows up: essay openers, "About us" pages, and course descriptions.

```slop
In the digital age, privacy is more important than ever.
Libraries must adapt to the digital age.
Our agency helps brands grow in the digital era.
```

Replace with:

- The specific technology and the year it changed things.
- The specific adaptation: "Libraries now lend e-books through Libby."
- The service you provide, named.
- Cut it when the claim holds without a time frame.

Rewrites:

```slop
In the digital age, privacy is more important than ever.
```

After: Since 2018, the GDPR fines companies up to 4% of revenue for privacy breaches.

```slop
Libraries must adapt to the digital age.
```

After: Our library now lends 12,000 e-books a month, a third of all loans.

```slop
Our agency helps brands grow in the digital era.
```

After: We run search ads and build Shopify stores for food brands.

- Literal use: for a historical period, name the years: "after the web went public in 1991".

#### 310. `digital landscape`

- Kind: phrase. Banned forms: `digital landscape`, `the digital space`, `digital world`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `digital landscape` turns a market into scenery so the writer can avoid naming the players. It comes paired with a movement verb (`navigate`, `stay ahead in`), which completes the metaphor and empties the sentence. Generated marketing copy reuses it across industries unchanged.
- Where it shows up: agency sites, LinkedIn posts, and strategy decks.

```slop
We help businesses succeed in the digital landscape.
The digital landscape is constantly changing.
Stand out in a crowded digital space.
```

Replace with:

- The market, named: "B2B payroll software in the UK".
- The specific change, with its date: "Google moved to mobile-first indexing in 2019."
- The channels you work in: search, email, App Store.
- Cut it when you cannot name the market; the sentence has nothing to say.

Rewrites:

```slop
We help businesses succeed in the digital landscape.
```

After: We build online stores for UK furniture makers.

```slop
The digital landscape is constantly changing.
```

After: Apple's 2021 privacy change cut our ad tracking by half.

```slop
Stand out in a crowded digital space.
```

After: Rank on page one for "custom oak tables" in 6 months.

- Literal use: for terrain in a game or a map, write "terrain" or "map".

#### 311. `let's dive`

- Kind: opener. Banned forms: `let's dive`, `let's dive in`, `let's jump in`, `let's get started`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `Let's dive in` closes an introduction that should not exist and announces the content instead of starting it. Chat models and generated tutorials use it as the bridge between a preamble and the first heading. The "let's" adds a fake sense of doing it together.
- Where it shows up: tutorials, YouTube scripts turned into posts, and chat answers longer than a few paragraphs.

```slop
Now that we've covered the basics, let's dive in.
Let's dive into the code and see how it works.
Ready to get started? Let's jump in.
```

Replace with:

- The first step, as a heading or an imperative: "Install the CLI."
- A one-line scope at the top: "This guide covers setup and the first deploy."
- Nothing; delete the introduction it closes.
- Cut it when the next line is the content; it always is.

Rewrites:

```slop
Now that we've covered the basics, let's dive in.
```

After: Step 1: install the CLI with `npm i -g fly`.

```slop
Let's dive into the code and see how it works.
```

After: The handler in `api/upload.ts` reads the file, checks its type, and writes it to S3.

```slop
Ready to get started? Let's jump in.
```

After: Create a project with `npm create vite@latest`.

- Literal use: for swimming, write "dive" in a sentence about the water: "Dive from the 3m board."

#### 312. `buckle up`

- Kind: opener. Banned forms: `buckle up`, `strap in`, `hold on tight`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `Buckle up` promises a thrilling ride before a post that is usually a list. Generated posts copy the hype tone of creator content, where the phrase signals length and excitement. It sets an expectation the content does not meet.
- Where it shows up: long-form blog posts, newsletters, and thread openers.

```slop
Buckle up, because this is going to be a long one.
Strap in for a wild ride through the history of CSS.
Buckle up: we're about to rethink everything you know about state.
```

Replace with:

- The length and scope: "This post is 3,000 words and covers 5 layout methods."
- The first point.
- A table of contents for long pieces.
- Cut it when there is no seatbelt.

Rewrites:

```slop
Buckle up, because this is going to be a long one.
```

After: This post is long (about 20 minutes). The summary is in the first section.

```slop
Strap in for a wild ride through the history of CSS.
```

After: This post traces CSS layout from tables (1996) to grid (2017).

```slop
Buckle up: we're about to rethink everything you know about state.
```

After: This post argues that most UI state belongs in the URL, and shows 3 examples.

- Literal use: for vehicle safety, write "fasten your seatbelt".

#### 313. `next level`

- Kind: phrase. Banned forms: `next level`, `next-level`, `to the next level`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `the next level` names an improvement with no scale, so the reader cannot tell what changes. It comes from game language and motivational copy, and models pair it with `take your X`. The level is never named, because there is none.
- Where it shows up: course pages, product heroes, and feature announcements.

```slop
Take your React skills to the next level.
This update brings performance to the next level.
Next-level tooling for next-level teams.
```

Replace with:

- The skill or result the reader will have afterward.
- The measured change.
- The tool's job, named.
- Cut it when there is no defined level; there never is.

Rewrites:

```slop
Take your React skills to the next level.
```

After: Learn to write custom hooks, profile renders, and split bundles by route.

```slop
This update brings performance to the next level.
```

After: This update halves render time on lists over 1,000 rows.

```slop
Next-level tooling for next-level teams.
```

After: Type-safe API clients generated from your OpenAPI file.

- Literal use: for a game or a tree, write "level 4" or "the level below the root".

#### 314. `the power of`

- Kind: phrase. Banned forms: `the power of`, `harness the power of`, `unlock the power of`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `the power of X` turns a tool into a force without saying what it does. Models write `harness the power of AI` or `the power of TypeScript` when the brief names a technology and no task. The phrase signals that the writer knows the noun but not its use.
- Where it shows up: product taglines, course titles, and conference talk abstracts.

```slop
Harness the power of AI to grow your business.
Discover the power of TypeScript in large codebases.
Experience the power of real-time collaboration.
```

Replace with:

- The task the tool does: "drafts replies to support tickets".
- The specific benefit in a large codebase: "renames across 400 files".
- What two people can do at once, named.
- Cut it when the noun alone carries the meaning.

Rewrites:

```slop
Harness the power of AI to grow your business.
```

After: The assistant drafts replies to support tickets; your team edits and sends them.

```slop
Discover the power of TypeScript in large codebases.
```

After: In a 400-file codebase, TypeScript lets you rename a field and see every caller that breaks.

```slop
Experience the power of real-time collaboration.
```

After: Two people can edit the same doc and see each other's cursor.

- Literal use: for exponents, write "2^10" or "2 to the 10th"; for electrical power, give watts.

#### 315. `at the forefront`

- Kind: phrase. Banned forms: `at the forefront`, `at the forefront of`, `leading the charge`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `at the forefront of` claims leadership in a field without a measure of it. Models use it in company descriptions (`at the forefront of innovation`), where the field is as vague as the claim. Every company that uses it is at the front of the same unnamed line.
- Where it shows up: "About" pages, press releases, and job ads.

```slop
We are at the forefront of AI innovation.
Our lab is at the forefront of battery research.
The company has been at the forefront of the industry for decades.
```

Replace with:

- The first or only thing you did, with its date.
- A count: papers, patents, customers, years.
- The specific research question and the result.
- Cut it when you have no evidence of being first.

Rewrites:

```slop
We are at the forefront of AI innovation.
```

After: We shipped on-device speech recognition for Android in 2023, a year before the platform did.

```slop
Our lab is at the forefront of battery research.
```

After: Our lab published the first solid-state cell to pass 1,000 charge cycles at room temperature.

```slop
The company has been at the forefront of the industry for decades.
```

After: The company has made industrial pumps since 1962 and holds 40 patents.

- Literal use: for the front of a physical space, write "at the front".

#### 316. `on the cusp`

- Kind: phrase. Banned forms: `on the cusp`, `on the cusp of`, `on the verge of`, `on the brink of`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `on the cusp of` places a result just ahead in time so the writer never has to say when it arrives. Models use it for breakthroughs and launches that have no date. The reader cannot tell whether `cusp` means next week or next decade.
- Where it shows up: research news, startup announcements, and investor updates.

```slop
We are on the cusp of a breakthrough in battery life.
The industry is on the cusp of a major shift to edge computing.
Our team is on the verge of launching something big.
```

Replace with:

- The date or the condition: "ships in March", "after the FDA review".
- The current status, named: "in private beta with 40 users".
- The specific result so far, with its number.
- Cut it when there is no date and no status; then there is no news.

Rewrites:

```slop
We are on the cusp of a breakthrough in battery life.
```

After: Our test cell holds 80% of its charge after 1,500 cycles; production samples are due in Q2.

```slop
The industry is on the cusp of a major shift to edge computing.
```

After: Three of our five largest customers asked to run inference on their own hardware this year.

```slop
Our team is on the verge of launching something big.
```

After: We launch shared workspaces on 12 November.

- Literal use: in geometry or astrology, `cusp` is a defined term; use it as a noun in that field only, in its technical sense.

#### 317. `pave the way`

- Kind: phrase. Banned forms: `pave the way`, `paves the way for`, `paving the way`, `lay the groundwork`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `paves the way for` describes a change by what it might enable later, so the change itself goes unnamed. Models use it to inflate a small step ("this refactor paves the way for future features"). The future features are never listed.
- Where it shows up: PR descriptions, roadmap posts, and grant applications.

```slop
This refactor paves the way for future improvements.
Her research paved the way for modern vaccines.
The new API lays the groundwork for a plugin system.
```

Replace with:

- "lets us" or "unblocks" followed by the named next step.
- "is required for" when the change is a prerequisite.
- The specific later result and the link between the two.
- Cut it when the future step is not planned; describe the change on its own terms.

Rewrites:

```slop
This refactor paves the way for future improvements.
```

After: This refactor splits `Editor` into 4 components, so we can lazy-load the toolbar next sprint.

```slop
Her research paved the way for modern vaccines.
```

After: Her 2005 paper showed how to stop the immune system attacking synthetic mRNA; both 2020 mRNA vaccines use that method.

```slop
The new API lays the groundwork for a plugin system.
```

After: The new API exposes hooks for save and export; plugins will register against them in v3.

- Literal use: for road work, write "pave the road" or "resurface the car park".

#### 318. `bridge the gap`

- Kind: phrase. Banned forms: `bridge the gap`, `bridges the gap between`, `bridging the gap`, `close the gap`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `bridges the gap between X and Y` names two groups and claims a connection without describing it. Models use it for any tool that sits between two roles, most often design and development. The mechanism, which is the only useful part, is left out.
- Where it shows up: product taglines, conference talk titles, and job descriptions.

```slop
Our tool bridges the gap between design and development.
This course bridges the gap between theory and practice.
We are bridging the gap between patients and doctors.
```

Replace with:

- The mechanism: what moves from one side to the other, and how.
- The specific thing learners do, for courses.
- The action either party takes, named.
- Cut it when you cannot name what crosses the gap.

Rewrites:

```slop
Our tool bridges the gap between design and development.
```

After: The plugin exports Figma color and spacing styles as CSS variables in one file.

```slop
This course bridges the gap between theory and practice.
```

After: Each week you read one paper and then implement its algorithm in Python.

```slop
We are bridging the gap between patients and doctors.
```

After: Patients book a video visit with a GP in under 10 minutes.

- Literal use: for a measured difference, give both numbers: "cut the gap between test and production timings from 300ms to 20ms".

#### 319. `stand out from the crowd`

- Kind: phrase. Banned forms: `stand out from the crowd`, `stand out from the competition`, `set yourself apart`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `stand out from the crowd` promises a difference and names neither the crowd nor the difference. Models write it for resume services, design agencies, and portfolio templates, so the same promise appears across every competitor. Copy that claims distinction in a stock phrase undercuts itself.
- Where it shows up: agency sites, resume advice, and app store descriptions.

```slop
Make your portfolio stand out from the crowd.
Our designs help your brand stand out from the competition.
Set yourself apart with a resume that gets noticed.
```

Replace with:

- The specific difference, named: what you have that the others do not.
- The outcome with a number: interview rate, click rate.
- The concrete service step.
- Cut it when the difference is not stated in the same sentence.

Rewrites:

```slop
Make your portfolio stand out from the crowd.
```

After: Show 3 projects, each with the problem, your role, and one result in numbers.

```slop
Our designs help your brand stand out from the competition.
```

After: We design packaging for coffee roasters; our last 5 clients moved into 2 national supermarket chains.

```slop
Set yourself apart with a resume that gets noticed.
```

After: We rewrite your resume around outcomes; clients report a 30% higher callback rate.

- Literal use: for visual contrast, give the values: "the button is #B4441C on #F7F5F0, the only orange on the page".

#### 320. `cut through the noise`

- Kind: phrase. Banned forms: `cut through the noise`, `cuts through the clutter`, `rise above the noise`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `cut through the noise` claims a filter without describing what it filters or by what rule. Models use it for newsletters, dashboards, and analytics tools. The phrase itself is one of the stock lines that makes up the noise.
- Where it shows up: newsletter signups, monitoring tool pages, and marketing plans.

```slop
Our newsletter cuts through the noise to bring you what matters.
The dashboard helps your team cut through the noise.
Cut through the clutter with smart notifications.
```

Replace with:

- The filter rule: what is shown and what is hidden.
- The count: "5 links a week", "one alert per incident".
- The source and the selection method.
- Cut it when there is no stated rule.

Rewrites:

```slop
Our newsletter cuts through the noise to bring you what matters.
```

After: Every Friday, 5 links on database engineering, each with a two-line summary.

```slop
The dashboard helps your team cut through the noise.
```

After: The dashboard shows only services with errors above 1% in the last hour.

```slop
Cut through the clutter with smart notifications.
```

After: Related alerts are grouped into one notification per incident.

- Literal use: for audio, name the method: "the noise gate removes hum below -40 dB".

#### 321. `ahead of the curve`

- Kind: phrase. Banned forms: `ahead of the curve`, `stay ahead of the curve`, `stay ahead`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `ahead of the curve` claims early adoption without naming what was adopted or when. Models use it in course pages and consulting copy that sell anxiety about falling behind. The curve is never drawn.
- Where it shows up: newsletters, course pages, and consulting pitches.

```slop
Stay ahead of the curve with our weekly AI briefing.
Our clients are always ahead of the curve.
This framework keeps your team ahead of the curve.
```

Replace with:

- What the reader learns, and how soon after it happens.
- The specific early move a client made, with its date.
- The concrete feature the framework has that others lack.
- Cut it when there is no date; "ahead" needs a time to be ahead of.

Rewrites:

```slop
Stay ahead of the curve with our weekly AI briefing.
```

After: Each Monday: the model releases and papers from the past week, in 10 minutes of reading.

```slop
Our clients are always ahead of the curve.
```

After: Two of our clients moved to passkeys in 2023, before their banks did.

```slop
This framework keeps your team ahead of the curve.
```

After: The framework supports React Server Components and streaming without a plugin.

- Literal use: for a chart or a grading curve, name the axis and value: "scores above the median".

#### 322. `push the boundaries`

- Kind: phrase. Banned forms: `push the boundaries`, `pushing the envelope`, `push the limits`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `push the boundaries` claims a limit was moved without naming the limit or the new position. Models use it for creative work and engineering alike. Most work described this way is ordinary work done well.
- Where it shows up: portfolio sites, design award entries, and company values pages.

```slop
We push the boundaries of what's possible on the web.
Her work pushes the boundaries of typography.
Our engineers push the limits of performance every day.
```

Replace with:

- The specific limit and the new value: "a 3D scene in 60 KB of JavaScript".
- What was done that others had not done, with a source.
- A number for performance.
- Cut it when the work is good but not new; say what it is.

Rewrites:

```slop
We push the boundaries of what's possible on the web.
```

After: Our product page renders a 3D model in 60 KB of JavaScript and runs at 60 fps on a 2019 phone.

```slop
Her work pushes the boundaries of typography.
```

After: She designed a variable font with a width axis that adjusts to the reader's screen size.

```slop
Our engineers push the limits of performance every day.
```

After: Our matching engine handles 2 million orders per second on 4 servers.

- Literal use: for a property line or a UI hit area, name the edge: "the drag handle extends 8px past the card border".

#### 323. `outside the box`

- Kind: phrase. Banned forms: `outside the box`, `think outside the box`, `out-of-the-box thinking`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `think outside the box` announces an unusual idea and delivers none. It is one of the oldest business clichés, and models use it in job ads and team values lists. The phrase is itself inside the box it names.
- Where it shows up: job descriptions, workshop invitations, and pitch decks.

```slop
We're looking for engineers who think outside the box.
Our team takes an outside-the-box approach to problem solving.
This workshop teaches you to think outside the box.
```

Replace with:

- The unusual idea, stated: what was tried that is not the default.
- The kind of problem candidates will solve, with an example.
- The exercise the workshop runs.
- Cut it when no unusual idea follows.

Rewrites:

```slop
We're looking for engineers who think outside the box.
```

After: You will cut our cloud bill; last year an engineer saved 30% by moving batch jobs to spot instances.

```slop
Our team takes an outside-the-box approach to problem solving.
```

After: Before writing code, we test each feature as a paper prototype with 5 users.

```slop
This workshop teaches you to think outside the box.
```

After: In this workshop you write 20 headline options in 10 minutes, then cut to 3.

- Literal use: for software defaults, write "by default" or "with no setup": "works with no config". For packaging, write "in the box" with the contents.

#### 324. `a wide range of`

- Kind: phrase. Banned forms: `a wide range of`, `a broad range of`, `a whole range of`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `a wide range of` stands in for a list the writer did not make or a count they did not check. Models produce it whenever a brief says a product supports many things. The reader cannot tell whether the range is 4 or 400.
- Where it shows up: feature pages, integration lists, and service descriptions.

```slop
We support a wide range of file formats.
The library works with a wide range of frameworks.
Our team has experience across a wide range of industries.
```

Replace with:

- The count and the top items: "42 formats, including PDF, DOCX, and HEIC".
- The full list, if it is under 8 items.
- The two or three industries with the most work, and the project count.
- Cut it when the list follows; the list proves the range.

Rewrites:

```slop
We support a wide range of file formats.
```

After: We read 42 formats, including PDF, DOCX, HEIC, and RAW files from 30 camera brands.

```slop
The library works with a wide range of frameworks.
```

After: The library works with React, Vue, Svelte, and plain JavaScript.

```slop
Our team has experience across a wide range of industries.
```

After: We have built 30 apps for banks and 12 for hospitals.

- Literal use: for a numeric range, give the range: "8 to 64 GB", "temperatures from -20 to 45 C".

#### 325. `a wide array of`

- Kind: phrase. Banned forms: `a wide array of`, `an array of`, `a broad array of`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `a wide array of` is the formal twin of "range", and models alternate the two within a page to avoid repeating themselves. The word "array" adds an air of precision to a phrase that has none. In technical writing it also collides with the data structure.
- Where it shows up: course catalogs, "Our services" pages, and generated documentation intros.

```slop
The platform offers a wide array of customization options.
Students can choose from a wide array of electives.
The SDK provides a wide array of helper functions.
```

Replace with:

- The specific options a user will look for first: colors, fonts, layout.
- A count with a link to the full list.
- The three helpers most people need, by name.
- Cut it when the next sentence lists the items.

Rewrites:

```slop
The platform offers a wide array of customization options.
```

After: You can change the logo, the accent color, the font, and the email sender name.

```slop
Students can choose from a wide array of electives.
```

After: Students choose 4 of 26 electives; the full list is on the course page.

```slop
The SDK provides a wide array of helper functions.
```

After: The SDK includes `retry()`, `paginate()`, and `signRequest()`, plus 18 smaller helpers.

- Literal use: for the data structure, give its type and size: "an array of 4,096 `u32` entries". For hardware, "a solar array of 24 panels".

#### 326. `look no further`

- Kind: opener. Banned forms: `look no further`, `search no more`, `you've come to the right place`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `Look no further` answers a question the reader did not ask and claims to end a search the page has not ended. It is a classifieds and SEO opener, and models reproduce it at the top of product and service pages. The sentence before it is usually a rhetorical question about the reader's needs.
- Where it shows up: SEO landing pages, local business sites, and app store blurbs.

```slop
Looking for a reliable hosting provider? Look no further.
Look no further for the perfect React component library.
If you need a plumber in Leeds, you've come to the right place.
```

Replace with:

- The offer, stated in the first sentence: who you are, what you do, where.
- The specific proof: uptime, price, coverage area.
- A direct call to action with the next step.
- Cut it when the headline already says what you sell.

Rewrites:

```slop
Looking for a reliable hosting provider? Look no further.
```

After: Managed Postgres hosting in Frankfurt with 99.95% uptime over the past 12 months.

```slop
Look no further for the perfect React component library.
```

After: 48 accessible React components, styled with CSS variables and no runtime dependency.

```slop
If you need a plumber in Leeds, you've come to the right place.
```

After: Plumbers in Leeds, same-day visits, call-out fee 60 pounds.

- Literal use: none.

#### 327. `whether you're`

- Kind: phrase. Banned forms: `whether you're`, `whether you are a`, `whether you're a beginner or a pro`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `Whether you're a beginner or a seasoned pro` names two poles of an audience to claim it serves everyone. Models write this two-pole sentence at the top of tutorials and product pages because briefs rarely name a reader. A text written for everyone fits nobody, and the phrase admits it.
- Where it shows up: tutorial intros, course pages, and product heroes.

```slop
Whether you're a beginner or a seasoned pro, this guide has something for you.
Whether you're building a blog or an enterprise app, our framework scales.
Whether you're on the go or at your desk, stay connected.
```

Replace with:

- The one reader you wrote for, named: "This guide is for developers who know Git and have never used rebase."
- Two paths with labels, if you serve two audiences: "New to Git: start at 2.1. Already use it: skip to 4."
- The actual limits: smallest and largest supported case, in numbers.
- Cut it when the poles are invented; pick the reader.

Rewrites:

```slop
Whether you're a beginner or a seasoned pro, this guide has something for you.
```

After: This guide is for developers who use Git daily and have never run `git rebase -i`.

```slop
Whether you're building a blog or an enterprise app, our framework scales.
```

After: Sites built with the framework range from 3 pages to 40,000; build time grows about linearly.

```slop
Whether you're on the go or at your desk, stay connected.
```

After: The app syncs between phone and desktop within 2 seconds.

- Literal use: in a form or a branching instruction, write the condition as "If you are X, do Y."

#### 328. `more than just`

- Kind: phrase. Banned forms: `more than just`, `not just a`, `so much more than`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `more than just a X` sets up a category so it can claim to exceed it, and then the extra is rarely named. Models use this reframe in product taglines and About pages (`more than just a to-do app`). It is a variant of the "not X, but Y" shape, which the house style bans.
- Where it shows up: taglines, About pages, and feature launch posts.

```slop
It's more than just a to-do app.
We're more than just an agency; we're your partner.
Our coffee is more than just a drink.
```

Replace with:

- The category, then the specific extra: "A to-do app with a shared calendar."
- What you do for the client, with a duration or count.
- The product facts: origin, roast, price.
- Cut it when the extra is a feeling; name a feature or drop the line.

```slop
It's more than just a to-do app.
```

After: A to-do app that blocks time on your calendar for each task.

```slop
We're more than just an agency; we're your partner.
```

After: We run your ads and join your weekly planning call; average client stay is 4 years.

```slop
Our coffee is more than just a drink.
```

After: Single-origin beans from Huila, Colombia, roasted on Tuesdays and shipped Wednesdays.

- Literal use: for a minimum, use a number: "more than 3 retries", "over 10 GB".

#### 329. `imagine a world`

- Kind: opener. Banned forms: `imagine a world`, `imagine a world where`, `imagine if`, `what if you could`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `Imagine a world where` opens a pitch with a fantasy so the product can arrive as its fulfillment. Models produce it for keynote openers and landing pages. The imagined world is a feature list in the future tense.
- Where it shows up: pitch decks, keynote scripts, and the first paragraph of launch posts.


- The measured time, for "minutes not months" claims.

```slop
Imagine a world where deployments never fail.
```

```slop
What if you could build an app in minutes, not months?
```

#### 330. `picture this`

- Kind: opener. Banned forms: `picture this`, `picture this:`, `imagine this`, `envision this`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `Picture this:` opens a staged scenario, usually a frustrated user at 2am, so the product can enter as the fix. Models use it to fake a story at the top of a blog post. The scenario is generic, so the reader does not see themselves in it.

```slop

Picture this: your team ships features twice as fast.
Imagine this: you open your laptop and your tasks are already sorted.
```

- The measured result, stated as fact.

- Cut it when the scenario is invented; use a real one or none.

```slop
Picture this: it's 2am and production is down.
```

After: At 02:14 on 9 May our payments API went down for 47 minutes because a certificate expired.

```slop
Imagine this: you open your laptop and your tasks are already sorted.
```

After: Each morning the app sorts your tasks by due date and blocks out meetings.

#### 331. `here's the thing`

- Kind: opener. Banned forms: `here's the thing`, `here's the kicker`, `here's why`, `here's what`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `Here's the thing:` builds suspense before a point that could have been the first sentence. It is a spoken tic copied into writing, and models use it to signal candor. The house style also bans the colon reveal it introduces.
- Where it shows up: opinion posts, LinkedIn posts, and chat replies that push back.

```slop

Here's why that matters: users notice slow pages.
```

- The point, as the first sentence.
- The fact placed with the others, at its normal weight.
- The cause and effect in one sentence with "because".
- Cut it every time; the clause after it stands alone.

```slop
Here's the thing: most apps don't need a microservices architecture.
```


#### 332. `the best part`

- Kind: phrase. Banned forms: `the best part`, `the best part?`, `best of all`, `and the best part is`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `The best part?` sets up a reveal with a fragment question and a one-line answer, usually the price or a feature. Models use the shape in marketing and social posts. The rhetorical question is banned by house style, and the reveal is usually a fact that belongs in a list.
- Where it shows up: product launches, social posts, and newsletter promos.

```slop
And the best part is, you don't need to write any code.
```

- The fact in the place where readers look for it: price in the pricing line, requirements in the setup section.

#### 333. `i hope this helps`

- Kind: closer. Banned forms: `i hope this helps`, `hope this helps`, `I hope this clarifies`, `I hope you found this useful`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `I hope this helps` is the default last line of a chat assistant answer, appended whether the answer was a fix, a list, or a refusal. It adds no information and asks the reader to absorb a pleasantry at the point they want to act. When agents leave it in code comments or commit messages, it shows that chat output was pasted without edits.
- Where it shows up: the last line of chat replies, Stack Overflow answers, and code comments written by assistants.

```slop
Let me know if you have any other questions. I hope this helps!
// Hope this helps! This function handles the edge case you mentioned.
I hope this clarifies the difference between `let` and `const`.
```

Replace with:

- The last step or the verification command, as the final line: "Run `npm test` to confirm."
- The one open question that changes the answer: "If you are on Node 16, use option B instead."
- In code comments, the reason for the code and nothing else.
- Cut it every time; end on the answer.

Rewrites:

```slop
Let me know if you have any other questions. I hope this helps!
```

After: Run `npm run build` again; the error should be gone. If it remains, send the full stack trace.

```slop

```

After: `// Returns null for empty input; callers in checkout rely on this.`

```slop
I hope this clarifies the difference between `let` and `const`.
```

After: Use `const` unless you reassign the variable; `let` is for counters and loop state.

- Literal use: none in technical text. In a personal letter, say what you hope for specifically: "I hope the move to Lyon goes smoothly."

#### 334. `happy coding`

- Kind: closer. Banned forms: `happy coding`, `happy hacking`, `happy building`, `happy debugging`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `Happy coding!` is the sign-off of generated tutorials and chat answers, added after the last code block. It came from forum and blog culture and models copy it as a friendly default. In a README or a code comment it reads as filler a reviewer will delete.
- Where it shows up: tutorial endings, README files, chat replies with code, and generated code comments.

```slop
Now you're ready to deploy. Happy building!
```

- A next step link: "Next: add authentication (part 3)."

#### 335. `feel free to`

- Kind: phrase. Banned forms: `feel free to`, `please feel free`, `you're welcome to`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `feel free to` grants permission the reader did not need. Chat assistants close almost every answer with `Feel free to ask if you have more questions`, and generated docs use it for every optional step. The phrase hides whether the action is required, optional, or a good idea.

- The imperative, when you want the action: "Open an issue."
- A condition, when it depends: "If requests time out on slow networks, raise `timeout` to 30s."

#### 336. `don't hesitate`

- Kind: phrase. Banned forms: `don't hesitate`, `do not hesitate to`, `don't hesitate to reach out`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `Don't hesitate to reach out` assumes the reader was hesitating and offers contact without saying how or when anyone will answer. Models end support replies and emails with it. It is customer-service boilerplate and readers skip it.

```slop

Don't hesitate to let me know if anything is unclear.
```

- The channel and the response time: "Email support@ (reply within 1 working day)."

```slop
Don't hesitate to let me know if anything is unclear.
```

After: (Delete the line. If one step is likely to confuse, explain that step.)

- Literal use: none.

#### 337. `great question`

- Kind: opener. Banned forms: `great question`, `good question`, `that's a great question`, `excellent question`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `Great question!` is the sycophantic opener tuned into chat assistants by preference training, where raters rewarded warmth. It praises the question before answering it, so every question gets the same grade. In a pull request reply or code comment it reads as a bot talking.
- Where it shows up: the first line of chat answers, support replies, and replies to code review comments.

```slop
Great question! The difference between `==` and `===` is type coercion.

Good question! Let me explain how the event loop works.
```

Replace with:

- The answer as the first sentence.

```slop
Great question! The difference between `==` and `===` is type coercion.
```



After: The event loop runs one task, then all queued microtasks, then renders, then picks the next task.

#### 338. `as an ai`

- Kind: opener. Banned forms: `as an ai`, `as an AI language model`, `as a large language model`, `I'm just an AI`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `As an AI language model, I cannot` is the refusal and disclaimer template of early chat assistants, and it now marks text as pasted from a chat window. It puts the speaker's nature ahead of the information, and often precedes an answer the model gives anyway. In code comments and docs it is a sign nobody edited the output.
- Where it shows up: chat refusals, generated reviews and essays, and code comments from assistants.

- The limit, stated as a fact about the task: "I have not run this code."

#### 339. `i'd be happy to`

- Kind: opener. Banned forms: `i'd be happy to`, `I'd be glad to`, `I'm happy to help`, `happy to help`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `I'd be happy to help!` opens a chat answer by announcing willingness before doing the work. Assistants tuned for politeness put it at the top of nearly every reply. The reader asked for the help, so the offer delays it.

- The scope of the simplification: what was removed or automated.
- The audience and the outcome.
- Cut it when the noun is the whole tagline; write a sentence.

Rewrites:

```slop
Invoicing made simple.
```

After: Send an invoice in 30 seconds; we chase late payers for you.

```slop
Kubernetes made easy for developers.
```

After: Deploy to Kubernetes from a `Procfile`; we write the manifests.

```slop
Accounting, simplified.
```

After: Bookkeeping for freelancers: connect your bank and we sort transactions into tax categories.

- Literal use: for a math or code operation, name it: "the reduced fraction", "the refactored function".

#### 346. `take your`

- Kind: phrase. Banned forms: `take your`, `take your X to the next level`, `take your business further`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `Take your X to Y` frames the product as a vehicle and the reader's work as cargo going somewhere better. Models use it as a call to action in every industry (`Take your workflow to new heights`). The destination is never a place the reader can check.
- Where it shows up: call-to-action buttons, hero subheads, and course ads.

```slop
Take your workflow to new heights.
Take your career further with our certification.
Take your photos from good to great.
```

Replace with:

- The result, measured: "Close tickets in half the time."
- What the certificate qualifies the reader to do, and its cost.
- The specific edit the tool makes.
- Cut it when there is no destination you can name.

Rewrites:

```slop
Take your workflow to new heights.
```

After: Replace your morning status meeting with a 5-line written update.

```slop
Take your career further with our certification.
```

After: The certificate prepares you for the AWS architect associate exam; it costs 300 pounds and takes 8 weeks.

```slop
Take your photos from good to great.
```

After: Fix exposure, straighten horizons, and remove dust spots in one pass.

- Literal use: for an instruction about carrying an object, use another verb: "Bring your passport to the desk", "There is no time limit."

#### 347. `in the world of`

- Kind: opener. Banned forms: `in the world of`, `in the realm of`, `in the space of`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `In the world of X,` opens a sentence by naming a field as if it were a separate place, so the writer can state a generality about it. Models use it to begin articles and sections (`In the world of web development, speed matters`). The field is the topic of the whole page, so naming it again adds nothing.
- Where it shows up: blog openers, section intros, and LinkedIn posts.

```slop
In the world of web development, performance is everything.
In the world of startups, speed matters.
In the world of finance, trust is key.
```

Replace with:

- The claim, scoped by a subject: "On e-commerce sites, each extra second of load time lowers conversion."
- The specific evidence for the generality.
- Nothing, if the field is the topic of the page.
- Cut it when the sentence after it is a platitude; cut the platitude too.

Rewrites:

```slop
In the world of web development, performance is everything.
```

After: On our store, conversion fell 7% for every extra second of load time.

```slop
In the world of startups, speed matters.
```

After: We had 9 months of runway, so we cut the launch scope to 3 features.

```slop
In the world of finance, trust is key.
```

After: Customers can see every fee before they confirm a transfer.

- Literal use: for geography, name the place: "in 40 countries".

#### 348. `when it comes to`

- Kind: phrase. Banned forms: `when it comes to`, `when it comes down to`, `in terms of`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `When it comes to X,` fronts the topic before the sentence starts, and the main clause then has a weak subject ("it", "there"). Models use the shape to change topics between paragraphs without a real transition. It adds four words and moves the subject to the wrong place.
- Where it shows up: comparison articles, advice posts, and chat answers.

```slop
When it comes to performance, Go is hard to beat.
When it comes to styling, there are many options.
When it comes to testing, it's best to start small.
```

Replace with:

- The topic as the subject of the sentence: "Go compiles to one binary and starts in 10ms."
- The options, listed, for "many options" lines.
- The instruction, directly: "Write one test for the checkout total first."
- Cut it when the topic is already the subject of the paragraph.

Rewrites:

```slop
When it comes to performance, Go is hard to beat.
```

After: Our Go service handles 4 times the requests of the Python one on the same hardware.

```slop
When it comes to styling, there are many options.
```

After: Style React with CSS modules, Tailwind, or a CSS-in-JS library; we use CSS modules.

```slop
When it comes to testing, it's best to start small.
```

After: Start with one test for the checkout total, the function that loses money when it breaks.

- Literal use: for an event that may happen, write "if" or "when" with a plain verb: "When the order arrives, scan the code."

#### 349. `the art of`

- Kind: phrase. Banned forms: `the art of`, `master the art of`, `the fine art of`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `the art of X` dresses a skill as a craft tradition so a guide can promise mastery. Models produce it for titles (`Mastering the art of prompt engineering`), applying it to tasks with a checklist. The phrase implies talent where the content teaches steps.
- Where it shows up: course titles, blog headlines, and book subtitles.

```slop
Master the art of writing clean code.
The art of the perfect pull request.
Learn the fine art of giving feedback.
```

Replace with:

- The skill as a task, with its scope: "How to split a 1,000-line PR into 4."
- The specific steps the guide teaches, named.
- The outcome the reader will have afterward.
- Cut it when the guide is a checklist; title it as one.

Rewrites:

```slop
Master the art of writing clean code.
```

After: Name functions after what they return, keep them under 40 lines, and test each one.

```slop
The art of the perfect pull request.
```

After: How to write a pull request: under 400 lines, one change, and a description with a test plan.

```slop
Learn the fine art of giving feedback.
```

After: Give feedback in three parts: what you saw, its effect, and what to change.

- Literal use: for actual art, name the artist or period: "Bauhaus posters", "work by Anni Albers".

#### 350. `the heart of`

- Kind: phrase. Banned forms: `the heart of`, `at the heart of`, `heart and soul`.
- Why it reads as machine text: `at the heart of` claims centrality for a value or component without showing it. Models write `At the heart of our platform is a commitment to X`, where X is a value every company lists. For components, the phrase replaces a diagram or a dependency count.
- Where it shows up: About pages, architecture overviews, and travel copy (`in the heart of the city`).

```slop
At the heart of our platform is a commitment to privacy.
The scheduler lies at the heart of the system.
Our hotel is located in the heart of Lisbon.
```

Replace with:

- The policy or mechanism that shows the value: "We store no message content; it is encrypted on your device."
- The dependency fact: "Every job passes through the scheduler; if it stops, nothing runs."
- The location with a distance: "200m from Rossio station."
- Cut it when the value is not backed by a policy.

Rewrites:

```slop
At the heart of our platform is a commitment to privacy.
```

After: Messages are encrypted on your device; our servers never see the content.

```slop
The scheduler lies at the heart of the system.
```

After: Every job passes through the scheduler; if it stops, no job runs.

```slop
Our hotel is located in the heart of Lisbon.
```

After: The hotel is in Baixa, 200m from Rossio station.

- Literal use: for an actual heart, drop the "of" construction: write "a patient's heart" or "the heart" and name the part, "the left ventricle".

## Part 8. Sentences, Structure and Microcopy

A page with flat surfaces, one accent and a 2px radius still reads as generated when the hero says `Unlock seamless workflows`. Readers spot machine copy before they notice the shadows, because they read the words first. This part covers the words: the sentence patterns that mark copy as model output, the punctuation and formatting rules that follow from them, microcopy for each interface context, and voice.

Conventions for this part. Every bad example sits in a `slop` fence. Every rewrite sits in a `text` fence or in plain prose, and you can paste it. Examples use a fictional invoicing product called Tidemark so that the rewrites can carry real-looking facts. Replace those facts with your own; never ship the sample numbers.

### 8.1 How tells work

A single tell proves nothing. People write "not this, but that" and lists of three every day. The signal is density and placement. When the same construction appears in every paragraph, in the same slot (first sentence, last sentence, every heading), the reader stops reading the content and starts reading the template.

Use these thresholds when you edit or review copy:

- One instance of a given tell per 500 words is style. Leave it.
- Two instances of the same tell per 500 words is a habit. Rewrite one.
- Three or more instances of any tells in a single paragraph is a template. Rewrite the paragraph from its facts.

Models produce these patterns for three concrete reasons. First, the training data is heavy with landing pages, keynote scripts, SEO blog posts and social threads, which use the same moves to sound persuasive. Second, preference tuning rewards answers that sound complete and confident, so constructions that signal "a point is being made" score well even when no point is made. Third, decoding favors high-probability continuations, and phrases like "Here is why" or "The result:" are among the safest bridges between two sentences. None of these reasons involves your reader.

The fastest edit procedure for a draft full of tells:

1. Delete the first and last sentence of every paragraph. Reread. If nothing is lost, leave them deleted. This removes most openers and summaries in one pass.
2. Replace each adjective with a number, a name or a noun. If you cannot, delete the adjective.
3. Read the text aloud at speaking pace. Anything you would not say to a colleague across a desk gets rewritten.
4. Run `scripts/lint.py` and the searches in Part 9 to catch what your ear missed.

### 8.2 Tells of framing and argument

These tells shape how a sentence makes its claim. Each one substitutes a rhetorical move for a fact.

#### The false contrast: "It is not X, it is Y"

The sentence denies a claim nobody made, then asserts the real one. Variants include "X isn't just A. It's B.", "This is not about A. It is about B." and the clipped "Less A, more B." The negated half exists only to make the second half feel like a reveal.

Models produce it because it is the most common move in keynote and landing page copy, and because the negated half costs nothing: it needs no evidence and adds no information. Preference tuning rewards it because it reads as an opinion with conviction.

```slop
Tidemark isn't an invoicing tool. It's a new way to run your business.
This is not a redesign. It is a rethink of how teams collaborate.
Onboarding isn't about features. It's about confidence.
We don't sell software. We sell peace of mind.
```

```text
Tidemark sends invoices, records payments and reminds late clients by email.
The new editor saves every 2 seconds and shows who else is typing.
The first screen asks for one thing: the name of your first client.
Tidemark costs $12 a month. Cancel from Settings at any time.
```

Rule: state the positive claim alone. Keep a contrast only when the negated half is a misconception your readers hold, you can name it, and you give evidence against it. Once per page at most.

#### "Not just X, but Y"

An escalation that claims more scope than the sentence delivers. Variants: `not only A but also B`, `more than just a tool`, `A, B, and so much more`, `and beyond`. The second item is almost always vaguer than the first, so the sentence ends weaker than it started.

Models use it to sound generous. When a prompt says "describe the product", the model has one concrete feature and an instruction to sound large, so it adds an abstract second half.

```slop
Tidemark is not just an invoicing tool, but a complete financial command center.
It's more than just a calendar. It's your team's heartbeat.
Not only faster, but smarter.
Track expenses, send invoices, and so much more.
```

```text
Tidemark sends invoices and emails late clients after 7, 14 and 30 days.
The calendar shows each person's working hours in their own time zone.
Search returns results in under 100ms on workspaces with 50,000 documents.
Track expenses, send invoices and export to Xero or DATEV.
```

Rule: name the second thing concretely or cut it. "And more" means the list is unfinished. Finish the list or end the sentence.

#### Tricolons and groups of three

Three adjectives, three parallel clauses, three short imperative sentences, three bullet points, three feature cards. "Fast, simple and secure." "Plan. Build. Ship." The cadence of three is the default rhythm of generated copy, and it shows up far more often than two or four.

The rule of three is drilled into speechwriting and advertising, and models learned that three items sound finished. Layout templates add pressure: the Tailwind UI feature section is `grid-cols-3`, so the copy is written to fill exactly three slots whatever the product actually has.

```slop
Fast, secure, and reliable.
Plan smarter. Build faster. Ship with confidence.
Simple to use, easy to scale, and built to last.
Collaborate in real time, track progress effortlessly, and deliver results that matter.
```

```text
Pages load in 0.8 seconds on a 4G connection.
Plan the sprint in Tidemark, then ship it. Releases link back to their tasks.
Setup takes 10 minutes. It runs on one Postgres database.
Two people can edit the same invoice, and each sees the other's cursor.
```

Rule: count the items you actually have. Two facts get two items; four facts get four. Never pad a list to three and never trim one to three. In front of a noun, use at most one adjective, and prefer a number.

#### The colon reveal

A short setup, a colon or question mark, then the payoff: "The result: ...", "The secret? ...", "One word: speed." It builds suspense for a sentence that does not need any.

Newsletter and social thread writing uses it to keep readers scrolling, and models absorbed the cadence. The setup phrases ("The result", "The catch", "The bottom line") are high-probability bridges that let the model emphasize without adding a fact.

```slop
The result: a workflow that finally makes sense.
The secret? Consistency.
One word: speed.
The bottom line: your team ships faster.
```

```text
After the switch, month-end close took 2 days instead of 5.
Teams that sent invoices on the same weekday each month were paid 6 days sooner on average.
Builds take 40 seconds, down from 3 minutes.
```

Rule: put the payoff in the subject or verb of a normal sentence. Use a colon to introduce a list, a quotation, an example or a definition. Never use it for suspense.

#### Rhetorical question openers

A section or page that opens with a question the reader did not ask, answered in the next sentence. "Tired of juggling spreadsheets?" "What if your inbox could sort itself?" "Ever wondered why your builds are slow?"

Copywriting formulas such as problem, agitate, solve open with a question, and so do most SEO blog introductions. A model told to `make it engaging` reaches for the question first because it is the most common opening in that register.

```slop
Tired of chasing late payments?
What if your documentation wrote itself?
Ever wondered why your builds are so slow?
Why settle for less?
```

```text
Tidemark emails clients when an invoice is 7 days late.
```
