```text
The CLI generates reference pages from your OpenAPI file.
Most slow builds re-download dependencies on every run. Cache the lockfile hash.
```

Rule: open with the answer. Questions belong where the reader asked them: FAQ headings, search placeholders, form fields and confirmation dialogs.

#### "Imagine..."

A second-person fantasy before the product appears. `Imagine never losing a receipt again.` `Picture this: it is Friday at 5pm and your inbox is empty.` The reader is asked to invent the benefit the copy failed to state.

Ad scripts and keynote openings use the move to set a scene. A model with no facts to report can generate a scene indefinitely, which makes this a reliable filler.

```slop
Imagine a world where meetings run themselves.
Picture this: it's Friday at 5pm and your inbox is empty.
Imagine never losing a receipt again.
What if invoicing just... happened?
```

```text
Tidemark posts meeting notes to the channel within a minute of the call ending.
Forward a receipt to receipts@tidemark.example and it is attached to the matching expense.
Recurring invoices go out on the date you set, with the hours from your timesheet.
```

Rule: describe the state the product produces, in the present tense, with the mechanism that produces it. Readers can imagine without instruction.

#### "Here is why"

A sentence that announces the next sentence. `Here's why that matters.` `Here's how it works:` `Here's the thing.` `And that's exactly why we built Tidemark.` It delays the content by one sentence and adds nothing.

Assistant tuning rewards answers that sign their structure, and thread-style writing uses the announcement as a hook before each point. It is cheap to generate and scores as "clear".

```slop
We rebuilt the sync engine. Here's why that matters.
Here's the thing: most teams don't need another dashboard.
Here's how it works:
And that's exactly why we built Tidemark.
```

```text
We rebuilt the sync engine, so edits made offline now merge without conflicts.
Most teams already have a dashboard. Tidemark sends a weekly email instead.
Connect your bank. Tidemark matches each payment to its invoice.
We built Tidemark after spending a full day each month on our own invoices.
```

Rule: delete the announcing sentence and start with the reason. "How it works" may stay as a heading above a numbered procedure.

#### The summary sentence that restates the paragraph

The last sentence repeats the paragraph in vaguer words. `In short, your data is always safe.` `Simply put, Tidemark saves you time.` `The takeaway? Small changes add up.` At section level it becomes a closing paragraph that starts with `In conclusion`.

School essay structure (topic sentence, support, conclusion) is all over the training data, and raters prefer answers that close neatly. The model ends every unit with a wrap-up whether the unit needs one or not.

```slop
Exports run nightly and are stored for 90 days. In short, your data is always safe.
Simply put, Tidemark saves you time.
The takeaway? Small changes add up.
All in all, it's a win-win for everyone.
```

```text
Exports run nightly and are stored for 90 days in a second region.
Tidemark fills in client details from your last invoice to that client.
Moving the default due date from 30 days to 14 cut the share of late invoices from 31% to 22%.
```

Rule: end the paragraph on its last new fact. A paragraph long enough to need a summary is long enough to split.

#### The "Whether you are A or B" opener

An opener that claims two opposite audiences at once: `Whether you're a solo founder or a Fortune 500 company...`, `for teams of all sizes`, `from beginners to experts`. Writing for everyone means the reader cannot tell whether the product is for them.

Prompts rarely specify the audience, so the model covers every possibility in one clause. The construction is also a standard SEO introduction.

```slop
Whether you're a freelancer or a Fortune 500 company, Tidemark scales with you.
Whether you're just starting out or a seasoned pro, there's something for everyone.
Built for teams of all sizes.
Loved by startups and enterprises alike.
```

```text
Tidemark is for freelancers and agencies with up to 50 active clients.
The free plan covers 5 clients and unlimited invoices.
Used by 2,300 accounting firms in Germany and Austria.
```

Rule: name one audience. If two audiences use the product differently, give each its own page or section and write each one for that reader.

#### "From X to Y" ranges

A range that implies full coverage of a process or market: "from idea to launch", "from onboarding to offboarding", "from solo creators to global teams". Two endpoints stand in for everything in between, and the reader is left to assume the middle exists.

The construction is a shortcut to sounding complete, the sentence-level version of the `end-to-end` claim. It also has a fixed rhythm that models reuse, often twice in one paragraph.

```slop
From idea to launch, we've got you covered.
Everything you need, from planning to payroll.
From first commit to production, all in one place.
From solo creators to global enterprises.
```

```text
Write the spec, assign the tasks, publish the release notes. Payroll is a separate product.
Tidemark covers invoicing and expenses. Payroll exports to Personio as a CSV.
Push to main and the preview deploys in about 90 seconds.
```

Rule: list the steps you actually cover and say where coverage ends. A stated limit is more believable than an implied infinity.

#### Sign-posting

Sentences about the text instead of the subject: "Let's break it down.", "In this guide, we'll explore...", "Without further ado", "Now let's take a closer look at...", "First things first." They describe the reading experience while the reader is having it.

Tutorial blogs and chat assistants use sign-posts to sound guided, and they pad length at almost no cost. Models emit them at every section boundary.

```slop
Let's break it down.
In this guide, we'll explore everything you need to know about invoicing.
Without further ado, let's dive in.
Now, let's take a closer look at the dashboard.
```

```text
An invoice needs four fields: client, line items, due date and currency.
The dashboard has two panels. Unpaid invoices are on the left, paid on the right.
```

Rule: cut every sentence that describes the document. Headings do the sign-posting; a table of contents does the rest.

#### The closing offer

Assistant residue at the end of text that is no longer a chat: `Let me know if you have any questions.`, `Feel free to reach out.`, `Hope this helps.`, `Happy coding.` It turns up in READMEs, docs, onboarding emails, commit messages and even interface copy.

Assistant tuning ends each turn with an offer to continue. When that output is pasted into a product or a repository, the offer comes with it and addresses the reader as a chat partner who cannot reply.

```slop
Let me know if you'd like me to adjust anything.
Feel free to reach out if you have any questions.
I hope this helps. Happy coding.
Don't hesitate to contact our friendly support team.
```

```text
Questions go to support@tidemark.example. We answer within one working day.
To report a bug, open an issue and include the version from Settings > About.
```

Rule: end product text with a contact route and a response time, or with nothing. In docs, code comments and commit messages, never address the reader as if they could answer back in the same window.

#### Sycophantic openers

Praise or agreement before the content: `Great question.`, `Absolutely.`, `You're absolutely right.`, `Certainly.` In interfaces it becomes cheerleading: `Awesome. You've added an item.`, `Nice work.`, `You're all set, superstar.`

Preference tuning rewards an agreeable tone, so the model leads with approval. The habit leaks into PR replies, docs written in chat, and success toasts.

```slop
Great question. Invoices can be edited until they're sent.
Absolutely. Here's an updated version of the component.
Awesome job. You've created your first project.
You're absolutely right, and that's a great catch.
```

```text
Invoices can be edited until they are sent.
Updated the component. The button now disables while the request runs.
Project created.
Fixed. The off-by-one was in the pagination offset.
```

Rule: start with the answer or the result. Praise the reader only where a person would, which in product copy is almost never. A person saving a form does not want to be congratulated.

### 8.3 Tells of texture

These tells sit inside sentences rather than in their framing. They survive a rewrite of the argument and need a second pass at the word level.

#### Em dash chains

The em dash used as an all-purpose connector: one or two per paragraph, often in pairs around an aside, often in front of a punchline. One dash in a long essay is unremarkable. A dash in every paragraph of a landing page is the most widely recognized marker of model output in English, and many readers now stop trusting a page at the second one.

Models learned the dash from edited magazine and book prose, where it is common, then use it at several times that rate because it lets a sentence keep going without choosing a relationship between its clauses. A comma, colon or period would each force a decision; the dash avoids it.

This file may not contain the dash character itself, so the slop examples below show each em dash as two hyphens.

```slop
Tidemark isn't just fast -- it's fast where it counts -- on your phone, offline, everywhere.
We built it for one reason -- you.
Sync -- the hard part -- is finally solved.
Your invoices, your clients, your rules -- all in one place.
```

```text
Tidemark works offline on your phone and syncs when you reconnect.
We built it because our own invoicing took a full day each month.
Sync is the hard part. Edits made offline now merge without conflicts.
Invoices, clients and payment rules live in one workspace.
```

Rule: no em dashes and no en dashes, in copy or in code comments. Choose the relationship. A break gets a period, a pause gets a comma, an aside gets parentheses, a list or definition gets a colon. Ranges use "to": "9 to 5", "pages 4 to 9", "Monday to Friday". Hyphens stay for compound words and ISO dates such as 2026-10-15.

#### Hedging stacks

Two or more hedges on a single claim: "can potentially help", "may possibly reduce", "could help to improve", "might be able to", "in some cases it may". Hype and hedging often appear together, which gives sentences like "can potentially transform the way you work", a large claim with its own escape hatch.

Safety tuning teaches models to avoid overclaiming, so they add a hedge to anything that sounds like a promise. Marketing training pushes the other way. The result is a sentence that claims a lot and commits to nothing.

```slop
This can potentially help improve your team's productivity.
Caching may possibly reduce load times in some cases.
It might be worth considering whether you could perhaps simplify the form.
Tidemark can help you potentially get paid faster.
```

```text
Teams using the shared inbox answered tickets 2 hours sooner at the median.
Caching the API response cut median load time from 1.4s to 0.6s.
Cut the form to four fields.
Clients who get a reminder on day 7 pay 5 days sooner on average.
```

Rule: one hedge per claim, and only when you can name the uncertainty: "on Chrome 120 and later", "for accounts created after March", "in our test with 40 users". Otherwise state the claim plainly or delete it.

#### Fake specificity

Numbers, names and sources that look precise and are invented or unverifiable: "Trusted by 10,000+ teams", "Save 10 hours a week", "3x faster", "99.99% uptime", "Studies show". Testimonials from "Sarah K., Product Manager" with a stock avatar. A row of famous company logos with no customer story behind any of them.

Prompts tell models to "be specific", and the model satisfies the instruction with plausible numbers. The signature is the round number with a plus sign or an "up to", and the source that cannot be checked.

```slop
Trusted by 10,000+ teams worldwide.
Save up to 10 hours every week.
3x faster than the competition.
"Tidemark changed how we work." -- Sarah K., Product Manager
Studies show that automated reminders increase on-time payments by 80%.
```

```text
Used by 2,314 teams as of 1 October 2026.
In our March 2026 survey of 412 customers, the median time saved was 3 hours a month.
Renders a 10,000-row table in 120ms on a 2020 MacBook Air. Version 2 took 380ms.
"We stopped writing reminder emails by hand." Dana Okafor, finance lead at Hollis and Reed.
```

Rule: every number states its source, its date and its method, or it comes out. An odd number such as 2,314 is fine when it is real; an invented round one is never fine. Testimonials use a full name, a role and an organization, with written permission. Without data, describe the mechanism instead of a result.

#### Adverb inflation

Adverbs propping up verbs and adjectives: `seamlessly integrates`, `effortlessly reorder`, `incredibly fast`, `truly unique`, `simply drag`, `easily manage`, `instantly see`. Remove them and the sentence usually means the same thing, which shows they were never carrying weight.

Intensifiers raise perceived enthusiasm, and marketing training rewards enthusiasm. "Simply" and "easily" come from documentation, where writers use them to signal that a step is short.

```slop
Seamlessly integrates with your existing tools.
Simply drag and drop to effortlessly reorder tasks.
An incredibly fast, truly delightful experience.
Easily manage your team's permissions.
```

```text
Connects to Slack, GitHub and Google Drive.
Drag a task to reorder it.
Opens in 300ms on a mid-range Android phone.
Set permissions per project: view, comment or edit.
```

Rule: delete the adverb. If the sentence gets weaker, the adverb was hiding a missing fact; add the fact. Never write "simply", "just" or "easily" in instructions. For the reader who is stuck, the step was not simple, and the word tells them the fault is theirs.

#### Uniform paragraph length

Every paragraph runs three or four sentences and 50 to 80 words. Each opens with a topic sentence and closes with a summary. Sentences cluster between 15 and 22 words. On screen the text forms blocks of equal height, like a wall of identical bricks.

Models generate at a steady length because nothing in the prompt asks them to vary it. A person writes a one-line paragraph when one fact deserves its own line and a long one when an argument needs room.

```slop
Invoicing is one of the most time-consuming tasks for small businesses. Between tracking hours, chasing payments, and reconciling accounts, it can take days each month. That's why we built Tidemark.

Tidemark automates the entire invoicing process from start to finish. It connects to your bank, tracks every payment, and sends reminders automatically. The result is less admin and more time for what matters.

Getting started takes just minutes. Simply connect your bank account, import your clients, and send your first invoice. It's that easy.
```

```text
Tidemark sends invoices and chases the late ones.

Connect your bank and Tidemark marks each invoice as paid when the money arrives. If an invoice is 7 days late, the client gets a reminder written in your name and you get a copy. After 30 days the reminders stop and Tidemark tells you, because by then a phone call works better than a fourth email.

Setup takes about 10 minutes.
```

Rule: let length follow content. On a 600-word page the longest paragraph should be at least three times the length of the shortest. Mix sentence lengths, and include some under 8 words. A one-sentence paragraph is allowed and often right.

### 8.4 Tells of layout

Structure carries tells too. A page can contain no banned word and no false contrast and still look generated because every answer is a bulleted list with bold labels under a title-case heading that makes a pun.

#### Bulleted everything

Every explanation becomes a list. Reasons, arguments and stories get broken into fragments with no connectives, so "because", "so" and "but" disappear and the reader has to rebuild the logic. Lists nest three levels deep. Some bullets hold a single word.

Chat interfaces render Markdown, and assistants were tuned to be "scannable", so lists became the default container for any content. Lists also hide missing logic: two fragments placed next to each other imply a relationship the writer never had to state.

```slop
Benefits:
- Faster invoicing
- Better cash flow
- Happier clients
- Peace of mind

Why we changed the pricing:
- Costs
  - Infrastructure
  - Support
- Fairness
- Simplicity
```

```text
We raised the Team plan from $12 to $15 per seat because storage costs doubled after we moved backups to a second region. Solo stays at $8. Existing customers keep their current price until March 2027.
```

Rule: use a list only when the items are parallel and independent: steps in order, requirements, options, specifications. Reasons, trade-offs and history go in sentences joined by "because", "so" and "but". A one-item list is a sentence. If list items run past two lines each, they are paragraphs.

#### Bold-label bullets

Each bullet starts with a bolded label and a colon, followed by a sentence that restates the label: `Speed: Tidemark is blazing fast.` The label and the sentence say the same thing twice. In chat answers and generated READMEs this is the default list format, and it is easy to spot from across a room.

Assistants produce it because it looks organized in a chat window and gives each item an apparent heading. It also lets the model generate a list of abstract nouns first and fill in sentences after.

```slop
- **Speed:** Tidemark is blazing fast.
- **Security:** Your data is protected with enterprise-grade security.
- **Simplicity:** An intuitive interface anyone can use.
- **Support:** Our team is here to help 24/7.
```

```text
- Pages load in under a second on a 4G connection.
- Data is encrypted at rest with AES-256 and backed up hourly to a second region.
- Support answers within 4 hours, Monday to Friday, 08:00 to 18:00 CET.
```

Rule: drop the label when the sentence already says it. Keep labels only in reference material where readers scan for a term (options, parameters, glossary entries), and then use a table or a definition list instead of bold text in a bullet.

#### Title case everywhere

Headings, buttons, navigation items, menu entries and toasts all in title case: "Get Started With Your Free Trial", "Manage Team Settings", "Your Invoice Has Been Sent Successfully". It reads as a press release and makes interface text look shouted.

Marketing templates and headline style guides use title case, and models apply it to anything that looks like a heading or a label. Component libraries reinforce it, since their demo buttons say "Sign Up" and "Learn More".

```slop
Get Started With Your Free Trial
Manage Your Team Settings
Your Invoice Has Been Sent Successfully
Frequently Asked Questions
```

```text
Start a free trial
Team settings
Invoice sent
Questions about billing
```

Rule: sentence case for all interface text and all headings. Capitalize the first word and proper nouns only. Product names and legal names keep their registered form.

#### Headings that are puns

Clever headings that hide what the section contains: `Show Me the Money`, `Sync or Swim`, `Where the Magic Happens`, `Ctrl+Alt+Delight`. A reader scanning headings to find the pricing section cannot tell which one it is.

Asked to be "fun" or "memorable", a model reaches for an idiom or a pop-culture line and bends it toward the topic. It picks the most predictable pun available, which is why the same ones appear on thousands of pages.

```slop
Show Me the Money
Sync or Swim
Where the Magic Happens
Ctrl+Alt+Delight
Invoice, Invoice, Baby
```

```text
Pricing
Offline sync
How payment matching works
Keyboard shortcuts
Recurring invoices
```

Rule: a heading names what the section contains, so a reader who sees only the headings can find what they need. If a joke belongs anywhere, it goes in the body, written by a person, once per page.

### 8.5 Punctuation and formatting rules

These rules apply to interface copy, marketing pages, documentation, commit messages and this handbook. The linter enforces the first three.

#### Dashes

- No em dash (U+2014) and no en dash (U+2013), anywhere, including code comments and alt text.
- A break between two thoughts is a period. A pause is a comma. An aside is in parentheses. A list, example or definition follows a colon.
- Ranges use "to": "9:00 to 17:00", "pages 4 to 9", "$8 to $15 per seat". In tables, "to" also works: "1 to 5 users".
- The hyphen stays for compound modifiers ("14-day trial"), ISO dates (2026-10-15), identifiers (INV-0042) and code.
- Negative numbers in financial tables use a minus sign or parentheses, never a dash. Pick one convention per product.

#### Exclamation marks

- Zero in interface copy. That includes success messages, empty states, onboarding, and above all error messages, where an exclamation mark reads as alarm or mockery.
- Zero in marketing headlines and buttons.
- Zero in documentation and commit messages.
- Personal email from a named person to a customer may contain one, if that person would write one. Never more than one per message.
- User-generated content is displayed as written.

#### Emoji

- None in interface text, headings, buttons, navigation, toasts, commit messages, PR titles, changelogs or docs.
- None as bullet markers, status indicators or section icons. A green circle is not a status; the word "Running" next to a 16px SVG icon is.
- None in code comments or log output. Logs are searched with grep; pictographs break searches and alignment.
- Icons come from one SVG set at 16 or 20px with a 1.5px stroke, always next to a text label or with an accessible name.
- Emoji typed by users (messages, reactions, names) are content. Render them unchanged. A reactions feature is a feature; decorating your own copy with emoji is a tell.

#### Bold and italics

- At most one bold phrase per screen of body text, and never a whole sentence.
- In step-by-step documentation, bold the visible name of a control the reader must find: "Select **Send invoice**." That is the only routine use.
- No bold labels at the start of bullets (see 8.4).
- Italics mark a term at the point where it is defined, or a title. Never use italics for emphasis in interface copy; screen readers ignore it and many fonts render it faintly.
- No underline except on links. No all-caps words for emphasis.

#### Headings

- Sentence case, no trailing period, under 8 words.
- A heading is a noun phrase ("Payment reminders") or an imperative ("Connect your bank"). Questions only on FAQ pages, where each heading is a question a customer actually asked.
- No colon subtitles ("Invoicing: A Complete Guide"). Pick the half that names the content.
- No skipped levels. One `h1` per page. Visual size follows the type scale (40, 32, 24, 21px for `h1` to `h4` on desktop), not the heading level alone.
- Never use a heading for emphasis. If text is not the title of the content below it, it is not a heading.

#### Lists

- Numbered lists for sequences the reader follows in order. Bulleted lists for unordered sets. Prose for everything else.
- 2 to 9 items. Over 9, group them under subheadings or use a table.
- Items are grammatically parallel: all imperatives, all noun phrases, or all full sentences.
- Fragments take no final period. Full sentences take periods. Do not mix the two in one list.
- Nest at most one level. A second level of nesting means the content wants a table or subheadings.
- No introductory sentence that says "The following list shows". The heading or the sentence before already does that.

#### Quotation marks, ellipses and ampersands

- Interface and marketing text uses typographic quotes and apostrophes. Code, config and commit messages use straight ones. Never mix the two in the same string.
- The ellipsis means "this continues" or "text was removed". Use it in loading text for an operation in progress ("Importing…") and in a menu item that opens a dialog ("Export…"). Never use it for suspense, and never trail a sentence off with one.
- "And" in prose and headings. The ampersand is for proper names (Hollis & Reed) and space-starved table headers.
- Slashes for real alternatives only ("and/or" is not one). Write "invoices or quotes".

#### Capitals and numbers in text

- Acronyms stay uppercase (PDF, VAT, API). Everything else is sentence case, including small uppercase labels: an eyebrow line set in caps with letter spacing above every heading is a template tell, and the heading should stand alone.
- No "NEW", "BETA" or "LIVE" pills. If something is new, say what changed and when in the release notes; if something is live, show the timestamp of the last update.
- Write numbers as digits in interface copy, including one to nine: "3 invoices", "2 minutes". Prose in long-form documents may spell out one to nine. Pick one rule per document and keep it.

### 8.6 Microcopy for controls and forms

Microcopy is the text inside the interface: button labels, field labels, messages. It is short, so every word shows. Generated microcopy is easy to spot because it is cheerful at the wrong moments and vague at the useful ones. Each context below gives the default slop, the rules, and a rewrite.

#### Buttons and calls to action

Generated buttons use generic verbs (`Submit`, `Continue`, `Get started`) or benefit slogans (`Unlock your potential`). Neither tells the person what will happen when they press it.

- Verb plus object, 1 to 3 words, sentence case: "Create invoice", "Send 3 reminders", "Export CSV".
- The label says what happens next. "Start 14-day trial" is better than "Get started" unless the next screen is the start of something.
- A dialog's primary button repeats the dialog's verb. A dialog titled "Delete invoice?" has a button labeled "Delete invoice".
- Name the count and the object on bulk and destructive actions: "Delete 12 invoices".
- Link text says where it goes: "Read the pricing FAQ", never "Click here" or a bare "Learn more".
- No arrow glyphs, no "->" appended to the label, no exclamation marks, no first-person mix ("Start my trial" next to "Your account").
- One primary button per view. A page with three filled accent buttons has no primary action.

```slop
Get Started
Submit
Unlock Your Potential
Let's Go!
Learn More ->
[Yes] [No]
```

```text
Create invoice
Send 3 reminders
Start 14-day trial
Read the pricing FAQ
[Delete invoice] [Keep invoice]
```

#### Form labels and help text

Generated forms put instructions in placeholders, mark every field with an asterisk, and open help text with "Please". Placeholders vanish on the first keystroke, so the instruction disappears at the moment the person needs it.

- The label is a short noun phrase above the field: "Work email", not "Enter your email address".
- Never use a placeholder as the label. A placeholder may show an example format, prefixed "e.g.", in `--ink-3`.
- Help text sits under the field, in 14px `--ink-2`, and states constraints before the person breaks them: "At least 12 characters."
- If most fields are required, mark the optional ones with "(optional)" and drop the asterisks.
- Explain why you ask for data people hesitate to give: "We send receipts here." under an email field, "Used only for tax on EU invoices." under a VAT number.
- No "Please", no exclamation marks, no adjectives about the input ("strong", "awesome").

```slop
Label: Enter your email address here
Placeholder: Your amazing project name...
Help: Please make sure your password is strong and secure!
Label: Company Name*
```

```text
Label: Work email
Help: We send invoices and receipts here.

Label: Project name
Placeholder: e.g. Q3 audit for Hollis & Reed

Label: Password
Help: At least 12 characters.

Label: VAT number (optional)
Help: Used only for tax on EU invoices.
```

#### Error messages

Generated errors are either cute (`Oops! Something went wrong`) or raw (`Error 422: Unprocessable Entity`). The cute ones hide the cause; the raw ones expose it in a language the person does not speak. Both leave them stuck.

- Structure: what failed, why (if known), what to do now. Usually two short sentences.
- Place the message next to the field or control that failed, in `--bad`, with an icon and text. Color alone is not enough.
- Use the person's terms ("card", "file", "date"), not the system's ("payload", "entity", "token").
- No blame ("You entered an invalid date"). State the requirement instead ("Enter a date after 1 January 2026").
- No apology theatre and no jokes. "Sorry" is allowed once, when the failure is ours.
- Keep what the person typed. Never clear a form because one field failed.
- Include an error code after the human text when support will need it.

```slop
Oops! Something went wrong.
Invalid input.
Uh-oh, looks like we hit a snag. Please try again later!
Error 422: Unprocessable Entity
We're sorry, but an unexpected error has occurred.
```

```text
Card declined. Your bank did not give a reason. Try another card or call your bank.
Enter a date after 1 January 2026.
Not saved. You are offline. Your changes are kept on this device and save when you reconnect.
The file is 14 MB. The limit is 10 MB.
Sorry, this failed on our side (error 5021). Try again in a minute. If it fails again, email support@tidemark.example and include the code.
```

#### Empty states

The generated empty state is a large illustration, a joke ("It's lonely in here"), and a button that says "Get started". The person learns nothing about what the screen is for.

- Say what will appear here and how it gets here, in one or two sentences.
- Offer the one action that fills the screen, as a single button.
- Separate three cases: first use (nothing created yet), cleared (everything done), and no results (a search or filter matched nothing). For no results, repeat the query and offer to clear the filters.
- No illustrations of floating people, no "Nothing to see here", no "yet" with an exclamation mark.
- An empty table keeps its column headers, so the person sees what data will appear.

```slop
Nothing to see here... yet!
It's a little lonely in here. Let's change that!
Your journey starts now. Create your first masterpiece.
No data
```

```text
No invoices yet. Invoices you create or import appear here.
[Create invoice]

No results for "hollis". Check the spelling or clear the Paid filter.
[Clear filters]

No reminders due. A reminder appears here when an invoice is 7 days late.
```

#### Confirmation dialogs

Generated confirmations ask "Are you sure?" and offer "OK" and "Cancel". The person has to remember what they clicked to know what "OK" will do.

- The title names the action and the object as a question: "Delete invoice INV-0042?"
- The body states the consequence and whether it can be undone, with counts: "The invoice and its 3 payment records are deleted."
- Buttons repeat the verb: "Delete invoice" and "Cancel". Never "Yes", "No" or "OK".
- For reversible actions, skip the dialog. Do the action and offer Undo for at least 10 seconds.
- For actions that destroy a workspace or an account, ask the person to type the name of the thing.
- The destructive button uses `--bad`, not the accent color, and it is not the default focus.

```slop
Are you sure?
This action cannot be undone. Are you sure you want to proceed?
[OK] [Cancel]

Whoa there! Are you really, really sure?
```

```text
Delete invoice INV-0042?
The invoice and its 3 payment records are deleted. Your client keeps the PDF they already received. This cannot be undone.
[Delete invoice] [Cancel]

Archived 12 invoices. [Undo]
```

#### Loading text

Generated loading text tries to entertain: rotating jokes, `Hang tight`, `Working our magic`. The jokes repeat on the third visit, and none of them tell the person how long to wait.

- Under 1 second: show nothing. A spinner that flashes for 200ms reads as a glitch.
- 1 to 3 seconds: a skeleton or a 16px spinner, no text.
- Over 3 seconds: one line saying what is happening, in the present participle: "Importing clients…"
- Over 10 seconds: show progress as a count or a percentage and let the person leave the page. Say how they will learn it finished.
- No jokes, no rotating messages, no "Almost there" when you do not know that.

```slop
Hang tight! We're working our magic...
Brewing something special for you...
Almost there! Good things take time.
Reticulating splines...
```

```text
Importing clients… 140 of 240
Generating 12 PDFs. You can leave this page. We will email you when they are ready.
Checking the bank feed. This usually takes under 10 seconds.
```

#### Success messages

Generated success messages celebrate: `Success!`, `Woohoo! Your invoice is on its way!`, confetti for saving a form. Routine actions do not need celebration, and celebrating them makes the rare real milestone feel the same.

- Past-tense verb and object, 1 to 4 words: "Invoice sent", "Changes saved".
- Add the one next fact or action when it helps: who received it, where to find it, an Undo.
- Autosave shows "Saved" next to the control or in the header, not a toast.
- A toast stays at least 5 seconds, 10 if it contains an action, and pauses while hovered or focused.
- No exclamation marks, no "Success", no "successfully" (the past tense already says it worked), no confetti.

```slop
Success!
Woohoo! Your invoice is on its way!
Awesome! Changes saved successfully.
You did it! Your profile is looking great.
```

```text
Invoice sent to dana@hollis.example. [View]
Saved
Logo updated. Clients see it on invoices you send from now on.
```

### 8.7 Microcopy for messages and pages

#### Notifications

Generated notifications hide the event behind a teaser: "You have a new notification", "Important update about your account", "Don't miss out". The person has to open the message to learn whether it mattered, and after the third empty teaser they stop opening any.

- The subject, title or first line names the event, the actor and the object: "Hollis & Reed paid INV-0042 ($1,200)".
- Push titles stay under 40 characters and bodies under 100, because lock screens truncate there.
- Email subject lines stay under 60 characters and front-load the noun the person will search for later.
- One event per notification. Batch low-priority events into a daily digest the person can turn off.
- Every notification type has its own off switch, and the email footer links straight to it.
- No urgency words ("Act now", "Last chance") unless a real deadline exists, and then state the date.

```slop
You have a new notification!
Important update about your account
Don't miss out on what's happening in your workspace
Great news! Something exciting just happened.
```

```text
Hollis & Reed paid INV-0042 ($1,200)
INV-0039 is 7 days late. Reminder sent to dana@hollis.example.
Your card expires on 30 November. Update it to keep the Team plan.
3 invoices are due this week
```

#### Onboarding

The generated onboarding flow opens with `Welcome aboard! Let's get you set up for success`, runs an eight-step tooltip tour of the navigation, and asks for job title, company size and `how did you hear about us` before the person has seen the product.

- Ask only for what the first real task needs. Everything else can wait until it is used.
- Say how many steps there are: "Step 2 of 3".
- The first session ends with real output: a sent invoice, a deployed page, an imported file. Not with a tour.
- Use a checklist of 3 to 5 real tasks, each one linking to the screen where it happens. Let people dismiss the checklist.
- Every step has a visible "Skip" that does not need a confirmation.
- Welcome text is one sentence or nothing. The product name in the header already says where they are.

```slop
Welcome aboard! We're so excited to have you here.
Let's get you set up for success in just a few easy steps.
Ready to embark on your invoicing journey?
Tell us a bit about yourself so we can personalize your experience.
```

```text
Step 1 of 3. Add your business details. They appear on every invoice.
Step 2 of 3. Add your first client. You can import a CSV instead.
Step 3 of 3. Send a test invoice to yourself.

Set up Tidemark
[ ] Add your logo
[ ] Connect your bank
[ ] Turn on reminders
```

#### Tooltips

Generated tooltips restate the label in a longer sentence ("Click here to edit your settings"), or hold information the person needs and cannot reach on a touch screen.

- A tooltip adds what the label cannot hold: a definition, a keyboard shortcut, a reason a control is disabled.
- Icon-only buttons need an accessible name, and the tooltip shows that same name: "Archive", "Duplicate (D)".
- Under 80 characters and one sentence. Longer content belongs in help text or a linked doc.
- Never hide required information in a tooltip. Hover does not exist on phones, and focus-triggered tooltips are easy to miss.
- A disabled button's tooltip says why it is disabled and how to enable it.

```slop
Click here to edit your settings!
This is where the magic happens.
Hover over me for more info!
This button lets you easily duplicate your invoice with just one click.
```

```text
Duplicate (D)
Net 14: payment is due 14 days after the invoice date.
Add a client before sending.
Archived invoices stay searchable and are excluded from reports.
```

#### 404 pages

The generated 404 is a joke: an astronaut, "Houston, we have a problem", "Looks like you're lost in space", a button reading "Take me home". It wastes the one moment when the person needs help finding something.

- Say plainly that the page does not exist or has moved.
- Show the requested path, so a mistyped URL is visible.
- Offer a search field and 2 to 4 links to the pages most often wanted from that section.
- If the page was removed on purpose, say what replaced it, with a link.
- Return a real 404 status code. A 200 response with error text hides the problem from crawlers and monitoring.

```slop
Oops! Looks like you're lost in space.
Houston, we have a problem.
This page took a vacation. Let's get you back on track!
404: Page not found :(
```

```text
There is no page at /docs/reminders-v1.

The reminders guide moved to /docs/reminders. Search the docs, or go to one of these:
- Reminders
- Recurring invoices
- Pricing
```

#### Pricing labels

Generated pricing pages use the same three columns: Starter, Pro, Enterprise, a "Most popular" ribbon on the middle one, check marks against vague features ("Advanced analytics", "Priority support"), and a struck-through price with no explanation.

- One line holds the price, the unit, the period and the tax status: "$12 per seat per month, billed yearly, excl. VAT".
- Show the monthly price billed monthly next to the yearly rate, so the discount is checkable.
- Limits are numbers: "5 clients", "10 GB", "3 seats". Never "Generous limits".
- Say what happens at the limit: "At 6 clients you are asked to upgrade. Nothing is deleted."
- Feature rows name the feature as it appears in the product. "Advanced analytics" is not a feature; "Revenue by client report" is.
- Name plans after who they are for ("Solo", "Team", "Firm") or after their size. Avoid "Ultimate" and "Pro Max".
- "Most popular" only if it is true this month. A badge on every middle column is a template default.
- "Contact sales" appears with a price floor or a reason: "From $400 a month. Needs a call because we migrate your data."

```slop
Pro
$29/mo
Most Popular
Everything in Starter, plus:
Advanced analytics
Priority support
Unlimited possibilities
```

```text
Team
$12 per seat per month, billed yearly ($14 billed monthly). Prices exclude VAT.
Up to 25 seats and 500 clients.
Everything in Solo, plus:
Shared client list
Revenue by client report
Email support, answered within 4 working hours
```

### 8.8 Microcopy for publishing and code

#### Headlines and subheads

Generated hero headlines are interchangeable: `Supercharge your workflow`, `The future of invoicing is here`, `Work smarter, not harder`, `Where teams do their best work`. Any company could put them on any product.

- The headline names what the product does, using a noun a customer would type into a search box: "Invoicing for freelancers that chases late payments".
- Under 10 words. If it needs more, the subhead carries the rest.
- The subhead gives one concrete mechanism or fact: who it is for, how it works, what it costs.
- Apply the swap test: put a competitor's name in front of the headline. If it is still true, rewrite it.
- No `the future of`, no `reimagined`, no imperative slogans aimed at the reader's potential.

```slop
Supercharge your workflow.
The future of invoicing is here.
Work smarter, not harder.
Invoicing, reimagined for the modern team.
```

```text
Invoicing for freelancers that chases late payments for you
Tidemark emails clients on day 7, 14 and 30, in your name, and stops when they pay. $8 a month.
```

#### Meta descriptions

Generated meta descriptions open with `Discover`, `Unlock` or `Look no further`, and the same description is copied to every page of the site.

- 120 to 155 characters, so search results show it whole.
- Product name, what the page offers, and one specific fact.
- One description per page, written for that page.
- No imperative openers aimed at the reader, no claims of being the best.

```slop
Discover the ultimate invoicing solution. Unlock seamless payments and take your business to the next level with Tidemark.
Look no further! Tidemark is the all-in-one platform for all your needs.
```

```text
Tidemark sends invoices and emails late clients on day 7, 14 and 30. Plans start at $8 a month for up to 5 clients.
Tidemark pricing: Solo $8, Team $12 per seat, Firm from $400 a month. Prices exclude VAT. Yearly billing saves 15%.
```

#### Commit messages

Generated commits announce themselves (`This commit enhances...`), list every file touched, use emoji shortcodes, and end with a summary of the summary.

- Subject line in the imperative, under 50 characters, no final period: "Stop reminders after invoice is paid".
- If the repository uses Conventional Commits, keep the prefix and still write a real subject: "fix(reminders): stop after invoice is paid".
- Blank line, then a body wrapped at 72 characters that says why the change was made and what it affects. The diff already shows what changed line by line.
- Reference the issue: "Fixes #412".
- No emoji or shortcodes, no "various improvements", no "updated files", no closing offer.

```slop
feat: :sparkles: Enhanced the reminder system with improved logic

This commit introduces several improvements to the reminder functionality,
making it more robust and efficient. Updated reminders.ts, queue.ts and
tests. Overall, this provides a better experience for users.
```

```text
fix(reminders): stop after invoice is paid

Reminders were queued at invoice creation and never cancelled, so a
client who paid on day 6 still got the day 7 email. The payment
webhook now deletes pending reminder jobs for the invoice.

Fixes #412
```

#### Pull request descriptions

Generated PR descriptions have the same skeleton: a Summary heading, a Changes list of bold-label bullets, an Impact section full of adjectives, and "Let me know if you have any questions" at the bottom. They describe the diff the reviewer is about to read and leave out what the reviewer cannot see.

- First line: what the change does and why, in one or two sentences.
- How to test it: the exact commands or steps, and the expected result.
- Risk: what could break, what you did not test, whether it needs a migration or a flag.
- Screenshots for any visual change, before and after, at the same viewport width.
- Leave out anything the diff already shows. Leave out headings for empty sections.

```slop
## Summary
This PR introduces a comprehensive overhaul of the reminder system.

## Changes
- **Reminders:** Enhanced reminder logic for better reliability.
- **Tests:** Added robust test coverage.

## Impact
This change will significantly improve the user experience.

Let me know if you have any questions!
```

```text
Stops payment reminders once an invoice is paid. Clients who paid early were still getting the day 7 email (#412).

The payment webhook now deletes pending reminder jobs for the invoice. Jobs already picked up by a worker check the invoice status before sending.

To test: run `make seed`, mark INV-0003 as paid, then run `make reminders-due`. No email should be queued for INV-0003.

Risk: reminder jobs created before this deploy are not cancelled by the webhook. The status check in the worker covers them. No migration.
```

#### README intros

The generated README opens with the project name, a rocket, a wall of badges and `A blazing-fast, lightweight, modern library for building amazing apps`. The reader still does not know what it does or whether to install it.

- First sentence: what the project is and what it does, in plain nouns: "`tidemark-pdf` renders invoices to PDF from a JSON file."
- Second: who it is for or what it replaces, if that is not obvious.
- Then the install command and the smallest working example, both copy-pasteable.
- Status in one line: maintained or not, supported versions, license.
- At most 3 badges (build, version, license). No emoji in the title or headings.

```slop
# tidemark-pdf
A blazing-fast, lightweight, and modern PDF generation library that empowers developers to create stunning invoices with ease.

## Features
- **Fast:** Lightning-fast rendering
- **Flexible:** Endlessly customizable
- **Developer-friendly:** Intuitive API
```

```text
# tidemark-pdf

tidemark-pdf renders invoices to PDF from a JSON file. It handles multi-page line items, VAT summaries and right-to-left scripts.

npm install tidemark-pdf

npx tidemark-pdf invoice.json --out invoice.pdf

Node 20 or later. MIT license. Maintained by the Tidemark team; issues are answered within a week.
```

#### Release notes

Release notes are for the people who use the product. Generated ones start with "We're thrilled to announce", group everything under "New features" and "Improvements", and describe changes in the vocabulary of the codebase.

- Lead with the change that affects the most people, in their terms: what they can now do, or what stopped happening.
- One short paragraph per change: what changed, who it affects, anything they need to do.
- Date and version at the top. Link to docs for anything that needs explaining.
- Say what was removed or changed incompatibly, plainly, with the date it takes effect.
- No "thrilled", "excited" or "proud". No "various bug fixes and performance improvements" as a line on its own; name the fixes or leave the line out.

```slop
We're thrilled to announce Tidemark 4.2, our most powerful release yet!
New features: Enhanced reminders, improved dashboard, and more.
Various bug fixes and performance improvements.
```

```text
Tidemark 4.2, 14 October 2026

Reminders stop when a client pays. Before, a client who paid on day 6 could still get the day 7 email.

The invoice list loads in under a second for accounts with 10,000 invoices. It took up to 6 seconds.

Removed: the old PDF template "Classic". Invoices already sent keep it. New invoices use "Plain" from 1 November.
```

#### Changelog entries

A changelog is for developers and integrators. It is a dated, versioned list of changes, grouped by type. Generated changelogs merge it with marketing, inflate every line, and paste commit subjects in bulk.

- Follow the Keep a Changelog groups: Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed, Security.
- Newest version first, with an ISO date: `## 4.2.0 (2026-10-14)`.
- One line per change, starting with the thing that changed, linking the issue or PR.
- Breaking changes are marked and explain the migration in one line.
- No adjectives, no emoji category markers, no "Misc".

```slop
## v4.2.0
### New Features
- :rocket: Supercharged reminders engine
- :sparkles: Improved dashboard experience
### Misc
- Various fixes
```

```text
## 4.2.0 (2026-10-14)

### Fixed
- Reminder jobs are cancelled when an invoice is paid (#412).

### Changed
- `GET /invoices` returns 100 items per page instead of 50 (#398).

### Removed
- BREAKING: the `classic` PDF template. Pass `template: "plain"` instead (#377).
```

### 8.9 Voice

Generated copy has a voice, and it is the same voice everywhere: upbeat, general and slightly breathless. Removing the tells in this part leaves text that is plain. Voice is what makes plain text sound like a particular company.

#### Sound like a specific person or team

Decide who is talking. "The two engineers who built Tidemark" and "a large finance software vendor" produce different sentences from the same facts. Write it down and give every writer and every model prompt the same page.

A voice sheet fits on one screen:

- Who is speaking, in one sentence: "The people who build Tidemark, writing to freelancers who would rather be doing their real work."
- Five words or phrases you use, taken from real support tickets and sales calls ("late invoice", "chase", "paid", "client").
- Five you never use, beyond the banned list (for Tidemark: "users", "accounts receivable", "workflow", "platform", "experience").
- Three opinions the team holds and will state: "Reminders should be polite. Invoices should fit on one page. Prices should be on the website."
- Two samples of real text in the target voice: one support reply, one release note, written by people on the team.

Then run the swap test on every page: replace the product name with a competitor's. Copy that still reads as true is generic, and generic is what models produce by default. Copy that becomes false belongs to you.

Collect the team's own language. Support replies, sales call notes and internal chat are full of the phrases customers actually use. Put the best ones in the voice sheet and in prompts, and models will copy them instead of their defaults.

#### Reading level

- Interface copy: grade 6 to 8 on the Flesch-Kincaid scale. Short words, one idea per sentence.
- Marketing and onboarding: grade 7 to 9. Average sentence length 12 to 18 words, no sentence over 30.
- Technical docs: as high as the subject needs, but sentence length stays under 25 words on average. Hard concepts get short sentences.
- Keep the domain terms your readers use. Accountants know what "accrual" means; replacing it with a vague paraphrase reads as condescending. Explain a term once, where it first appears.
- Measure with a tool such as the `textstat` Python package, and treat the score as a check, not a target. A readable page with a grade 10 score is fine.

#### Contractions

- Use them in interface copy and marketing: "you'll", "can't", "it's", "we're". People speak in contractions, and text without them reads as a translated manual.
- Write "do not" and "cannot" in full for warnings where the negative must not be missed: "This cannot be undone."
- Avoid stacked or rare contractions ("it'll've", "mightn't") and contractions of nouns ("Tidemark'll").
- Pick a rule per document and keep it. This handbook uses few contractions because it is a reference; a product's onboarding should use more.

#### Second person

- Address the reader as "you". Refer to the company as "we" and to the product by name.
- Labels use "your" or no pronoun at all: "Your invoices" or "Invoices". Never "My invoices" in one place and "Your settings" in another.
- Never call the reader "the user" in text they read. "Users" belongs in internal documents.
- "We" appears in interface copy only when people at the company did or will do something: "We emailed you a receipt." System actions are described without a pronoun: "Receipt sent."
- Do not tell the reader how they feel ("You'll love...", "You're going to be amazed"). Describe the product and let them decide.

#### Numbers

- Digits for all numbers in interface copy, including 1 to 9: "3 invoices", "2 minutes ago".
- Thousands separators for numbers of 5 digits and more, following the reader's locale: 10,000 or 10 000 or 10.000.
- Dates that cannot be misread: "1 October 2026" or "Oct 1, 2026", by locale. Never 01/10/26. ISO dates (2026-10-01) in logs, changelogs and file names.
- Times include the time zone when people in more than one zone see them: "09:00 CET".
- Relative times ("3 minutes ago") for the last 24 hours, absolute dates after that. Show the absolute timestamp on hover and to screen readers.
- Currency with its symbol in single-currency products, with its ISO code when several currencies can appear: "EUR 1,200".
- Round in headlines only when the rounding is honest and stated nearby: "2,300 firms" above a footnote with "2,314 as of 1 October 2026".
- Units follow one style per product. This handbook writes durations as in CSS (300ms) and file sizes with a space (10 MB).

### 8.10 A full rewrite, start to finish

The tells rarely appear alone. Below is a feature section of the kind a model writes when asked for "a features section for an invoicing app", followed by the edit, step by step.

```slop
## Invoicing, Reimagined

Tired of chasing payments? You're not alone. Whether you're a freelancer or a growing agency, getting paid shouldn't feel like a full-time job -- and with Tidemark, it doesn't.

Tidemark isn't just an invoicing tool. It's your financial command center. From creating invoices to tracking payments, we've got you covered.

- **Smart Reminders:** Automatically follow up with clients so you don't have to.
- **Seamless Integrations:** Connect effortlessly with the tools you already love.
- **Powerful Insights:** Make data-driven decisions with real-time analytics.

The result? More time for what matters. Join 10,000+ businesses who trust Tidemark to get paid faster.
```

Tell count for those 100 or so words: a pun-adjacent title-case heading, a rhetorical question opener, a "Whether you are" opener, an em dash, a false contrast, a "From X to Y" range, three bold-label bullets (a tricolon of features), adverb inflation twice, a colon reveal, fake specificity, and eight banned words. Nothing in it is wrong in a way a fact-checker could catch. Nothing in it is true in a way a reader could use.

The edit, in order:

1. List the facts. Ask the product team what the feature does, in numbers. For this section the answers were: reminders go out on day 7, 14 and 30 in the sender's name; they stop when the bank feed shows the payment; there is a Xero and DATEV export; 2,314 teams were active on 1 October 2026; the median customer got paid 5 days sooner after turning reminders on, measured over 6 months for 1,100 accounts.
2. Throw away the draft. Editing generated sentences one word at a time keeps their shape, and the shape is the problem.
3. Write one sentence per fact, in the order a customer would ask about them.
4. Pick a heading that names the section.
5. Read it aloud and cut anything you would not say to a customer on the phone.

```text
## Payment reminders

Tidemark emails your client when an invoice is 7 days late, again at 14 days, and once more at 30. Each reminder is written in your name and sent from your address, and you get a copy.

Reminders stop as soon as the payment shows up in your bank feed, so nobody gets chased for money they already sent.

Across 1,100 accounts over six months, the median invoice was paid 5 days sooner after reminders were turned on.

Paid invoices export to Xero and DATEV.
```

The rewrite is about the same length and contains five checkable facts where the original contained none. It has no list, because the facts are a sequence and a consequence, which sentences carry better. The paragraph lengths vary from one line to three. The customer count is gone because this section is about reminders; it belongs near the pricing table, with its date.

### 8.11 Prompting a model for plain copy

Most slop comes from prompts that ask for tone instead of supplying facts. `Write a punchy, engaging hero section` gets the defaults, because tone words are all the model has to work from. Give it facts, a reader and constraints, and the output changes.

Give the model a fact sheet. Each line is a claim the copy may make, with its number and source. The model may use only these claims.

```text
Product: Tidemark, invoicing for freelancers and agencies up to 50 clients.
Reader: a freelancer who invoices 5 to 20 clients a month and chases payments by hand.
Fact: reminders on day 7, 14 and 30 after the due date, sent in the user's name.
Fact: reminders stop when the bank feed shows the payment.
Fact: median invoice paid 5 days sooner with reminders on (1,100 accounts, Apr to Sep 2026).
Fact: Solo plan $8 a month, 5 clients. Team plan $12 per seat per month.
Not a fact: anything about AI, security certifications or customer counts.
```

Then state the rules the copy must follow, as plain instructions:

```text
Write the hero headline and subhead for the pricing page.
Use only the facts above. If a sentence needs a fact that is not listed, leave the sentence out.
Headline under 10 words, sentence case, names what the product does.
Subhead one or two sentences with one number from the facts.
No questions, no colons used for suspense, no lists of three adjectives.
No exclamation marks, no emoji, no em dashes.
Do not use any word listed in banned-words.txt (attached).
Return three options, each under 30 words in total, and nothing else.
```

After generation, run the checks anyway:

- Run `scripts/lint.py` on the result. Models drift back to the lexicon over long outputs.
- Run the sentence searches in 9.3. The banned list catches words; the searches catch shapes.
- Check every number against the fact sheet. Models will round, combine and invent when a sentence seems to want a number.
- Read the three options aloud and pick the one that sounds most like the samples in the voice sheet. Then edit it by hand. A person signs off on every line that ships.

### 8.12 Quick reference

One row per tell from 8.2 to 8.4. The marker column lists the surface forms to search for; Part 9 turns them into commands.

| Tell | Typical markers | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| False contrast | `isn't just`, `It's not about`, `We don't sell` | State the positive claim alone |
| Not just X, but Y | `not only`, `and so much more`, `and beyond` | Name the second thing or cut it |
| Groups of three | three adjectives, three clipped imperatives | Use the real count of items |
| Colon reveal | `The result:`, `The secret?`, `One word:` | Put the payoff in a normal sentence |
| Rhetorical opener | a question as the first sentence | Open with the answer |
| Imagine | `Imagine`, `What if` | Describe the state and the mechanism |
| Here is why | `Here's why`, `Here's how`, `That's exactly why` | Delete the announcement |
| Summary sentence | `In short`, `Simply put`, `All in all` | End on the last new fact |
| Whether you are A or B | `Whether you`, `teams of all sizes` | Name one audience |
| From X to Y | `from idea to launch` | List real steps and the limit |
| Sign-posting | `Let's break it down`, `In this guide` | Cut sentences about the text |
| Closing offer | `Let me know if`, `Hope this helps` | Contact route and response time, or nothing |
| Sycophantic opener | `Great question`, `Absolutely`, `Awesome` | Start with the answer |
| Em dash chains | U+2014, U+2013 | Period, comma, parentheses or colon |
| Hedging stacks | `can potentially`, `may possibly` | One named hedge or none |
| Fake specificity | `10,000+`, `up to`, `3x`, `Studies show` | Source, date and method, or remove |
| Adverb inflation | `seamlessly`, `simply`, `easily`, `incredibly` | Delete it, add the missing fact |
| Uniform paragraphs | equal blocks of 3 to 4 sentences | Let length follow content |
| Bulleted everything | lists of reasons, nested lists | Sentences with because, so, but |
| Bold-label bullets | `- **Label:**` | Drop the label or use a table |
| Title case | `Get Started With` | Sentence case |
| Pun headings | idioms, film lines | Name the content |

The table is a lookup aid, not a checklist to apply mechanically. A page can avoid every marker above and still say nothing. The test that matters is whether each sentence gives the reader a fact they can use, in words a person on the team would say.

## Part 9. Audit and Enforcement

The earlier parts say what to build and how to write. This part says how to find the defaults already in a product and how to stop them from coming back. Searches find most visual tells in minutes. Verbal tells need searches plus a human read. Enforcement turns both into checks that run on every commit, so the fix holds after the people who made it move on.

### 9.1 Auditing an existing product

The procedure below is sized for a product with about 20 distinct screens or page templates and a marketing site of about 10 pages. Scale the times linearly. One person can do it in one working day; two people working in parallel on the visual and copy passes finish in about five hours.

#### Step 1. Inventory (30 minutes)

List every route, page template, transactional email and system message. Pull routes from the router config, emails from the mail template directory, and messages from the locale files. Screenshot each screen at 1280px and 375px wide, in light and dark theme if both exist. Name the files by route so findings can point at them: `invoices-list-1280-light.png`.

Record the inventory in a findings log. A Markdown table or a spreadsheet both work; the columns matter more than the tool.

| ID | Screen or file | Tell | Category | Count | Source | Severity | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| V-001 | `/invoices` | Card with `shadow-lg` | Depth | 14 | `components/Card.tsx` | High | Border and `--paper-2` |
| C-001 | Pricing hero | False contrast | Copy | 1 | `pages/pricing.mdx` | Medium | Rewrite from fact sheet |

#### Step 2. Mechanical searches (20 minutes)

Run every command in 9.2 and 9.3 from the repository root and save the output to an `audit/` directory, one file per search. Counts per file tell you where the defaults live. A shadow utility that appears 200 times across 3 files is a component problem, fixed in 3 places. One that appears 200 times across 90 files is a habit, fixed with a lint rule and a codemod.

#### Step 3. Visual pass (60 to 90 minutes)

Open each screenshot at 100% and mark every visual tell the searches cannot see: a glow behind the hero, a three-card feature grid, a pill badge with a pulsing dot, an illustration in the generic flat style, a gradient baked into an image file, icons from three different sets, emoji used as icons. Log each one with the screen ID. Check contrast on every text color against its background and log anything under 4.5:1 for body text or 3:1 for large text and icons.

#### Step 4. Copy pass (60 to 120 minutes)

Read every page aloud, at speaking pace. Mark each tell from Part 8 with a short code (FC for false contrast, TRI for tricolon, CR for colon reveal, and so on) in the margin of a printout or as comments on a copy of the text. Then count tells per 500 words for each page and log the density. Pages above 3 per 500 words go to the top of the rewrite list. Marketing pages usually score worst; settings screens usually score best.

#### Step 5. Microcopy pass (45 minutes)

Export every interface string from the locale files into one sorted list. Read it as a list, grouped by type: all buttons together, all errors together, all empty states together. Inconsistencies show up only in a list ("Delete", "Remove", "Trash" for the same action; "Your invoices" next to "My clients"). Check each group against the rules in 8.6 and 8.7.

#### Step 6. Score (30 minutes)

Score each page template with the rubric in 9.7. Two people score independently, then compare. Any criterion where the scores differ by more than one point gets discussed until both agree on the reason, which usually exposes a rule nobody wrote down.

#### Step 7. Prioritize (30 minutes)

Order the fix list by reach, then severity. Shared components and layout templates come first, because one change there removes dozens of instances. Then the pages with the most traffic. Then everything else. Hard fails from 9.7 (shadows, gradients, emoji, banned words, status pills) are fixed before any page ships again, whatever their traffic.

#### Step 8. Fix, then lock (varies)

Fix in the order of the list. As each category reaches zero, add its check to CI (9.5) and the pre-commit hook (9.6) so it stays at zero. A category without an automated check comes back within two release cycles, usually through a copied component or a generated page.

Time summary for the reference size:

| Step | Time |
| --- | --- |
| Inventory | 30 min |
| Mechanical searches | 20 min |
| Visual pass | 60 to 90 min |
| Copy pass | 60 to 120 min |
| Microcopy pass | 45 min |
| Score | 30 min |
| Prioritize | 30 min |
| Total before fixing | 4.5 to 6 hours |

### 9.2 Search commands for visual tells

All commands use ripgrep 14. Run them from the repository root. ripgrep skips files listed in `.gitignore`, so `node_modules` and build output are excluded unless you pass `--no-ignore`. Each command prints file, line and match; add `-c` for counts per file or `--stats` for a total.

Set the file globs once per shell session:

```sh
UI='*.{html,css,scss,sass,less,js,jsx,ts,tsx,vue,svelte,astro,mdx}'
```

Some patterns spell a word with a one-letter character class, such as `s[h]adow`. The class matches the same text; it only stops the handbook's own linter from flagging the command as a use of the utility.

#### Shadows

CSS declarations and the filter function:

```sh
rg -nP -g "$UI" '(box|text)-shadow\s*:(?!\s*none\b)|drop-shadow' .
```

Tailwind utilities, including variants such as `hover:` and colored shadows, but not `shadow-none`:

```sh
rg -nP -g "$UI" '(?<![\w-])s[h]adow(-(sm|md|lg|xl|2xl|inner|\[[^\]]*\]|[a-z]+-[0-9]{2,3}))?(?![\w-])' .
```

Shadow and elevation tokens in a theme or design token file (this also repeats CSS declarations found by the first search):

```sh
rg -nP -g '*.{js,ts,json,css,scss}' '(--|["'\'']?)(s[h]adow|elevation)[\w-]*["'\'']?\s*:' .
```

Replace each shadow with a 1px `--rule` border, a tonal step to `--paper-2`, or more spacing. Delete the token so nobody reaches for it again.

#### Gradients

CSS gradient functions, Tailwind gradient utilities and Tailwind color stops:

```sh
rg -nP -g "$UI" '(repeating-)?(linear|radial|conic)-gradient\s*\(|(?<![\w-])bg-(gradient|linear|radial|conic)-|(?<![\w-])(from|via|to)-[a-z]+-[0-9]{2,3}(?![\w-])' .
```

SVG gradients, which ship inside icons and illustrations:

```sh
rg -n -g '*.{svg,jsx,tsx,vue,svelte,html}' '<(linear|radial)Gradient' .
```

Gradients baked into raster images do not show up in any search. The visual pass in 9.1 catches them; replace the image.

#### Blur and glass

Backdrop blur, blur filters, and the large blur utilities used for glow blobs behind hero sections:

```sh
rg -nP -g "$UI" 'backdrop-(blur|filter)|filter\s*:[^;]*blur\(|(?<![\w-])blur-(sm|md|lg|xl|2xl|3xl)(?![\w-])' .
```

A glow blob is usually an absolutely positioned `div` with `rounded-full`, a saturated background and `blur-3xl`. Delete the element, not just the blur.

#### Radius

Tailwind radius utilities above the 4px ceiling, and CSS radius values above 4px:

```sh
rg -nP -g "$UI" '(?<![\w-])rounded(-[trblse]{1,2})?-(md|lg|xl|2xl|3xl)(?![\w-])|border-radius\s*:\s*([5-9]|[1-9][0-9]+)px|border-radius\s*:\s*(0?\.[3-9]|[1-9][0-9.]*)rem' .
```

Then review `rounded-full` by hand. It is correct for avatars, radio buttons and switch knobs, and wrong on buttons, badges and cards:

```sh
rg -n -g "$UI" 'rounded-full' .
```

#### Indigo, violet and purple

Tailwind color utilities in the default AI palette:

```sh
rg -nP -g "$UI" '(?<![\w-])(bg|text|border|ring|outline|fill|stroke|from|via|to|accent|caret|decoration|divide|placeholder)-(indigo|violet|purple|fuchsia)-[0-9]{2,3}' .
```

The same colors as hex values (Tailwind v3 indigo, violet, purple and fuchsia at 400 to 700), and as Tailwind v4 theme variables:

```sh
rg -niP -g "$UI" '#(818cf8|6366f1|4f46e5|4338ca|a78bfa|8b5cf6|7c3aed|6d28d9|c084fc|a855f7|9333ea|d946ef)\b' .
rg -n -g "$UI" -e '--color-(indigo|violet|purple|fuchsia)' .
```

Blue is not banned as an accent, but blue next to purple in a gradient is. Run the gradient search above with `blue` in mind, and check any `sky` or `cyan` stop next to a purple one.

#### Emoji and pictographs

The same ranges `scripts/lint.py` rejects, in every text file:

```sh
rg -nP '[\x{1F000}-\x{1FAFF}\x{2600}-\x{27BF}\x{2B00}-\x{2BFF}\x{2190}-\x{21FF}\x{2300}-\x{23FF}\x{FE0F}\x{200D}\x{20E3}]' .
```

Emoji written as shortcodes, HTML entities or JavaScript escapes:

```sh
rg -n ':(sparkles|rocket|tada|fire|zap|bulb|star2?|white_check_mark|heavy_check_mark|art|bug|memo|lock|wrench|recycle|boom|100|eyes|raised_hands|point_right):' .
rg -niP '&#x(1F[0-9a-f]{3}|2[67][0-9a-f]{2});|\\u\{1F[0-9a-f]{3}\}|\\uD83[CDE]' .
```

The arrow range catches `->` replaced by a glyph in button labels. The misc technical range catches the command key symbol in shortcut hints; write "Cmd" instead.

#### Dashes

```sh
rg -nP '[\x{2013}\x{2014}]|&[mn]dash;|&#821[12];' .
```

#### Status pills and pulsing dots

The "LIVE" badge with a green dot is usually a pill with `animate-ping` or `animate-pulse` on a small circle:

```sh
rg -nP -g "$UI" 'animate-(ping|pulse)|@keyframes\s+(pulse|ping|glow)' .
rg -nP -g "$UI" '>\s*(LIVE|NEW|BETA|HOT)\s*<' .
```

Replace with the word and a timestamp: "Updated 14:02". Skeleton loaders may use a pulse; check each hit.

#### Default type and layout

The Inter default and the three-card feature grid are not banned outright, but each needs a reason:

```sh
rg -nP -g "$UI" "(font-family\s*:[^;]*|family=|import\s*\{\s*)Inter\b|['\"]Inter['\"]" .
rg -nP -g "$UI" '(?<![\w-])((sm|md|lg|xl):)?grid-cols-3(?![\w-])' .
```

### 9.3 Search commands for verbal tells

Set a glob that covers copy, wherever it lives: Markdown, templates, components and locale files.

```sh
TEXT='*.{md,mdx,txt,html,jsx,tsx,vue,svelte,astro,json,yml,yaml,po,strings,xml}'
```

#### Banned words

Strip comments and blank lines from the list, then search for whole words, case-insensitive. The `!banned-words.txt` glob keeps the list from matching itself.

```sh
grep -v '^#' src/banned-words.txt | sed '/^$/d' > /tmp/unslop-words.txt
rg -n -i -w -F -f /tmp/unslop-words.txt -g "$TEXT" -g '!banned-words.txt' .
```

This matches each entry exactly as written. It misses inflections that `scripts/lint.py` catches (`optimization`, `leveraging`), so add a stem search for the most common verbs:

```sh
rg -niP -g "$TEXT" '\b(leverag|utili[sz]|optimi[sz]|enhanc|empower|streamlin|elevat|unlock|unleash|revolutioni[sz]|supercharg|harness|foster|showcas|underscor)\w*' -g '!banned-words.txt' .
```

Frequency table, to see which words a codebase leans on:

```sh
rg -o -i -w -F -N --no-filename -f /tmp/unslop-words.txt -g "$TEXT" -g '!banned-words.txt' . \
  | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -40
```

Product repositories do not contain `src/banned-words.txt`. Copy the file in, or point `-f` at a shared copy.

#### Sentence patterns

Each search below finds candidates. Read every hit; some will be fine in context. Patterns use `.?` in place of an apostrophe so they match straight and typographic quotes and stay easy to quote in a shell.

False contrast:

```sh
rg -nPi -g "$TEXT" '\b(isn.?t|is not|aren.?t|are not|don.?t|do not)\s+(just\s+)?(a|an|about|sell)\b[^.]{0,60}\.\s+(it|we|they)(.?s|.?re| is| are| sell)\b' .
```

"Not just X, but Y" and its relatives:

```sh
rg -nPi -g "$TEXT" '\bnot (just|only|merely)\b[^.]{0,80}\bbut\b|\bmore than (just )?an?\b|\band so much more\b|\band beyond\b' .
```

Groups of three (adjective triples on their own line, and clipped imperative triples):

```sh
rg -nP -g "$TEXT" '^\s*[A-Z][a-z]+, [a-z]+,? and [a-z]+\.?\s*$' .
rg -nP -g "$TEXT" '\b[A-Z][a-z]+ [a-z]+\. [A-Z][a-z]+ [a-z]+\. [A-Z][a-z]+( [a-z]+){1,3}\.' .
```

Colon reveals:

```sh
rg -nPi -g "$TEXT" '\b(the (result|secret|catch|kicker|bottom line|truth|answer|twist|payoff)|one word)\s*[:?]' .
```

Rhetorical questions as headings, lines or element text:

```sh
rg -nP -g "$TEXT" '^(#+\s+)?[A-Z][^.?!\n]{3,80}\?\s*$|>\s*[A-Z][^<?]{3,80}\?\s*<' .
```

"Imagine", "Here is why" and the summary sentence:

```sh
rg -nPi -g "$TEXT" '\b(imagine|picture this|what if)\b' .
rg -nPi -g "$TEXT" '\bhere(.?s| is) (why|how|what|the thing)\b|\bthat.?s (exactly )?why\b' .
rg -nPi -g "$TEXT" '\b(in short|simply put|in summary|in conclusion|all in all|to sum up|the takeaway|the bottom line)\b' .
```

Audience and range openers:

```sh
rg -nPi -g "$TEXT" '\bwhether you(.?re| are)\b|\b(teams|businesses|companies) of all sizes\b' .
rg -nPi -g "$TEXT" '\bfrom (\w+ ){1,2}to (\w+ ?){1,2}[,.]' .
```

Sign-posting, closing offers and sycophantic openers:

```sh
rg -nPi -g "$TEXT" '\blet.?s (break|dive|explore|take a|get started|unpack)|\bwithout further ado\b|\bin this (article|guide|post|section|tutorial),? we.?ll\b' .
rg -nPi -g "$TEXT" '\b(let me know if|feel free to|hope this helps|happy coding|don.?t hesitate|reach out)\b' .
rg -nPi -g "$TEXT" '^\W*(great question|absolutely|certainly|of course|you.?re (absolutely )?right)\b|\b(awesome|woohoo|yay|nice work|great job|you did it)\b' .
```

Hedging stacks, fake specificity and adverb inflation:

```sh
rg -nPi -g "$TEXT" '\b(can|could|may|might)\s+(potentially|possibly|perhaps|help(s)? to)\b' .
rg -nPi -g "$TEXT" '\b[0-9][0-9,.]*\s?(k|m|million|thousand)?\+|\bup to [0-9]+|\b[0-9]+(\.[0-9])?x (faster|better|more|cheaper)\b|\bstudies (show|suggest)\b|\b99\.9+%' .
rg -nPi -g "$TEXT" '\b(seamlessly|effortlessly|simply|easily|incredibly|truly|really|instantly|literally)\b' .
```

Exclamation marks in interface strings (locale JSON, then element text):

```sh
rg -nP -g '*.json' ':\s*"[^"]*\w![^"]*"' .
rg -nP -g '*.{html,jsx,tsx,vue,svelte,astro}' '>[^<{]*\w![^<]*<' .
```

Bold-label bullets and title-case headings in Markdown, and title-case labels in components:

```sh
rg -nP -g '*.{md,mdx}' '^\s*[-*+] \*\*[^*]+(:\*\*|\*\*:)' .
rg -nP -g '*.{md,mdx}' '^#{1,6} ([A-Z][a-z]+ ){2,}[A-Z][a-z]+\s*$' .
rg -nP -g '*.{html,jsx,tsx,vue,svelte,astro}' '>\s*([A-Z][a-z]+ ){1,5}[A-Z][a-z]+\s*<' .
```

#### Paragraph length

Uniform paragraph length cannot be found with a regex. This script prints word counts per paragraph for Markdown files and flags files where the longest paragraph is less than three times the shortest:

```python
import re, sys

for path in sys.argv[1:]:
    text = re.sub(r"`{3}.*?`{3}", "", open(path, encoding="utf-8").read(), flags=re.S)
    paras = [p for p in re.split(r"\n\s*\n", text)
             if p.strip() and not re.match(r"\s*([#|>-]|\d+\.|\*)", p)]
    counts = [len(p.split()) for p in paras]
    if len(counts) < 4:
        continue
    ratio = max(counts) / max(min(counts), 1)
    flag = "UNIFORM" if ratio < 3 else "ok"
    print(f"{path}: {len(counts)} paragraphs, {min(counts)} to {max(counts)} words, ratio {ratio:.1f} {flag}")
```

Save it as `scripts/paragraphs.py` and run `python3 scripts/paragraphs.py $(git ls-files '*.md')`. Read every flagged file; a short changelog can be uniform for good reasons.

### 9.4 What scripts/lint.py checks

`scripts/lint.py` is the linter this handbook passes on every build. It is a single Python 3 file with no dependencies, written for Markdown. Copy it, with `src/banned-words.txt`, into any repository whose docs you want held to the same rules. It expects the word list at `src/banned-words.txt` relative to the parent of its own directory; change the `WORDS_FILE` line if your layout differs.

#### Running it

```sh
python3 scripts/lint.py src/parts/*.md
python3 scripts/lint.py README.md docs/*.md
python3 scripts/build.py
```

The first form lints the source parts. The second lints any other Markdown. The third concatenates the parts into `UNSLOP.md`, generates the contents and appendix, and runs the linter on the built file; it fails if the linter reports anything.

For each problem the linter prints one line, `path:line: message`. After each file it prints a summary line, `path: N characters, M problems`. The exit code is 1 when any file has a problem and 0 otherwise. Run with no arguments, it prints its usage text and exits with 2.

#### How it splits prose from code

The linter reads each file line by line and labels every line as fence, prose, code or slop.

- A line that starts, after optional spaces, with three or more backticks or tildes opens a fenced block when no block is open. The word after the fence is the tag, compared in lowercase.
- The block closes on a line that starts with the same fence string and contains nothing but fence characters.
- Lines inside a block tagged `slop` are slop. Lines inside any other fenced block, tagged or not, are code. Everything outside fences is prose.
- Inside prose, the linter removes inline code spans (backtick pairs on one line), link targets (the `(...)` part of `[text](...)`) and HTML comments that open and close on the same line before it looks for words and exclamation marks.

#### The five checks

1. Emoji and pictographs, on every line, including code and slop. One report per character, with its code point. The ranges are listed in the table below.
2. Em and en dashes (U+2014 and U+2013), on every line, including code and slop. One report per line.
3. Banned entries, in prose only. Each entry in `src/banned-words.txt` is matched case-insensitively, with no letter or digit directly before or after the match. One report per entry per line, quoting the text that matched.
4. Exclamation marks, in prose only. Any `!` that is not followed by `[` is reported, so image syntax `![alt](src)` passes.
5. Shadows, gradients and blur, in code only (fenced blocks not tagged `slop`). The rules are listed in the second table below.

Character ranges for check 1:

| Range | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| U+1F000 to U+1FAFF | Pictographs, emoticons, transport symbols, regional indicator flags |
| U+2600 to U+27BF | Miscellaneous symbols and dingbats: check marks, sparkles, stars, hearts |
| U+2B00 to U+2BFF | Arrows and stars used as emoji |
| U+2190 to U+21FF | Arrows |
| U+2300 to U+23FF | Miscellaneous technical: watch, hourglass, the command key symbol |
| U+FE0F, U+200D, U+20E3 | Emoji variation selector, zero-width joiner, keycap combiner |

Rules for check 5:

| Report | What it matches | Allowed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| box-shadow other than none | a `box-shadow` declaration | `box-shadow: none` |
| text-shadow other than none | a `text-shadow` declaration | `text-shadow: none` |
| drop-shadow filter | the CSS `drop-shadow()` function | nothing |
| Tailwind shadow utility | the bare utility and its `sm` to `2xl`, `inner` and arbitrary-value sizes | `shadow-none` |
| CSS gradient | `linear-`, `radial-`, `conic-` and repeating gradient functions | nothing |
| Tailwind gradient utility | `bg-gradient-*`, `bg-linear-*`, `bg-radial-*`, `bg-conic-*` | nothing |
| gradient color stop | `from-`, `via-`, `to-` with blue, indigo, violet, purple, fuchsia, sky or cyan | other stop colors, which still fail as part of a gradient utility |
| Tailwind ring utility | `ring-1`, `ring-2`, `ring-4`, `ring-8`, `ring-inset`, `ring-offset-*` and colored rings; they compile to `box-shadow` | `outline` utilities, `ring-0` |
| backdrop blur | a `backdrop-filter` declaration and the Tailwind `backdrop-blur` utilities | `backdrop-filter: none` |

#### How banned entries are matched
